[The suffix] -ghata- is for what purpose? [In the examples: *rattiyaṃ*, *itthiyā*, *dhenuyā*, *vadhuyā*.

Therefore, there is optionally the substitution of *y* for *o*.

120, 243. *Amha* (my) and *mama* (my), when accompanied by a case ending, undergo the substitution of *me* before the case ending *se*.

For every *ntu*-suffix, including its case-ending, the substitute *nto* occurs when the first person plural suffix *ya* follows.
*Guṇavanto tiṭṭhanti* ("The virtuous ones stand").
For what purpose is *ntusseti* used? [To show: "All beings go.

*To*: in *tā*, *sa*, *smiṃ*, and *nāsu*.

*Guṇavato*, *guṇavantassa*, *guṇavati*, *guṇavantasmiṃ*, *guṇavatā*, *guṇavantena*; *satimato*, *satimantassa*, *satimati*, *satimantasmiṃ*, *satimatā*, *satimantena*.

[To exclude cases such as: *guṇavanto tiṭṭhanti*, *satimanto tiṭṭhanti*.

For the word *ima*, including its case endings, when it is in the neuter gender, the substitution of *idaṃ* occurs optionally before the endings *-aṃ* and *-si*.
Do you see this mind? This mind stands. Do you see this mind? This mind stands.
What is the purpose of *nathuṃsaka*? [It is used when one says: "Do you see this person? or "This person stands.

For the entire word *amu*, including its case ending, when it occurs in the neuter gender, there is the substitution of *aduṃ* before the endings beginning with *aṃ*.
"You see that flower; that flower shines.
For what purpose is the term "neuter" (napuṃsake) used? [Example: "You see that king; that king stands there. 131.
The number of feminine, masculine, and neuter.
“Feminine, masculine, and neuter number”—this should be understood as having the sense of a governing heading (adhikāra).

for the two numbers, when they occur in the feminine, masculine, and neuter [genders] along with their case endings, the form *dve* occurs in place of *yo* and *iccete*.
Two women, two things. Two forms.
For what purpose [is] *yosvī*? It means "in two.

By the inclusion of *ca*, there are also *duve*, *dvaya*, *ubha*, *ubhaya*, and *duvi* before these suffixes: *-nā*, *-na*, *-am*, and *-icce* (i.e., *-icc-ehi*). 133, 230. *Ticatuṇṇaṃ*: For the numerals three (*ti*) and four (*catuṇṇaṃ*) when they occur with case endings in the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders, these substitutes—*tisso*, *catasso*, *tayo*, *cattāro*, *tīṇi*, and *cattāri*—occur respectively in place of *yo* and so forth.
Examples: *tisso vedanā*, *catasso disā*; *tayo janā*, *jane*; *cattāro purisā*, *purise*; *tīṇi āyatanāni*, *cattāri ariyasaccāni*.
What is the purpose of *yosvīti*? [It applies] to three or four.
134. 251. *Pañcādīnamakāro*:

For the numbers beginning with five (*pañca*), when they occur in the feminine, masculine, or neuter genders, the vowel *a* replaces the final vowel of the word together with its case-ending (*savibhattissa antassa sarassa*) before the suffixes *yo*, *iccete*, and so forth.
Five, five, six, six, seven, seven, eight, eight, nine, nine, ten, ten.
For what purpose [are] "five and so forth"? [To exclude] two, three.
135, 118. *Rājassa*, *rañño*, *rājino*, *se*.
In place of the entire word *rājasadda* together with its case ending, the substitutes *rañño* and *rājino* occur before that same case ending. [Examples:
*rañño*, *rājino*.
Why is *se* (before that) mentioned? [To show it does not apply] in *raññā*.
136, 119. *Raññaṃ naṃmhi vā*.
In the case of the *naṃ* case-ending, the substitution *raññaṃ* optionally occurs for the entire word *rāja*, including its case-ending. Thus:
*raññaṃ* or *rājūnaṃ idaṃ raṭṭhaṃ* ("this kingdom belongs to the kings").

In the case of the word *rāja* (king) together with its case ending, the substitute *raññā* optionally occurs before the case ending *nāmhi*.
Thus: *raññā kataṃ* or *rājena kataṃ*.
What is the purpose of [the rule] "nāmhīti"?
It is for the sake of [the forms] *rañño* and *raññe*.

When the suffix *smiṃ* occurs, the words *rañño* and *rājini* are the substitutes for the entire word *rāja*, including its case ending. That is, when the case suffix *smiṃ* follows, these two—*rañño* and *rājini*—are the replacements for the word *rāja*.
The virtue of the king and the queen remains.
139, 245. *Tayi* and *mayi*:
for all the words *tumha* (you) and *amha* (we), together with their case endings, these substitutes *tayi* and *mayi* occur respectively when the locative singular (*smiṃ*) case ending follows.
*Tayi*, *mayi*.
For what purpose [is] *sminhi*? "You are," "I am. 140, 232. *Tvaṃ ahaṃ simhi ca*.
For all forms of *tumhe* and *amhe*, including their case endings (*savibhattīnaṃ*), the substitutions *tvaṃ* and *ahaṃ* respectively occur when the nominative singular (*simhi*) case ending follows.
Thus: *tvaṃ*, *ahaṃ*.
For what purpose is "in the nominative singular" (*simhi*) stated? [To show that it does not apply elsewhere: *tayi*, *mayi*.
By the inclusion of the word *ca*, there is also *tuvaṃ*. *Tuvaṃ* is the teacher (*satthā*).

For all the words *tumha* and *amha*, together with their case endings, these substitutes *tava* and *mama* occur respectively before the case ending *se*.
*Tava*, *mama*.

142, 242. [It means] "for you" and "for me."

*Tuyhaṃ, mayhaṃ dhanaṃ dīyate* ("Wealth is given to you, [to] me").
Why is *se* mentioned? [To exclude other cases: *Tayā, mayā*.
143, 235. *Taṃ* and *maṃ*.
For all forms of the pronoun *tumha* accompanied by case endings, *taṃ* and *maṃ* are the respective substitutes when the case ending *amhi* follows.
That is, *taṃ* and *maṃ*.
What is the meaning of *amhīti*? It means "by you" and "by me.
(144, 234) *Tavaṃ* and *mamaṃ* are optional [substitutes].

For all instances of the words *tumha* and *amha*, when accompanied by case endings (*savibhattīnaṃ*), these substitutes *tavaṃ* and *mamaṃ* respectively occur optionally in place of them in the *amhi* case ending.

What is the purpose of [mentioning] "of the consonants"? It is for the sake of [indicating the agent], namely, by death (*maccunā*).
What is the purpose of including the word "cause" (*kāra*)? It is for the purpose of establishing the substitution of *m* for the letter *y*. An illustration: 270, 120.
[The suffixes] *-amha*, *-tumha*, *-ntu*, *-rāja*, *-brahma*, *-tta*, *-sakha*, *-satthu*, *-pitā*, etc., are not [applied] after [words ending in] *-i* or *-u*.
In such expressions as *amha*, *tumhaṃ*, *tuyhaṃ*, *rājā*, *brahmā*, *atta*, *sakha*, *satthu*, *pitū*, and so forth, the term *smā* (the nominative singular ending) is not to be seen.
[The forms are] *mayā*, *tayā*, *guṇavatā*, *raññā*, *brahmunā*, *attanā*, *sakhinā*, *satthārā*, *pitarā*, *mātarā*, *bhātarā*, *dhītarā*, *kattārā*, *vattārā*.
For what purpose [are these examples given]? [To show: *purisā*.
Thus ends the fifth section, the Section on Names (Nāmakappa). 3.
The Section on Agents (Kārakakappa)
The Sixth Section (Chaṭṭhakaṇḍa) 271, 88, 308. That from which one departs, or that from which one takes fear, is the *apādāna*.
Or, that from which one departs, or from which fear arises, or from which one takes [something], that agent receives the designation *apādāna*.

How so? "Sages depart from the village," "The king has gone out from the city," "Fear arises for the thieves," and "The disciple receives the training from the teacher and preceptor. What is the purpose of this mention of the ablative (*apādāna*)?

[It is to indicate that] the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the ablative. (Pāṇini 2.3.28) [And] by connection with a prefix (*upasarga*), the suffixes *mā* and *na* are used in both senses. (Pāṇini 5.4.47)
In the employment of verbal roots (dhātu), as well as in connection with prefixes (upasagga) and so forth, that *kāraka* receives the designation of *apādāna*.
First, regarding the employment of verbal roots: when the root *ji* preceded by *parā* is employed, that which is "unable to endure" (*asaha*) is designated as *apādāna*.
For example: *Buddhasmā parājenti aññatitthiyā* ("The followers of other sects are defeated by the Buddha").
When the verb *papubbassa* (preceded by *pa-*) is used with this root *bhū*, that from which its origin is not severed is designated as the ablative (*apādāna*). How is that so?
"The five great rivers originate from the Himalayas; the great lakes originate from Anavatatta; the small streams originate from the Aciravatī.
Even when used with a noun, that grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is designated as the ablative.
How so? A son born from the breast, a sap emerged from the earth, a son well-born from both—mother and father.
When used in conjunction with a prefix, that *kāraka* receives the designation of *apādāna*.
How so? "Merchants come from the hall," "The sound rises up as far as the Brahma-world, from the mountain above."
The god rains; from the Buddha, Sāriputta addresses the bhikkhus with a Dhamma teaching for three months;
he gives him a vessel full of oil; he gives him a blue lotus from among the lotuses; he gives him gold from among the bullion.

By the inclusion of "etcetera" (ādiggahaṇena), the fifth case ending occurs even in the midst of a compound. From this side the hunter pierces the deer; he pierces the elephant from the temple; he eats food from the month.
By the inclusion of the word *api*, the fifth case ending occurs even in connection with indeclinables (*nipāta*), as do the second and third cases. For example:
*rahita* (devoid of) *mātujā* (mother-born/son), having performed merit, gives a gift—[one says] *rahito mātujā*, *rahito mātujan-taṃ*, or *rahito mātujena*.
*Rite* (without) *saddhammā* (from the True Dharma)—where would one obtain happiness? [One says] *rite saddhammaṃ* or *rite saddhammena*. Those bhikkhus went forth from various families.
Apart from the true Dhamma, no other protector exists in the world—whether expressed as *vinā saddhammā*, *vinā saddhammaṃ*, or *vinā saddhammena*.
[Likewise] apart from the Buddha, *vinā buddhasmā*, *vinā buddhaṃ*, or *vinā buddhena*.
By the inclusion of the particle *ca*, the fifth case ending (*pañcamīvibhatti*) occurs in other instances as well: "Sister, since I was born with the noble birth."
As far back as I remember, since I have attained the age of discretion, there has been no occasion where, while dwelling with the faculty of the eye unrestrained,
covetousness and dejection— evil, unwholesome states— might have invaded me.
This is the point desired for protection.
In the application of elements (*dhātu*) for the purpose of guarding, that which is intended as the agent is designated as the ablative (*apādāna*).
"The rice grains guard against the crows" (*kāke rakkhanti taṇḍulā*); "the barley prevents the cows" (*yavā paṭisedhenti gāvo*).
Or [it is so called] by means of which there is seeing.
Alternatively, that which is intended as the locus of non-seeing is designated as the ablative (*apādāna*) case.
For example: "The pupil disappears from the preceptor" (*upajjhāyā antaradhāyati sisso*); "The son disappears from both mother and father" (*mātarañca pitarañca antaradhāyati putto*).
Why is the word *vā* used? It is for the purpose of including the locative case (*sattamī vibhatti*). For example: "The Blessed One disappears in Jeta’s Grove" (*jetavane antaradhāyati bhagavā*).

275, 312. [The following suffixes occur] after words expressing distance, proximity, measurement of space, measurement of time, elision of the suffix *tvā*, connection with a direction, that which is divided, connection with the particle *āra*, purity, release, the sense of cause, the sense of being secluded, measure, prior connection, the sense of binding, and words expressing qualities; as well as when used in the sense of "a little" (*thoka*).

[In detail: in the sense of distance, in the sense of proximity, in the measurement of space, in the measurement of time, in the elision of the suffix *tvā*, in connection with a direction, in that which is divided, in connection with the particle *āra*, in purity, in release, in the sense of cause, in the sense of being secluded, in measure, in prior connection, in the sense of binding, and in words expressing qualities.
In these senses—namely, questioning, telling, slightness, and the non-agent—as well as in various applications, that *kāraka* receives the designation of *apādāna*. Regarding the sense of distance:
"How far from here is Naḷakāra village? or "having gone from afar," or "those foolish men are far removed from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
[Examples of] the second and third cases: "from afar from the village" (*dūraṃ gāmaṃ āvato*), or "having come by means of the distant village" (*dūrena gāmena vā āgato*).
"Far from this Dhamma and Vinaya," or "by means of this Dhamma and Vinaya," and so forth. Regarding the sense of proximity:
*antikaṃ gāmā* (near the village), *āsannaṃ gāmā* (close to the village), *samīpaṃ gāmā* (in the vicinity of the village), *samīpaṃ saddhammā* (in the vicinity of the True Dhamma).
[In these cases] both the second and third cases are used: *antikaṃ gāmaṃ*, *antikaṃ gāmena vā*; *āsannaṃ gāmaṃ*, *āsannaṃ gāmena vā*.
Regarding proximity: "near the village," or "by means of the nearby village"; "near the True Dhamma," or "by means of the near True Dhamma," and so forth. Regarding the measurement of distance:
"From here, four *yojanas* from Mathurā, there is a city named Saṅkassa, where many people dwell," and so forth. Regarding the measurement of time:
"Monks, ninety-one aeons ago from now, the Blessed One named Vipassī appeared in the world; after the passing of three months from now, he will attain final Nibbāna," and so forth.
In the case of elision (*tvālope*) regarding actions and locations: "He might cross from palace," or "having ascended the palace";
"he might cross from mountain," or "having ascended the mountain"; "he might cross from the back of an elephant," or "having ascended the back of an elephant";
"he might rise from his seat," or "having sat down on the seat"—and so forth.
Regarding the separation from directions: within the space from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence, many classes of beings dwell;
where there was safety, there is now fear. From the east, the south, the west, and the north, fires blaze forth.
[This refers to the passage beginning: "From what they had heard of the Blessed One: 'From the soles of the feet upward, and from the hair of the head downward,' and so forth."

*Vibhatte* (in the sense of being distinguished): because there is nothing more excellent or more sublime [than it]. For example: "Of the ninety-six sects, this is the most excellent teaching, namely, the Discipline of the Well-Gone One" (*Sugata-vinaya*), and so forth.
*Ārappayoge* (in connection with abstention): "Abstaining from, refraining from, desisting from village-dharma, outcaste-dharma, and unrighteousness;

the avoidance of taking life," and so forth. *Suddhe* (in the sense of purity): "Pure and unadulterated by qualities that lead to greed; pure on the mother’s side and the father’s side, unadulterated, untainted, and irreproachable," and so forth.
In the sense of release: “I am fully freed from suffering,” so I say; “I am released from the bonds of Māra”; “They are not released from death”—and so forth.
In the sense of cause: “For what reason? “By what cause? “For what cause? “Why indeed do your children not die?
“Why will death occur right here?”—and so forth. In the sense of seclusion: “Secluded from evil states”; “Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states”—and so forth.

In the sense of measure (*pamāṇe*): "It should be made nine *vidatthi*s in length according to the measure of the Sugata’s *vidatthi*; for a man of medium height, twelve and a half cubits," and so forth. In the sense of prior connection (*pubbayoge*):
"Even before, there was a greeting," and so forth. In the sense of binding (*bandhanatthe*):
"A man bound by a hundred. And with the third case: "A man bound by a hundred by the king on account of a debt," and so forth.

In the case of words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*): "Through merit they go to a happy destination; through generosity, abundant wealth; through wisdom, a mind liberated; through sovereignty, the king protects his people," and so forth.

In the case of questions (*pañha*), with elision (*tālopa*), and in the cases of the object (*kamma*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*): "They question from the Abhidhamma," "having heard the Abhidhamma," or "standing in the Abhidhamma.
"They question from the Vinaya," "having heard the Vinaya," or "standing in the Vinaya. And [the same applies to] the second and third cases.
Abhidhamma, or by means of Abhidhamma; Vinaya, or by means of Vinaya. Likewise: Suttas, Geyyas, Gāthās, Veyyākaraṇas, Udānas, Itivuttakas, Jātakas, Abbhutadhammas, Vedallas, and so forth.
Regarding the act of speaking, in the case of the accusative and locative cases—*abhidhammā kathayanti*, *abhidhammaṃ sutvā*, *abhidhamme*.
Or "having stood. They speak by means of the Vinaya, having heard the Vinaya, or having stood in the Vinaya. And the second and the third [cases] are:
by means of the Abhidhamma, or through the Abhidhamma; by means of the Vinaya, or through the Vinaya. Likewise:
the Suttas, Geyyas, Gāthās, Veyyākaraṇas, Udānas, Itivuttakas, Jātakas, Abbhutadhammas, Vedallas, and so forth.

*Thoka*: "They are released little by little" (*thokā muccanti*). They are released slightly, they are released with difficulty. And the third [case]. Such as "by a little," "by a slight amount," or "with difficulty," and so forth.
*Akattarica*: "And even when not the agent. For example: "Because of the performance, the accumulation, the intensification, and the expansion of karma, eye-consciousness arises," and so forth.

By the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), those remaining applications of the ablative (*apādāna*) which have not been taught by me should be applied appropriately by those skilled in grammatical usage.
276, 302. That person for whom one wishes to give, or who approves [of the gift], or who maintains [the object], is the recipient (*sampadāna*).
Alternatively, whether it be the one for whom one wishes to give, the one who approves, or the one who maintains, that *kāraka* (participant in the action) receives the designation of recipient.
For example: "He gives a robe to the ascetic"; "The truth pleases the ascetic"; "Yajñadatta maintains the golden parasol for Devadatta."
What is the purpose of using the term *sampadāna* (recipient)? [The rule] "the fourth case (*catutthī*) is used for the recipient" applies.

The word *vā* ("or") is employed for the sake of providing an alternative; it serves to provide an alternative meaning when there is the employment of a verbal root or a noun, or the employment of a prefix (*upasagga*), or the employment of a particle (*nipāta*).
277, 303. *Silāgha*, *hanu*, *ṭhā*, *sapa*, *dhāra*, *piha*, *kudha*, *duhi*, *ssosūya*, *rādhi*, *kkha*, *paccāsuṇa*.

The dative case is used after verbs meaning "to follow" (*anupatati*), after verbs expressing the sense of "informing" (*kattārocana*) such as *pubba*, *tad-attha*, *tuma-ttha*, *ālama-ttha*, and *maññāna*; after verbs having the sense of "going" (*gatyattha*) when followed by an object;
after verbs having the sense of "wishing" (*āsīsattha*); after words denoting social convention (*sammuti*);

and in the sense of the locative (*sattamyattha*). It is also used in connection with the roots *silāgha*, *hanu*, *ṭhā*, *sap*, *dhāra*, *piha*, *kudha*, *duha*, *issa*, and others, as well as after verbs having the sense of "envy" (*usūyattha*).

The agent (kāraka) is designated as the recipient (sampadāna) when used with the verb *payujjati*, with verbs meaning "to please" (*rādhi-kkhappayoga*), with those that follow the word "having promised" (*paccāsuṇānupatiggaṇhana*) as the prior agent,

in the sense of "informing" (*ārocanattha*), in the sense of "for that purpose" (*tadattha*), in the sense of the infinitive suffix *-tu* (*tum-attha*), in the sense of "enough" (*alam-attha*), with verbs meaning "to think" (*maññati*) used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*) provided no sentient being is involved,

with roots having the sense of "going" (*gatyattha*) in the sense of the object (*kamman*), in the sense of "wishing" (*āsīsattha*), and frequently in the sense of the locative case (*sammuti bhiyya sattamy-atthesu*).

First, regarding the application of *silāgha* (to praise): "He praises the Buddha," "He praises the Dhamma," "He praises the Saṅgha," "He praises his own preceptor," "He praises you," "He praises me"—and so forth.
Regarding the application of *hana* (to strike): "He strikes you alone," "He strikes me alone"—and so forth.

Regarding the application of *ṭhā* (to stand/serve): "A carpenter might attend upon the sons of the Sakyans; a bhikkhunī might attend upon a bhikkhu while he is eating with water or a fan"—and so forth.
In connection with *sapati* (to envy): “Your envy, my envy,” and so forth.
In connection with *dhāreti* (to wear/bear): “He wears gold for you,” and so forth.

In connection with *pihayati* (to envy/long for): “The followers of other sects envy the Buddha; the gods long to see them; ‘I long for the venerable one’; the poor envy those who have attained success,” and so forth.
In the application of the roots *kudh*, *duh*, and *usū*: "The god is making Devadatta angry; O Great Hero, be angry with him, lest this kingdom perish!
The cloud oppresses the quarters; the heretics envy the ascetics out of greed for virtue;
the heretics envy the ascetics out of greed for gain; the wicked envy those possessed of virtue out of greed for virtue."
"What envy for those who understand? and so forth.

In the employment of these roots, *radh* and *ikṣ*, that unexpressed factor which is the object of inquiry and intended to clarify the action receives the designation *sampadāna* (recipient), and the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is also used. Examples:

*ārādhohaṃ rañño* ("I have pleased the king"), *ārādhohaṃ rājānaṃ* ("I have pleased the king"); *kyāhaṃ ayyānaṃ aparajjhāmi* ("How am I offending the masters?"), *kyāhaṃ ayye aparajjhāmi* ("How am I offending the masters?").
"The eye is for the seeing of people; I think it is like that," [said] Upatisso, who was desirous of the full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the Venerable Elder Upāli;
or "the Venerable one," and so forth.

When used in connection with *paccāsuṇāti* (to promise), the agent of the prior action is designated as the recipient (*sampadāna*). That is to say, when *suṇoti* is used in conjunction with *paccā*, whatever was the prior agent of that action, that becomes the recipient designation.
How is that? The Blessed One said this to the bhikkhus.
"Bhikkhus" refers to an unspoken action; "this" refers to a spoken action.
He who was the agent of the prior action is designated as "the Blessed One" by the scriptural statement, "He who acts is the agent. Thus, regarding whichever action...
That which is the agent of a preceding action is designated as the *sampadāna* (recipient).
How so? "Those monks responded to the Blessed One" (*te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ*), [or] "the monks listen to the Buddha" (*āsuṇanti buddhassa bhikkhū*).
In connection with the verb *anupatati* ("to follow"), that which is the agent of a preceding action is designated as the *sampadāna*.
How so? A monk proclaims the Dhamma to people; those people follow that monk, those people accept that monk.
He who speaks is called the "agent";
what is spoken of is called "action."
"One who receives [the gift]—
know that as the 'recipient' (sampadāna).
And so forth.

In the sense of announcing: “I announce to you, monks; I address you, monks; I inform you, monks; I announce to you, Great King; I address you, Great King; I inform you, Great King”—and so forth. In the sense of that [purpose]:
“That robe-cloth must be deposited for the sake of completing what is deficient; for the sake of the Buddha, for the sake of the Dhamma, for the sake of the Saṅgha, I renounce my life”—and so forth.

"Out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans, a Buddha arises in the world. The Vinaya was laid down for the comfortable dwelling of the bhikkhus," and so forth.

Regarding the application of *alam* in the sense of "sufficiency": *alam* is used in the sense of "worthy of" (*arahati*) among those [meanings] that are excluded [from the primary senses]. Examples include:

*alam me buddho* (the Buddha is enough for me), *alam me rajjam* (sovereignty is enough for me), *alam bhikkhu pattassa* (the bowl is sufficient for the bhikkhu), *alam malle mallassa* (one wrestler is a match for another wrestler). In the sense of "worthy of," it is said: *malle mallassa arahati*. When used in the sense of "prohibition" (*paṭikkhitte*), it is said: *alam te*.
"Form is to be done; enough for me with gold and bullion," and so forth.

In the construction with *maññati* (to think), when expressing disregard (*anādara*) toward something inanimate (*appāṇika*), [the particle *tuvaṃ* is used]: *tuvaṃ maññe kaliṅgaraṃ* ("I think you are a mere block of wood").
Why "when expressing disregard"? [Observe: *suvaṇṇaṃ viya taṃ maññe* ("I think you are like gold").
For what purpose is the term *appaṇinī* used? It is used in such expressions as "you think [it] a donkey," and so forth.

Regarding the object of a verb meaning "to go": *gāmassa pādena gato* (he went by foot to the village), *nagarassa pādena gato* (he went by foot to the city), *appo saggāya gacchati* (the person goes to heaven), or *saggassa gamanena* (by means of going to heaven), *saṅgho mūlāya paṭikasseyya* (the Saṅgha should expel [him] from the root). And in the second case: *gāmaṃ pādena gato*, *nagaraṃ*.
"He has gone on foot; few go to heaven, or by going to heaven," "The Saṅgha should overturn the root," and so forth.
In the sense of wishing: "May the Venerable One be long-lived; may it be well with you; may it be wholesome for you; may there be freedom from illness for you;
may there be happiness for you; may there be a welcome for you; may there be prosperity for you; may there be welfare..."
"May it be so for you," and so forth.

Regarding the usage of *sammuti* (consent/agreement): except for the consent of the Saṅgha, it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to speak of his own consent; as in: "It would be well if I had the consent to see that Blessed One," and so forth.
Regarding the usage of *bhiyyo* (more/further): as in "to a greater degree," and so forth.
In the sense of the locative (*sattamyatthe*): “I reveal this to you,” “Sakka appeared to me”—in such passages as these.
By the inclusion of the word "sense" (*attha*), it is seen in many applications of syllables.
For example: “I shall make a simile; I shall teach you the Dhamma.”
And regarding the essential meaning: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus. It will be for their comfort and well-being.
We shall send word to him so that the Blessed One might explain it to us, and we too shall explain it to them. The accumulation of wealth is permissible for recluses.
We have need for jewels; what use have I for a Buddha? My own welfare is better; they are very helpful to me."
"Venerable sir, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī was very helpful to the Blessed One"; "Monks, parents are of great assistance to their children"—such are the examples.
Regarding the other applications of words (*akkharappayoga*), other usages should also be formulated by those skilled in the application of words.

The inclusion of the particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing in the mention of the word *vā* (or), which serves the sense of an alternative. The particle *vā* is employed here for the purpose of including any words that involve the dative case (*sampadānappayogika*) which have not been taught by me.
For example: "The Blessed One is the master of the community of monks; this king is the master of the country;

this householder is the master of the field; this hunter is the master of the forest," and so forth. In some instances, the second, third, fifth, sixth, and seventh cases are also used in the sense of "master."
178, 320. *Ādhāro tamokāsaṃ*.
That which is a support (*ādhāra*) is designated as "space" (*okāsa*). That support is fourfold: pervasive (*byāpika*), adhesive (*opasilesika*), inherent (*vesayika*), and proximate (*sāmīpika*).
Among these, first, the pervasive [support]: milk stays in water, oil in sesame seeds, and juice in sugarcane.
The locative of proximity (*opasilesika*): "The king lies on a couch; the Saṅgha is seated on a chair.
The locative of pervasion (*vesayika*): "People walk upon the grounds; the wind blows in the sky; birds fly through the air. The locative of vicinity (*sāmīpika*):
"Elephants roam in the forest; there is a sound at the Ganges; they milk the cows in the pen; he dwells at Jetavana in Sāvatthī."
What is the purpose of designating "location" (okāsa)? [It is for the sake of] the locative case (sattamī) in the sense of location.
279, 292. Or, that by which something is performed is the instrument (karaṇa).
Whatever performs an action, whatever sees, or whatever hears—that agent is designated as the instrument (karaṇa-saññā).
With the hand one reaps grain; with an axe one hews wood; with a hatchet one cuts a tree; with a spade one digs the earth; with a knife one performs work. With the eye one sees form.
What is the purpose of the term *karaṇa* (instrument)? The third case ending is used for the instrument (*karaṇe tatiyā*).
That which one performs is the object (*kamma*).
Whatever one does, whatever one sees, or whatever one hears—that becomes the agent and the perception of the action (*kamma-saññā*).
One makes an umbrella, one makes a chariot, one sees a form, one hears a sound, one tramples a thorn, one swallows poison.
What is the purpose of the term "action" (*kamma*) here? It is for the sake of the grammatical case [ending] in the sense of an object (*kammatthe dutiyā*).
281, 294. He who acts is the agent (*kattā*).
That which acts receives the designation "agent.
A man bitten by a snake; an elephant killed by a *garuḷa*. Māra was conquered by the Buddha; Māra was bound by Upagupta.
What is the purpose of the term *kattuiccanena*? It is for the sake of [the designation] *kattari*.
282, 295. He who causes another to act is the cause (*hetu*).
He who causes the agent (*kattā*) to act receives the designation *hetu*, and he is also the agent.

Thus, one person causes that person to perform the work; that person causes the other person to perform the work; that person causes his own work to be performed by him. In this way, it is applied to *hāreti*, *pāṭheti*, *pāceti*, *dhāreti*.
What is the purpose of the suffix *hetu*? The suffixes *ṇe*, *ṇaya*, *ṇāpe*, and *ṇāpayā* are caused forms (*kārita*) added to verbal roots (*dhātu*) in the sense of causation (*hetvatthe*).
283, 316. Or, he whose possession [it is] is the owner (*sāmī*).
Or, that which is one's possession is the perception of "mine.
This is the monk’s share, this is the monk’s bowl, this is the monk’s robe, [and] his own mouth.
What is the purpose of the term "mine"? It is the genitive case in the sense of "mine."
284, 283. The Nominative Case in the Sense of Gender. The first case ending occurs merely to express the sense of gender.
Examples: *puriso* (a man), *purisā* (men); *eko* (one), *dve* (two); *ca*, *vā*, *he*, *ahe*, *re*, *are*.
285. 70. And in addressing (*ālapana*). The nominative case ending occurs in the sense of addressing, when there is an excess [of one], and when expressing merely the gender and number. For example:
*bho purisa* (O man), *bhavanto purisā* (O men); *bho rāja* (O king), *bhavanto rājāno* (O kings); *he sakhe* (O friend), *he sakhino* (O friends).
286, 291. The third case ending is used for the instrument. The third case suffix occurs in the sense of the instrumental case.
He burns the hut with fire; with a mind that is corrupted, or with a mind that is serene, one performs an action by means of the body.
287, 299. And in the sense of association with "saha" (together with). The third case ending occurs in the sense of association with "saha. For example:
"The Saṅgha may perform the Uposatha together with the Gagga," or "even without the Gagga," or "together with a great community of bhikkhus," or "measured as equal to a thousand."
288, 293. And in the sense of the instrument (kattari).
And in the sense of the instrument, the third case ending occurs.
A man killed by a king; a boon granted by a yakṣa; a man bitten by a snake.
289, 297. And in the sense of cause.
The third case ending occurs also in the sense of cause (*hetvattha*). For example:
*annena vasati* (he dwells because of food), *dhammena vasati* (he dwells because of the Dhamma), *vijjāya vasati* (he dwells because of knowledge), *sakkārena vasati* (he dwells because of honor).
290, 298. And in the sense of the locative case.
The third case ending occurs also in the sense of the locative case.
For example: *tena kālena*, *tena samayena* (or *yena kālena*, *yena samayena*); *tena kho pana samayena*.

291, 299. *Yenaṅgavikāro* (By which there is a modification of the whole through a member). When a modification of the whole (*aṅgin*) is characterized by a diseased member (*aṅga*), the third case ending occurs therein. Examples:

"blind in the eye" (*akkhinā kāṇo*), "crippled in the hand" (*hatthena kuṇī*), "he sees with a blind eye" (*kāṇaṃ passati nettena*), "lame in the foot" (*pādena khañjo*), "hunchbacked in the back" (*piṭṭhiyā khujjo*).
292, 300. And in the sense of specification (*visesana*).
The third case ending occurs also in the sense of specification:
"The Lord is Gotama by clan; he is handsome because of his gold; he is supreme because of his asceticism."
293, 301. The fourth case is used for the recipient (sampadāna). The fourth case ending occurs when there is a recipient kāraka. For example:
"He gives a gift to the Buddha, or to the Dhamma, or to the Saṅgha"; or "he is a donor to a recluse or to a brahmin."
294, 305. Also in cases such as *namo-yoga*.
The fourth case ending also occurs in cases such as *namo-yoga*.
Examples: *Namo te buddha vīratthu*, *sotthi pajānaṃ*, *namo karohi nāgassa*, *svāgataṃ te mahārāja*.
295, 307. The fifth case ending is used for the ablative (*apādāna*). The fifth case suffix occurs when the ablative factor (*kāraka*) is expressed:
"One should restrain the mind from evil, like the moon released from clouds; that person is liberated from fear."
296, 314. The suffix *ḍha* is used in the sense of cause (*kāraṇatthe*).
Furthermore, the fifth case ending occurs in the sense of cause.
Due to non-comprehension, due to non-penetration, and due to not seeing the Four Noble Truths as they really are.
297. 284. The second case ending occurs in the sense of the object (*kamma*). The second case ending occurs in the sense of the object. For example:

*gāvaṃ hanati* (he kills a cow), *vīhayo lunāti* (he reaps rice), *satthaṃ karoti* (he makes a knife), *ghaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a pot), *rathaṃ karoti* (he makes a chariot), *dhammaṃ suṇāti* (he listens to the Dhamma), *buddhaṃ pūjeti* (he worships the Buddha), *vācaṃ bhāsati* (he speaks words), *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* (he cooks rice), *coraṃ ghāteti* (he causes the thief to be killed).

298. 287. *Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge*. When there is absolute connection with time (*kāla*) or distance (*addhāna*), the second case ending occurs. Examples: "He eats meat and rice for a month" (*māsaṃ maṃsodanaṃ bhuñjati*);

"The river is beautiful throughout autumn" (*saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī*); "He studies for a month" (*māsaṃ sajjhāyati*); "A row of forest trees [extends] for a league" (*yojanaṃ vanarāji*); "A mountain is long for a league" (*yojanaṃ dīgho pabbato*); "He studies for a *kosa*" (*kosaṃ sajjhāyati*).
For what purpose is the term *accantasamyoga* (absolute connection) used? [Example: *saṃvacchare bhojanaṃ bhuñjati* ("he eats a meal every year").
299, 288. Regarding construction with a verb of motion (*kammappavacanīya*).
When there is construction with a verb of motion, the second case ending occurs.
Furthermore, such a glorious report has arisen concerning that venerable Gotama:
"They went forth following his going forth. (300, 286) *Gati-buddhi-bhuja-paṭha-hara-kara-sayādīnaṃ kārite vā*.
When there is a causative suffix (*kārita*) after verbs such as *gati*, *buddhi*, *bhuja*, *paṭha*, *hara*, *kara*, and *saya*, the second case ending optionally occurs.

A man causes a man (or a village) to go; a man [causes] by means of a man; a man [causes] for a man. Likewise: he awakens, he feeds, he causes to read, he causes to take away, he causes to do, he causes to lie down. Thus it is in all instances regarding the causative suffix (*kārita*).
301, 215. Regarding the possessive: the sixth case ending occurs in the sense of possession. The sixth case ending is used in the sense of possession.
The share of that monk, the bowl of that monk, the robe of that monk, and one’s own face.
302, 319. The locative case: the seventh grammatical case occurs when expressing location or the agent of an action.
The mind delights in what is deep, at the water’s edge, and in evil; yet a clansman leads the holy life under the Blessed One.
(303, 321) *Sāmī*, *issara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, *sakkhīpatibhū*, and *pasutakusalehi*: with these terms, the sixth case ending occurs, as well as the seventh.
*Master*, *lord*, *ruler*, *heir*, *witness*, and *one who has been instructed in skill*: with these usages, the sixth case ending is used, and also the seventh.
Master of oxen, master in oxen; lord of oxen, lord in oxen. Overlord of oxen, overlord in oxen.
Heir of oxen, heir in oxen. Witness of oxen, witness in oxen; surety for oxen, surety in oxen.
Devoted to oxen, devoted in oxen. Skilled in oxen, skilled in oxen.
304, 322. And in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
In the sense of selection, the sixth case ending occurs, as does the seventh.

"Among cows, the black one has the most excellent milk" (*kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā*); "among cows, the black one has the most excellent milk" (*kaṇhā gāvīsu sampannakhīratamā*). "Among women, the dark-complexioned one is the most beautiful" (*sāmā nārīnaṃ dassanīyatamā*).
Among women, Sāmā is the most beautiful; among men, the Kshatriya is the most courageous; among men, the Kshatriya is the most courageous;
among travelers, the one running is the swiftest; among travelers, the one running is the swiftest.
And [it applies] to disrespect.
In expressions of disregard, the sixth case ending occurs, as well as the seventh.
He went forth while the child was crying; he went forth while the child was crying.
(306, 289) In some instances, the second case occurs in the sense of the sixth.
In certain instances where the sense of the sixth case (genitive) occurs, the second case (accusative) ending is used.
Furthermore, Aggivessana, three similes occurred to me.
[The same applies] for the third and seventh cases as well.
In the sense of the third and seventh cases, the second case ending occurs in some instances.
"If the ascetic Gotama addresses me, and you do not speak to me"—this is in the sense of the third case.
"Having dressed in the morning time," "at one time the Blessed One"—these are in the sense of the seventh case.
308, 317. And the sixth [case]. In the sense of the third and seventh cases, the sixth case-ending (chaṭṭhī vibhatti) occurs in some instances.
"A good deed was done by me" (kato me kalyāṇo), "an evil deed was done by me" (kataṃ me pāpaṃ). Thus it is in the sense of the third case.
“Skilled in dance and song are these four women, and you are skilled in the parts and components of a chariot”—thus it is used in the sense of the locative (*sattamī*).
Why [is the particle] *kvaci* used? “Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya which have been taught and laid down by me for you—Ānanda is discerning regarding their meanings.
(309, 318) And [the suffixes] of the second and fifth cases [are also used].
In certain instances, the sixth case ending occurs in the sense of the second and fifth cases. For example:
*tassa bhavanti vattāro* (there are speakers concerning him), *sahasā kammassa kattāro* (those who perform an action impulsively)—thus in the sense of the second case.
*Assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti* (through not hearing the Dhamma, they decline); *kinnu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi* (why indeed should I fear that pleasure?); *sabbe tasanti* (all tremble).
All fear punishment; all fear death; one who fears the four venomous snakes of terrible poison fears the serpent of terrible poison.
Thus [is used] in the sense of the ablative.
310, 324. The locative case is used in the senses of object, instrument, and cause.
The seventh case ending occurs in the senses of the object (*kamma*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the sign (*nimitta*).
"Friends, these Ājīvakas salute the bhikkhus"—thus in the sense of the object.
"They wander for alms with their hands," "they wander for alms with their bowls," "they go on the paths"—thus in the sense of the instrument.
The leopard is killed for its skins; the elephant is killed for its tusks—thus it is in the sense of a characteristic mark (nimitta). 311, 325.
And in the sense of the recipient (sampadāna), the seventh case ending occurs. And in the sense of the recipient, the seventh case ending is used.
"What is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit; O Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha! When you have given it to the Saṅgha, I too shall be honored.
(312, 326). And in the sense of the ablative case:
the seventh case ending also occurs in the sense of the fifth case.
They protect the elephants in the plantain groves (kadalīsu).
Also, in the case of time and state (kālabhāvesu):
when the agent is employed, the seventh case ending occurs in the sense of time and state.

He went at the time of forenoon and returned at the time of evening. He went while the monks were being fed and returned when they had finished eating. He went while the cows were being milked and returned when they had been milked.
314, 328. Regarding the use of the locative case in expressions of superiority and sovereignty:
when these terms—*upa*, *adhi*, etc.—are employed in expressions denoting superiority or sovereignty, the seventh case ending occurs.
A *doṇa* is a measure for a *khāri*; a *kahāpaṇa* is a measure for a *nikkha*. The Pañcālas are superior to Brahmadatta; Gotamī is superior in dancing; the Buddha is superior among the gods.

(315, 329) **[Sūtra 315:]** *Maṇḍitu-ussukesu tatiyā.* In the sense of "adorned with" (*maṇḍita*) and "eager for" (*ussuka*), the third case ending occurs, as well as the seventh. **[Sūtra 329:]** *Maṇḍita-ussukka-iccetesvatthesu tatiyāvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca.* In these meanings—namely, "adorned with" and "eager for"—the third case ending occurs, and also the seventh.
One who has confidence through knowledge, or one who has confidence in knowledge; one who strives for knowledge, or one who strives in knowledge—the Tathāgata or one of the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Thus ends the sixth section, the Section on the Designation of Names, concerning the Section on the Doer.
The Section on the Doer is finished.
4. Samāsakappa, Seventh Chapter, Sections 316 and 331:
A compound (*samāsa*) of nouns is that which possesses a combined meaning (*yuttattha*).
The connected meaning (*yuttattha*) of those names when their constituent word-meanings are employed is designated as a compound (*samāsa*). Examples:

*kathinadussaṃ* (kaṭhina-cloth), *āgantukabhattaṃ* (food for guests), *jīvitindriyaṃ* (life-faculty), *samaṇabrāhmaṇā* (ascetics and brahmins), *sāriputtamoggallānā* (Sāriputta and Moggallāna), *brāhmaṇagahapatikā* (brahmins and householders).
For what purpose is the phrase "of names" (*nāmānaṃ*) used? [To exclude cases such as: Devadatta cooks; Yaññadatta cooks.
What is the purpose of the term *yuttattha*? [It is to indicate: "The king’s son was supported by Devadatta.

What is the purpose of selecting the compound (*samāsa*)? In some cases, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for those words ending in a case-suffix that have entered into a compound (Pāṇini 5.4.68–74).
317, 332. For these, the case-suffixes are elided.
For those compounds whose meanings are properly joined, case endings and elisions occur. For example:
*kathinadussaṃ* (a kathina-cloth) and *āgantukabhattaṃ* (food for guests).

By the inclusion of the word "those" (*tesaṃ*), there are elisions of case endings, suffixes, words, syllables, and augmentations in compounds, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), and participles (*kitaka*). For example: *vāsiṭṭho* (a descendant of Vasiṣṭha) and *venateyyo* (a descendant of Veṇatā).
The inclusion of "ca" (and) is for the purpose of restriction: [the names] Pabhaṅkara, Amata-ddada, Medhaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara.
Regarding the base form of that which ends in a vowel:
when case endings have been elided, the original forms of that gender ending in a vowel become the base forms.
*cakkhusotaṃ* (eye-ear), *mukhanāsikaṃ* (mouth-nose), *rājaputto* (king’s son), *rājapuriso* (king’s man).
319, 330. A compound preceded by a prefix (*upasagga*) or an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*) is called an indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva*).
A compound preceded by a prefix or an indeclinable particle receives the designation of an indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva*).

That which occurs in the vicinity of a city is "near the city" (*upanagara*); the absence of distress is "free from distress" (*niddaratha*); the absence of mosquitoes is "free from mosquitoes" (*nimmakasa*);
the sequence according to seniority is "according to age" (*yathāvuḍḍha*), or "those who are seniors, according to their seniority" (*ye ye vuḍḍhā vā yathāvuḍḍhaṃ*);
the extent of the limit of life is "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajīvaṃ*); those phenomena that proceed with the mind as their basis are "pertaining to the mind" (*adhicitta*).

"Beyond the mountain" means from one side of a mountain to the other; "against the current" means a boat moving upstream against the flow of a stream; "inside the palace" means within the interior of a palace.

What is the purpose of the term *abyayībhāva*? [It is for the rule: "The indeclinable compounds (*abyayībhāva*) ending in *m* take the accusative case endings. (Pāṇini 2.4.83). [And: "That [compound] is neuter in gender. (Pāṇini 2.4.19). (Suttas 320, 335).
Thus, the *avyayībhāva* compound should be understood as being exclusively neuter in gender.
"The discourse proceeds with reference to young girls" is *adhikumāri*; "the discourse proceeds in the vicinity of the daughter-in-law" is *upavadhu*;
"the discourse proceeds in the vicinity of the Gaṅgā" is *upagaṅgaṃ*; [and] "the discourse proceeds in the vicinity of the jewel-casket" is...
*Kathā* means "comparison.
321, 349. *Digussekattaṃ*:
A *digu* compound becomes singular and takes the neuter gender.
Three worlds are *tiloka*; three staffs are *tidaṇḍa*; three eyes are *tinayana*; three horns are *tisiṅga*. Four directions are *catuddisa*; five faculties are *pañcindriya*.

(322, 359) Likewise, in a *dvanda* compound, there is unity and neuter gender for such terms as *pāṇi-tūriya* (hand and musical instrument), *yogga-senaṅga* (chariot and army component), *khuddajantuka* (small creatures), *vividhaviruddha* (various enemies), and *visabhāgattha* (incompatible things), and so forth.
Thus, in a *dvanda* compound, there is unity and neuter gender for *pāṇi*, *tūriya*, *yogga*, *senāṅga*, *khuddajantuka*, *vividhaviruddha*, *visabhāgattha*, and similar items.

How so? "Eye and ear" is *cakkhusotaṃ*; "mouth and nose" is *mukhanāsikaṃ*; "skin, flesh, and blood" is *chavimaṃsalohitaṃ*. Thus it is in the sense of parts of the body. "Conch and drum" is *saṅkhapaṇavaṃ*;
"song and instrumental music" is *gītavāditaṃ*; "daddara and ḍiṇḍima drums" is *daddariḍiṇḍimaṃ*. Thus it is in the sense of parts of musical instruments.
"Plowshare and plow-beam" is *phālapācanaṃ*; "yoke and plow" is *yuganaṅgalaṃ*. Thus it is in the sense of parts of a vehicle.

A sword and a shield are "sword-and-shield" (*asicamma*); a bow and a quiver are "bow-and-quiver" (*dhanukalāpa*); an elephant and a horse are "elephant-and-horse" (*hatthiassa*); a chariot and a foot-soldier are "chariot-and-foot-soldier" (*rathapattika*).

Thus it is used in the sense of military divisions. Gnats and mosquitoes are "gnats-and-mosquitoes" (*ḍaṃsamakasa*); ants and termites are "ants-and-termites" (*kunthakipillika*); insects and reptiles are "insects-and-reptiles" (*kīṭasarīsapa*).

Thus it is used in the sense of small creatures. A snake and a mongoose are "snake-and-mongoose" (*ahinakula*); a cat and a mouse are "cat-and-mouse" (*biḷāramūsika*); a crow and an owl are "crow-and-owl" (*kākolūka*). Thus it is used in the sense of various natural enemies.

Virtue and wisdom are "virtue-and-wisdom" (*sīlapaññāṇa*); serenity and insight are "serenity-and-insight" (*samathavipassana*); knowledge and conduct are "knowledge-and-conduct" (*vijjācaraṇa*). Thus, [these are examples] where the meanings are dissimilar (*visabhāga*).
What is the purpose of including "and so forth" (*ādi*)? [It is to include: a female slave and a male slave are "slaves, male and female" (*dāsidāsa*);
a woman and a man are "woman and man" (*itthipuma*); a bowl and a robe are "bowl and robe" (*pattacīvara*); a sunshade and sandals are "sunshade and sandals" (*chattupāhana*); a triad and a tetrad...
The triad and tetrad: *veno ca rathakāro ca* becomes *venarathakāram*; *sākuṇiko ca māgaviko ca* becomes *sākuṇikamāgavikam*;
*dīgho ca majjhimo ca* becomes *dīghamajjhimam*, and so forth. 323, 360.
There is optionally [the elision of the case-ending] for words such as *rukkha*, *tiṇa*, *pasu*, *khana*, *dhanna*, and *janapada*.
In a *dvanda* compound, there is optionally a singular number and a neuter gender for such things as trees, grass, cattle, wealth, grain, and countries.
For example: *assattho ca kapītano ca* becomes *assatthakapītanaṃ* or *assatthakapītanā*;
*usīrañca bīraṇañca* becomes *usīrabīraṇaṃ* or *usīrabīraṇā*; *ajo ca eḷako ca* becomes *ajeḷakaṃ* or *ajeḷakā*; and *hiraññañca*... [and so forth].
Gold and bullion-gold: *hirañña-suvaṇṇaṃ*, or *hirañña-suvaṇṇā*. Rice and barley: *sāli-yavaṃ*, or *sāli-yavā*. Kāsī and Kosala: *kāsī-kosalaṃ*, or *kāsī-kosalā*.
What is the purpose of including the word "and" (*ca*) at the beginning?
Faulty and faultless: *sāvajja-anavajjaṃ*, or *sāvajjā-anavajjā*. Low and sublime: *hīna-paṇītaṃ*. Or *hīna-paṇītā*. Black and white: *kaṇha-sukkaṃ*, or *kaṇha-sukkā*.
324, 339. A *kammadhāraya* compound occurs when two words have the same grammatical case (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).
When two words with the same grammatical case are compounded, that compound receives the technical designation *kammadhāraya*.
For example: "He is both great and a man" becomes *mahāpuriso*; "He is both black and a snake" becomes *kaṇhasappo*; and "It is both blue and... [becomes *nīlañca...*].
"Taṃ uppalañca" means "that blue lotus"; "lohitañca taṃ candanañca" means "red sandalwood"; "brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā ca" means "a brahmin girl";
and "khattiyā ca sā kaññā ca" means "a kshatriya maiden. What is the purpose of this designation as a *kammadhāraya* compound?
It is for the sake of the technical designation (*saññā*) of a *kammadhāraya*.
325, 348. Numeral-Prefix Dvigu.
A *kammadhāraya* compound that has a numeral as its prefix is designated as a *dvigu*.

Examples: three impurities = *timalaṃ*; three fruits = *tiphalaṃ*; three worlds = *tilokaṃ*; three staffs = *tidaṇḍaṃ*; four directions = *catuddisaṃ*; five faculties = *pañcindriyaṃ*; seven Godāvarīs = *sattagodāvaraṃ*.
What is the purpose of the *digui* suffix?
It is for the sake of forming a *digus* compound. 326, 341.
Both are *tappurisa*. Both types of compounds—the *digu* and the *kammadhāraya*—are designated as *tappurisa*.
There is no Brahmin nor non-Brahmin; no outcaste nor non-outcaste; no monk nor non-monk; no one with five-year-old [cattle] nor one without five-year-old [cattle];
no one with five bundles nor one without five bundles; no one with seven Godāvarī [cows] nor one without seven Godāvarī [cows]; no one with ten cows nor one without ten cows;
no one with five cows nor one without five cows.
What is the purpose of the mention of *tappurisa*? [It is for the rule:
"In a *tappurisa*, the word *attaṃ* is elided. (327, 351).
*Amā* and the others [are compounds] with subsequent words. When those beginning with *amā* are compounded with nouns as subsequent words, that compound is designated as a *tappurisa*.

One who has gone to the earth is "earth-gone" (*bhūmigata*); one who is beautiful throughout the entire night is "all-night-beautiful" (*sabbarattisobhaṇa*). One who has gone to a state of loss is "gone-to-loss" (*apāyagata*);

that which is made by a lord is "lord-made" (*issarakata*); pierced by an arrow is "arrow-pierced" (*sallaviddha*); cloth for the Kathina ceremony is "Kathina-cloth" (*kathinadussa*); food for a guest is "guest-food" (*āgantukabhatta*);
free from sexual intercourse is "free-from-sexual-intercourse" (*methunāpeta*); fear of thieves is "thief-fear" (*corabhaya*).
The son of a king is a *rājaputta*; a heap of grain is a *dhaññarāsi*; perception of forms is *rūpasaññā*; suffering in *saṃsāra* is *saṃsāradukkha*.
(328, 352) Regarding the meaning of other words:
when two nouns or many nouns are compounded in the sense of other words, that compound is designated as a *bahubbīhi*.
The ascetics have come to this monastery; it is this monastery to which the ascetics have come. The faculties have been conquered by this ascetic;
he is this ascetic who has conquered his faculties. A tax has been given to that king; he is this king to whom the tax was given.
People have departed from this village; it is this village from which the people have departed. The hand has been cut off from that man; he is this man whose hand has been cut off.
A man whose hand has been cut off is a "cut-hand man. A country in which crops have flourished is a "land of abundant harvests.

One who is well-rounded like a banyan tree is "banyan-rounded"; a prince who is well-rounded like a banyan tree is a "banyan-rounded prince. Alternatively, he is one who is well-rounded like a banyan tree.
The prince whose body is rounded like a banyan tree—that is this prince.
He who has become the eye, become as the eye, who is like one who has become the eye—that Blessed One is "become the eye" (cakkhubhūta).
The color of gold is "golden-colored" (suvaṇṇavaṇṇa); he whose color is like the color of gold—that Blessed One is "golden-colored."
The voice of Brahmā is the "Brahmā-voice"; the Blessed One whose voice is like the voice of Brahmā is "Brahmā-voiced," the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "subsisting on wind, water, and fallen leaves, flowers, and fruits": leaves, flowers, and fruits are "leaves-flowers-fruits";
those that have fallen by themselves are "self-fallen"; and those self-fallen leaves, flowers, and fruits are "self-fallen-leaves-flowers-fruits."

Wind and water are "wind-and-water. Leaves, flowers, and fruits that have fallen of their own accord, as well as wind and water, are "leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water that have fallen of their own accord.

Those for whom leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water that have fallen of their own accord constitute food are "those whose food consists of leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water that have fallen of their own accord"—namely, the seers (*isayo*).
What ought to be said regarding this has already been stated below. This, moreover, is a compound consisting of a *dvanda* within a *kammadhāraya*.

[This is] a *bahubbīhi* compound with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). Alternatively: those whose food consists of leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water that have fallen of their own accord are "those whose food consists of leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water that have fallen of their own accord" (*sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā*).

This, however, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*). [Regarding the phrase] "plateaus scented by flowers fallen from various trees": various kinds of trees are "various trees" (*nānādumā*); [the flowers] fallen from these various trees are...
"Various trees" means those [trees] that have fallen from various trees; "flowers fallen from various trees" refers to those flowers which have fallen from various trees.
"Fragrant with flowers fallen from various trees" means scented by those flowers fallen from various trees.

That king of mountains whose ridges (*sānu*) are fragrant with flowers fallen from various trees is the one called "the king of mountains whose ridges are fragrant with flowers fallen from various trees. This is [the description].
However, it is a *bahubbīhi* compound with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) that contains within it a *kammadhāraya* and a *tappurisa*.
Alternatively: "the slopes are scented" (*vāsitasānu*)—even though there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekkhatta*), the compound is formed because the meaning is clear.

That king of mountains whose slopes are scented by flowers fallen from various trees is "the king of mountains whose slopes are scented by flowers fallen from various trees" (*nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu pabbatarājā*).
This, however, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with a split referent (*bhinna-adhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "its peak kissed by drops from clouds of various shapes": it bears water, thus it is a "water-bearer" (*ambudhara*). Who is that? It is Pajjunna (the rain-god). Various shapes are "variegated shapes" (*byālambo*);
and that which is both variegated in shape and a water-bearer is a "cloud of variegated shapes" (*byālambambudhara*). [Of] that cloud of variegated shapes...
"Byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭa" refers to that king of mountains whose peak (kūṭa) is kissed by drops (bindu) from clouds (ambudhara) that hang down (byālamba). This,
moreover, is a *tulyādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) *bahubbīhi* compound containing within it a *kammadhāraya* and a *tappurisa*.
Alternatively: *cumbita-kūṭa* means "kissed peak. Even though there is a sense of expectancy (*sāpekkhatta*), it forms a compound because it conveys a complete meaning.
That king of mountains whose peaks are kissed by the droplets from the hanging clouds is "the one whose peaks are kissed by the droplets from the hanging clouds" (*byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭa*).
This, however, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*).
"Amitabalaparakkamajuti" means: *amitā* is that which is not measured (*na mitā*); *bala*, *parakkama*, and *juti* are "strength, prowess, and splendor";
he who possesses immeasurable strength, prowess, and splendor is "Amitabalaparakkamajuti. This, moreover, is a *tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi* compound containing within it a *kammadhāraya-dvandva*.
"Pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu" means that the chest (*ura*), the collarbone (*akkha*), the shoulder (*aṃsa*), and the arm (*bāhu*) constitute "chest-shoulder-arm" (*urakkhaṃsabāhu*);

the Blessed One whose chest, shoulders, and arms are full is "one with full chest-shoulder-arms" (*pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu*). This, moreover, is a *dvanda-vagga* (compound of pairs) functioning as a *tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi* (appositional possessive compound).
"Pīṇagaṇḍavadanathanūrujaghana" means the cheek (*gaṇḍa*), the face (*vadana*), the breast (*thana*), the thigh (*ūru*), and the hip (*jaghana*).
One whose cheeks, face, thighs, and hips are full is "one with full cheeks, face, thighs, and hips" (*pīṇagaṇḍavadanathanūrujaghanā*).
This too is a coordinate-compound-inclusive (*dvandagabbha*) appositional determinative compound (*tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi*).
[The mountain] was struck by the mass of rocks kissed by the crests of the crowns of the gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, serpents, and gandharvas.
The gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, bhujagas, and gandhabbas—these are the "gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, bhujagas, and gandhabbas.
Furthermore, those who are the most excellent among the gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, bhujagas, and gandhabbas are the "excellent gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, bhujagas, and gandhabbas.
The crowns of these excellent gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, bhujagas, and gandhabbas are the "crowns of the excellent gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, bhujagas, and gandhabbas."
The peaks of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas, and gandhabbas are "peaks of the crowns of the most excellent gods,
asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas, and gandhabbas"; those mountains kissed by the peaks of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas,
and gandhabbas are "mountains kissed by the peaks of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas, and gandhabbas."
He is the Tathāgata whose feet are struck by the peaks of the mountains kissed by the crests of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas, and gandhabbas;
he is the one whose feet are thus struck by the peaks of the mountains kissed by the crests of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas, and gandhabbas;

he is the one whose feet are struck by the peaks of the mountains kissed by the crests of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas, and gandhabbas—thus he is "the one whose feet are struck by the peaks of the mountains kissed by the crests of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, bhujangas, and gandhabbas."
"Tathāgata"—this, moreover, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi*), which itself contains within it a *dvanda*, a *kammadhāraya*, and a *tappurisa*.
Alternatively: "the feet are struck" (*saṅghaṭṭitā caraṇā*) is *saṅghaṭṭitacaraṇā*; even though there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekkhatta*), the compound is formed because the meaning is clear.
[The feet] whose soles are kissed by the tips of the crests on the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḷas, humans, serpents, and gandhabbas.

The Tathāgata whose feet are touched by the impact of the mountain peaks kissed by the crests of the crowns of the most excellent gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, nāgas, and gandharvas—this, moreover, is a *bhinnādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi* compound.
"In the four directions" (*catuddiso*) means he to whom there are four directions; that is the Blessed One.
"Pañcacakkhu" means one who has five eyes; such a Tathāgata is "pañcacakkhu.
"Dasabala" means one who possesses ten powers; such a Blessed One is "dasabala.
"Anantañāṇa" means that which has no end is infinite; a Tathāgata whose knowledge is infinite is "anantañāṇa," the Tathāgata.

"Amitaghanasarīro" means: "amita" is that which is not measured (na mitaṃ); "ghanasarīraṃ" is a body that is solid (ghanaṃ eva sarīraṃ); the Tathāgata whose solid body is immeasurable is "Amitaghanasarīro," the Tathāgata.
"Amitabalaparakkamappatto" means: "amitā" is that which is not measured; "balañca parakkamo ca" are strength and prowess; "amitabalaparakkamā" are immeasurable strengths and prowess;
he by whom these immeasurable strengths and prowess have been attained is "Amitabalaparakkamappatto."
The Blessed One. This, moreover, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), containing within it a *kammadhāraya* and a *dvanda*.
The mountain cave is beautified by flowering creeper-trees and *nāga*-trees kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees. "Intoxicated bees" (*mattabhamarā*) means bees that are intoxicated;
"swarms of intoxicated bees" (*mattabhamaragaṇā*) means groups of intoxicated bees; [by] those swarms of intoxicated bees...

"Kissed by intoxicated bees" means kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees; "blooming flowers" means flowers that have indeed blossomed; those which possess blooming flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees are "those with blooming flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees";
"creepers and *nāga*-trees" refers to *mallī* creepers and *nāga*-trees;
and thus they are "the creepers and *nāga*-trees with blooming flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees."
The mountain king whose caves are adorned by *nāga* trees with blossoming creepers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees,
which are themselves beautified by *nāga* trees with blossoming creepers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees,
is this very [mountain] whose blossoming creeper-trees are kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees.

The *vallināgarukkha* (creeper-tree-mountain), the *bhītakandara* (fear-inspiring-cave), and the *pabbatarāja* (king-of-mountains). This, however, is a *tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi* (co-referential possessive compound) containing within it *dvanda*, *kammadhāraya*, and *tappurisa*.
Alternatively: "caves beautified" (*upasobhitakandarāni*)—even though there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekkhatta*), it is understood because it is expressive.

This is a compound. That king of mountains whose caves are adorned by *nāga* trees with flowering creepers being kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees is "the king of mountains whose caves are adorned by *nāga* trees with flowering creepers being kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees.
This, however, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*).

"A cave adorned with various fallen tree-flowers": "trees and grass" is *rukkhatiṇāni*; "various kinds of trees and grass" is *nānārukkhatiṇāni*; "fallen among various trees and grass" is *nānārukkhatiṇapatitāni*;
those flowers which have fallen among various trees and grass are *nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphāni*; [the cave is adorned] by means of these various fallen tree-grass-flowers.

Adorned with various trees, grasses, and fallen flowers; that king of mountains whose caves are adorned with various trees, grasses, and fallen flowers is "the king of mountains adorned with various trees, grasses, and fallen flowers.
This, moreover, is a coordinate determinative (*dvanda-kammadhāraya*) compound within a relative tatpuruṣa, functioning as a common-appositional possessive (*tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi*).
Alternatively: "Upasobhitakandarāni" means "caves that are adorned. (This is a compound despite the presence of expectancy [between the members], because the meaning is clear.
That king of mountains whose caves are adorned by various trees, grasses, and fallen flowers is "nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphopasobhitakandaro," the king of mountains.
This, however, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with different substrata (*bhinna-adhikaraṇa*).
"With various pestles, ploughshares, rocks, trees, logs, arrows, bows, clubs, swords, and javelins in their hands"—
that is, pestles, ploughshares, rocks, trees, logs, arrows, bows, clubs, swords, and javelins;
pestles, ploughshares, rocks, trees, logs, arrows, bows, clubs, swords, and javelins of many different kinds.
Various clubs, plows, rocks, trees, *kaliṅgara* stones, spears, bows, maces, swords, and javelins;

those who have these various clubs, plows, rocks, trees, *kaliṅgara* stones, spears, bows, maces, swords, and javelins in their hands are "those with various clubs, plows, rocks, trees, *kaliṅgara* stones, spears, bows, maces, swords, and javelins in hand.
This, however, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with diverse referents (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), containing within it a *dvanda* and a *kammadhāraya*.
What is the purpose of mentioning *bahubbīhi*? [It is for the rule:
"And in the case of *bahubbīhi*" (329, 357). A collection of nouns is a *dvanda*.
Whatever is a collection of nouns that share the same case-ending is designated as a *dvanda*.
The moon and the sun are "the moon and the sun"; the ascetic and the brahmin are "the ascetic and the brahmin";
Sāriputta and Moggallāna are "Sāriputta and Moggallāna"; the brahmin and the householder are "the brahmin and the householder";
Yama and Varuṇa are "Yama and Varuṇa"; Kuvera and Vāsava are "Kuvera and Vāsava."
What is the purpose of the mention of *dvanda*?
It is for the sake of *dvanda* compounds. 330, 340. *Mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade*:
For those words containing the term *mahant*, the substitution *mahā* occurs when they stand in grammatical apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) with another word.
And because that man is great, he is a "Great Man" (mahāpurisa); and because that queen is great, she is a "Great Queen" (mahādevī);

and because that army is great, it is a "Great Army" (mahābala); and because that elephant is great, it is a "Great Elephant" (mahānāga); and because that glory is great, it is "Great Glory" (mahāyasa);
and because that lotus grove is great, it is a "Great Lotus Grove" (mahāpadumavana); and because that river is great, it is—
A great river (*mahānadī*) and a great gem (*maṇi*) are a "great gem" (*mahāmaṇi*); a great householder (*gahapatika*) is a "great householder" (*mahāgahapatika*);
that which is great wealth (*dhana*) is "great wealth" (*mahādhana*); and that which is great merit (*puñña*) is "great merit" (*mahāpuñña*).

By the inclusion of the plural form, in some instances the word *mahanta* undergoes the substitution *mahā*. That which is great fruit (*phala*) is "great fruit" (*mahapphala*), "great power" (*mahabbala*), likewise "great wealth" (*mahaddhana*), and "great fear" (*mahabbhaya*).

331, 353. When a word denoting a female has been stated as masculine, it should be regarded as masculine even when referring to a female, provided it stands in grammatical apposition with another word denoting a female. For example:
*dīghajaṅgho* (he whose shanks are long), *kalyāṇabhariyo* (one who has a beautiful wife), *pahūtapañño* (one possessed of abundant wisdom).

What is the purpose of the term *bhāsitapuma*? It is [to indicate] that the wife is a "kinsman of a brahmin" (*brāhmaṇabandhu*), and she is also the wife of one who is a "kinsman of a brahmin," thus forming the compound *atibrāhmaṇabandhubhariyā*.
And in the case of a *kammadhāraya* designation:

In a compound designated as a *kammadhāraya*, when there are two words in the feminine gender with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), if the preceding word is one whose masculine form has been stated (*bhāsitapuma-itthī*), then the masculine form alone is to be seen [as the substitute]. Examples: *brāhmaṇadārikā* (brahmin girl), *khattiyakaññā* (noble maiden), *khattiyakumārikā* (noble young woman).
What is the purpose of [the rule] *bhāsitapume*? [Examples: *khattiyabandhudārikā*, *brāhmaṇabandhudārikā*.
333, 344. *Attaṃ nassa tappurise*:
In a *tappurisa* compound, when the word *nassa* is the first member (*pūrvapada*) and another word is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), *atta* is substituted for *nassa*.
He is not a brahmin, not a non-brahmin; not an outcaste, not a monk; [not] five years [old], not five cows.
In a *tappurisa* compound, the substitute *ana* occurs for the word *na* when followed by a vowel.
"Na asso anasso, anissaro, anariyo. (335, 346).
When does *ku* become *kada* before a vowel? It becomes *kada*. "Kadā kussa.
When does *ku* become *kada* when a vowel follows? It becomes *kada*.
*Kucchitaṃ* means contemptible; *annaṃ* is food, thus *kadannaṃ*; *asanaṃ* is eating, thus *kadassanaṃ*.

For what purpose does it remind [us]? Those for whom there are contemptible wives (*kucchitā dārā*)—namely, those who perform unmeritorious deeds—they are *kudārā*, [and] *kujanā*. Likewise, *kuputtā*, *kugehā*, *kuvatthā*, *kudāsā*. 336, 347.
And [the suffix -ka occurs] after words denoting contempt.
What [substitute] occurs for *ku* and *icceta* before words meaning "undesirable"?
[The substitutes are] *kālavaṇaṃ* and *kāpupphaṃ*.
What is the purpose of including the plural number? [It is so that] in some instances, *kā* also occurs for *ku* and *icceta* even before words not meaning "undesirable," as in *kāpurisā*.

337, 350. In some cases, there is an *a* at the end of words that have become the final members of a compound. In certain instances, the vowel at the end of nouns that have reached the status of being the final member of a compound becomes the letter *a*.

Examples include: *devānaṃ rājā* (king of the gods) becomes *devarājā*; *devānaṃ sakhā* (friend of the gods) becomes *devasakhā*; *pañca ahāni* (five days) becomes *pañcāhaṃ*; *sattāhaṃ* (seven days); *pañcagavaṃ* (five cows); *chattupāhanaṃ* (umbrella and sandals); *upasaradaṃ* (approaching); *visālakkho* (large-eyed); *vimukho* (turned away).

What is the purpose of including the suffix -kāra? It is so that [the suffixes] ending in -i and -ī may be included. That which possesses manifest phenomena (paccakkha-dhamma) is called *paccakkhadhammā*;
fragrant scent is *surabhigandhi*; beautiful scent is *sugandhi*; putrid scent is *pūtigandhi*;
loathsome scent is *kugandhi*; that which possesses foul scent is *dugandhi*.
"Pūtigandhi" means a putrid odor;
the suffix *ka* occurs at the end of a compound after words ending in *nadī* (river) and *kattṛ* (agent).
That country in which there are many rivers is "bahunadika"; that person whose agents are many is "bahukattuka."
338, 356. And from *nadī*.
The suffix *ka* occurs at the end of a compound after the word *nadī*.
That in which many rivers flow is *bahunadika*. He for whom many desires flow is *bahukantika*. [Likewise] *bahunārika*.
339, 358. *Jāyāya tudaṃ jāni patimhi*.
When *pati* follows, *jāyā* is replaced by *tudaṃ* and *jāni*.
Thus, *tudaṃpatī* and *jānipatī*.
340, 355. And from *dhanus*.
The suffix *āp* occurs after *dhanus* at the end of a compound.
He whose bow is the *gāṇḍīva* is *gāṇḍīvadhanvā*.
341, 336. *Aṃ* is the [substitute] for case-endings after indeclinable compounds (*abyayībhāva*) ending in *a*.
Therefore, after indeclinable compounds ending in *a*, the form *aṃ* occurs in place of certain subsequent case-endings:
*adhicittaṃ*, *yathāvuḍḍhaṃ*, *upakumbhaṃ*, *yāvajīvaṃ*, *tiropabbataṃ*, *tiropākāraṃ*, *tirokuṭṭaṃ*, *antopāsādaṃ*.
What is the purpose of [the word] *kvaci*? It is for the sake of a monk who is intent on higher consciousness (*adhicitta*).
342, 337. *Saro rassō napuṃsake*:
In the case of a neuter gender, the vowel of a noun that forms part of an indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva-samāsa*) becomes short.
“*Adhikumāri*” means “speech that proceeds with reference to maidens” (*kumārīsu adhikicca pavattati kathā*). Examples include *upavadhu*, *upagaṅgaṃ*, and *upamaṇikaṃ*.
**343, 338.** *Aññasmā lopa ca*:
After an indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva-samāsa*) ending in a vowel other than *a*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the subsequent case endings (*vibhatti*).
*Adhitthi*, *adhikumāri*, *upavadhu*.
Thus ends the seventh section, the Chapter on Compounds, within the Chapter on Names.
The Chapter on Compounds is finished.

[The suffix] -apacca after vāṇa.
The suffix *Ṇa* optionally occurs in the sense of "his offspring" (*tassāpacca*).
The offspring of Vasiṭṭha is *Vāsiṭṭha*; [alternatively], the offspring of Vasiṭṭha is *Vāsiṭṭhī*, or the offspring of Vasiṭṭha is *Vāsiṭṭhaṃ*.
Likewise, *Bhāradvāja*, *Bhāradvājī*, and *Bhāradvājaṃ*. *Gotama*,...
Gotamī, Gotama; Vāsudevī, Vāsudeva, Vāsudeva; Bāladevī, Bāladeva, Bāladeva;
Vesāmittī, Vesāmitta, Vesāmitta. 345, 366.
From *vaccha* and others, the suffixes *ṇāyana* and *ṇāna* [are applied].

The descendant of Vaccha is *Vacchāyano*, *Vacchāno*; or the descendant of Vaccha is *Vacchāyanī*, *Vacchānī*;
the descendant of Vaccha is *Vacchāyanaṃ*, *Vacchānaṃ*. The descendant of Sakaṭa is *Sākaṭāyano*.
*Sākaṭāno*, *sakaṭassa apaccaṃ* (the offspring of Sakaṭa), *sākaṭāyanī*, *sā kaṭānī*, *sākaṭāyanaṃ*, *sākaṭānaṃ*. Likewise:
