*Aggivessāyano*, *aggivessāno*, *aggivessāyanī*, *aggivessānī*, *aggivessāyanaṃ*, *aggivessānaṃ*.
Gacchāyano, gacchāno, gacchāyanī, gacchānī, gacchāyanaṃ, gacchānaṃ. Kappāyano, kappāno, kappāyanī, kappānī, kappāyanaṃ, kappānaṃ.
Moggallāyano, moggallāno, moggallāyanī, moggallānī, moggallāyanaṃ, moggallānaṃ. Muñcāyano, muñcāno, muñcāyanī, muñcānī, muñcāyanaṃ.
*Muñcānaṃ*. *Saṅghāyano*, *saṅghāno*, *saṅghāyanī*, *saṅghānī*, *saṅghāyanaṃ*, *saṅghānaṃ*.
*Lomāyano*, *lomāno*, *lomāyanī*, *lomānī*, *lomāyanaṃ*, *lomānaṃ*. *Sākamāyano*, *sākamāno*, *sākamāyanī*, *sākamānī*, *sākamāyanaṃ*, *sākamānaṃ*.
*Nārāyano*, *nārāno*, *nārāyanī*, *nārānī*, *nārāyanaṃ*, *nārānaṃ*. *Corāyano*, *corāno*.
Corāyaṇī, corānī, corāyanaṃ, corānaṃ; āvasālāyano, āvasālāno, āvasālāyanī, āvasālānī, āvasālāyanaṃ, āvasālānaṃ.
Dvepāyano, dvepāno, dvepāyanī, dvepānī, dvepāyanaṃ, dvepānaṃ.
Kuñcāyano, kuñcāno, kuñcāyanī, kuñcānī, kuñcāyanaṃ, kuñcānaṃ. Kaccāyano, kaccāno.
*Kaccāyanī*, *kaccānī*, *kaccāyanaṃ*, *kaccānaṃ*. 346, 367.
*Ṇeyyo* [is added] after *kattika* and so forth.
After those groups of clans beginning with *kattika*, the suffix *ṇeyya* optionally occurs in the sense of "her offspring" (*tassā apacca*).
*Kattikeyya* means the offspring of *Kattikā*, or [the offspring] of *Kattikā*. In the same way:
*Venateyya*, *Rohiṇeyya*, *Gaṅgeyya*, *Kaddameyya*, *Nādeyya*, *Āleyya*, *Āheyya*, *Kāmeyya*; *Soceyya* means the offspring of *Sucī*; *Sāleyya*, *Bāleyya*, *Māleyya*, *Kāleyya*. 347, 368.
After this, the suffix *-ṇi* is optionally applied.
Therefore, the suffix *ṇi* occurs after a word ending in *a* in the sense of "that person's offspring" (*tassāpacca*).
For example: *dakkhassa apaccaṃ* is *dakkhi*, or "the offspring of Dakkha"; *duṇassa apaccaṃ* is *doṇi*, or "the offspring of Duṇa.
Likewise: *vāsavi*, *sakyaputti*, *nāṭaputti*, *dāsaputti*, *dāsavi*, *vāruṇi*, *gaṇḍi*, *bāladevi*.

From *pāvaki*, *jenadatti*, *buddhi*, *dhammi*, *saṅghi*, *kappi*, and *anuruddhi*, the suffix *ṇika* occurs in the sense of "descendant" (*vāti vikappanatthena*) when the meaning is "his descendant" (*tassāpacca*). For example: the descendant of the son of the Sakyan is a *Sakyaputtika*. Likewise, a *Nāṭaputtika* and a *Jenadattika*.
[Rule 148, 371: The suffix *ṇava* [is applied] after *apakva* and others.
The suffix *ṇava* occurs after words such as *upaku* in the sense of "his descendant" (*tassāpacca*).
For example: *upakussa apaccaṃ* is *opakavo*, or "the descendant of Upaku. *Manuno apaccaṃ* is *mānavo*, or "the descendant of Manu.
*Bhaggussa apaccaṃ* is *bhaggavo*, or "the descendant of Bhaggu. *Paṇḍussa apaccaṃ* is *paṇḍavo*, or "the descendant of Paṇḍu."
*Apaccaṃ* (offspring), *bāhu-apaccaṃ* (many offspring), or *bahussa apaccaṃ* (offspring of many).
349, 372. *Ṇera vidhavādito*.
After that [stem] beginning with *vidhavā*, the suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs in the sense of "her offspring."
The offspring of a widow is a *vedhavero*, or the offspring of a widow. The offspring of a *bandhuki* woman is a *bandhukero*, or the offspring of a *bandhuki* woman.
The offspring of an ascetic (*samaṇa*) is a *sāmaṇero*, or the offspring of an ascetic. Likewise:
*sāmaṇerī*, *sāmaṇeraṃ*; *nāḷikero*, *nāḷikerī*, *nāḷikeraṃ*.
350, 373. The suffix *ṇika* is optionally applied in the sense of "with which one is mixed," "by which one crosses," "by which one moves," or "by which one is carried.
That with which one is mixed, by which one crosses, by which one moves, or by which one is carried—in these senses, the suffix *ṇika* occurs optionally.
For example: *telikaṃ* (oil-mixed) food is that which is mixed with sesame (*tila*), or it is mixed with sesame. Likewise: *goḷikaṃ*, *ghātikaṃ*.
One who crosses by means of a boat is a *nāvika*, or one who crosses by boat. Likewise, a *oḷumpika*.
One who travels by means of a cart is a *sākaṭika*, or one who travels by cart. Likewise, a *pattika*, a *daṇḍika*, a *dhammika*, and a *pādika*.

One who carries on the head is a *sīsika*, or one who carries on the head. One who carries on the shoulder is an *aṃsika*, or one who carries on the shoulder. Likewise, a *khandhika* and an *aṅgulika*.
The suffix *ṇika* also occurs in other senses, in the sense of "belonging to" (*vikappana*).
One who dwells in Rājagaha is called a *rājagahika*, or one who dwells in Rājagaha. One born in Rājagaha is a *rājagahika*, or one born in Rājagaha. In the same way:
*māgadhika*, *sāvatthika*, *kāpilavatthika*, *pāṭaliputtika*, *vesālika*.

351, 374. The suffix *ṇika* optionally occurs in the sense of "he studies that," as well as in the senses of "one who is occupied with that," "appointed to that," "that is his craft," "that is his merchandise," and "that is his livelihood.
In the sense of "he studies that": *vinayam adhīte* → *venayiko*, or *vinayam adhīte*. Likewise: *suttantiko*, *ābhidhammiko*, *veyyākaraṇiko*.
Action performed by the body is bodily (*kāyika*), or it is action performed by the body. Likewise for vocal (*vācasika*) and mental (*mānasika*).
Feeling that resides in the body is bodily (*sārīrika*), or [it is so called] because it resides in the body; likewise for mental feeling.
A gatekeeper is one appointed at the gate, or one who is appointed at the gate. Likewise for a treasurer (*bhaṇḍāgārika*), a citizen (*nāgarika*), and a laborer (*nāvakammika*).

The lute (*vīṇā*) is his craft, or he is one whose craft is the lute: thus, a lute-player (*vīṇāvādaka*). Likewise, a drummer (*pāṇavika*), a player of the *modiṅga* drum (*modiṅgika*), and a flute-player (*vaṃsika*).
Perfume is his merchandise, or he is one whose merchandise is perfume: thus, a perfumer (*gandhika*).

Likewise, an oil-seller (*telika*) and a sugar-candy merchant (*goḷika*). He lives by killing sheep: thus, a butcher of sheep (*orabbhika*), or one who lives by killing sheep. He lives by killing deer: thus, a deer-hunter (*māgavika*), or one who lives by killing deer. Likewise, a pork-butcher (*sokarika*) and a fowler (*sākuṇika*).
By taking "ādi" (beginning) as a reference, the suffix *ṇika* should be applied in other instances as well. One struck with a net is a *jālika*, or one who strikes with a net.
One bound with a cord is a *suttika*, or one who binds with a cord.
One whose weapon is a bow is a *cāpika*, or one whose weapon is a bow. In the same way: *tomarika*, *muggarika*, *mosalika*.
Wind is his affliction: *vātiko*, or "wind is his affliction. Likewise for *semhiko* (phlegmatic) and *pittiko* (bilious).
One who has faith in the Buddha: *buddhiko*, or "one who has faith in the Buddha. Likewise for *dhammiko* (one who has faith in the Dhamma) and *saṅghiko* (one who has faith in the Saṅgha).
That which belongs to the Buddha: *buddhikaṃ*, or "that which belongs to the Buddha. Likewise for *dhammikaṃ* (belonging to the Dhamma) and *saṅghikaṃ* (belonging to the Saṅgha).

An article bought with cloth is "cloth-bought" (*vatthika*), or it is an article bought with cloth. Likewise, there are "pot-bought" (*kumbhika*), "plough-bought" (*phālika*), "grain-bought" (*kiṃkaṇika*), and "gold-bought" (*sovaṇṇika*).
A pot is its measure, thus it is "pot-measured" (*kumbhika*), or it is that which has a pot as its measure.
A heap of pots is "pot-heap" (*kumbhika*), or it is a heap of pots.
One who is worthy of a water-pot (*kumbha*) is a *kumbhika*; or, he is worthy of a water-pot.
One who plays with dice (*akkha*) is an *akkhika*; or, he plays with dice. In the same way: *sālākika*, *tindukika*, *ambaphalika*, *kapiṭṭhaphalika*, *nāḷikerika*, and so forth.
[The suffix] *ṇa* [is added after a word denoting passion] in the sense of "one who has subdued that" and other similar senses.
The suffix *Ṇ* occurs optionally after the word *rāga* in the sense of "dyed by that" (*tena rattaṃ*), as well as in other senses such as "belonging to this" (*tassedaṃ*).
A cloth dyed with *kasāva* is *kāsāva*, or alternatively, a cloth dyed with *kasāva*. Likewise: *kosumbhaṃ*, *hāliddaṃ*, *pāṭaṅgaṃ*, *rattaṅgaṃ*, *mañjiṭṭhaṃ*, *kuṅkumaṃ*.
Meat belonging to a pig is *sokaraṃ*, or alternatively, meat belonging to a pig. Likewise: *māhisaṃ*.
A celestial mansion (vimāna) existing not far from an udumbara tree is "odumbara," or a celestial mansion existing not far from an udumbara tree.
A dwelling (nivāsa) in the vicinity of a corner (vidisā) is "vedisa," or a dwelling in the vicinity of a corner.
One born in Mathurā is "māthura," or one born in Mathurā.
One who has come from Mathurā is called *māthura*, or [the word] "Mathurā" itself when derived from one who has come from Mathurā.

A month connected with the month of Kattikā is called *kattika*, or [the word] "Kattikā" itself when connected with the month. In this same way: *māgasira*, *phussa*, *māgha*, *phagguṇa*, *citta*, *vesākha*, *jeṭṭha*, *āsāḷha*, *sāvaṇa*, *bhadda*, *assayuja*.
There is no lengthening [of the vowel] in words such as *nīla* or *pīta* when they function as suffixes (*paccaya*).
The syllable *pha* is for the word *phussa*;
say *sira* for the head (*sīsa*). A collection of trainings is *sikkha*; a collection of alms is *bhikkha*. Likewise: *kāpota*, *māyūra*, *kokila*.
For the Buddha, his deity is *buddha*. Likewise: *bhadda*, *māra*, *māhinda*, *vessavaṇa*, *yāma*, *soma*, *nārāyaṇa*.
He studies for a year; thus, *saṃvacchara* means "a year. Likewise, *mohutta*, *nemitto*, *aṅgavijjo*, *veyyākaraṇo*, *chando*, *bhāsso*, *cando*.
A region that is the domain for the giving of cattle is *vāsāda*; likewise, *kumbho*, *sākunto*, *ātisāro*.

Because there are *udumbara* trees in this place, it is *odumbaro*. That which is produced from the oceans is *sāgaro*. His dwelling is at *Sāgala*, thus he is *sāgalo*. His dwelling is at Mathurā, thus he is *māthuro*. He is the lord of Mathurā, thus he is *māthuro*. In this manner, such examples are to be applied.
353, 378. *Jātādīnam imiyā ca*: The suffixes *-imiyā* and others occur in the sense of words such as *jāta*.

For example: *pacchājāto* (born later) becomes *pacchimo*; likewise, *antimo*, *majjhimo*, *purimo*, *uparimo*, *heṭṭhimo*, *gopphimo*. One born of the lineage of Bodhisattvas is *bodhisattajātiyo*; similarly, *assajātiyo*, *hatthijātiyo*, *manussajātiyo*.

By the inclusion of the word *ādi* ("beginning with"), these suffixes—*ima*, *iya*, and *ika*—occur after a word that is either connected in meaning with "beginning" (*niyutta-ādī*) or has "beginning" as its own meaning (*tadassa-atthī*).

The word *antima* means "connected with the end" (*anto niyutto*). Likewise, there are *antiya* and *antika*. [The suffix] *ima* occurs: one who has a son, or in whom a son exists, is called *puttimo*. Similarly, there are *puttiya* and *puttika*; likewise, *kappima*, *kappiya*, and *kappika*.

By the inclusion of the particle *ca* ("and"), the suffix *kiya* occurs in the sense of being connected with something. That which is connected with birth is *jātikiya*; that which is connected with the blind is *andhakiya*. One who is blind by birth is *jaccandha*; that which is connected with those who are blind from birth is *jaccandhakiya*.
354, 379. *Kaṇa* and *ṇa* [are used] in the sense of a collection (*samūha*).
The suffixes *kaṇa* and *ṇa* occur in the sense of a collection.
A collection of princes is *rājaputtaka*. Likewise: *rājaputta*, *mānussaka*, *mānussa*, *māyūraka*, *māyūra*, *māhiṃsaka*, *māhiṃsa*.
355, 380. *Gāma*, *jana*, *bandhu*, *sahāya*, etc., [take] the suffix *-tā* (*tāpaccaya*) in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). The collection of villages is *gāmatā*.
Likewise, *janatā*, *bandhutā*, *sahāyatā*, and *nagaratā*.
356, 381. *Tadassa ṭhāniyo ca*.
In the sense of “that is its place,” the suffix *-iya* occurs.

For example: the place of intoxication is *madaniya*; the place of binding is *bandhaniya*; the place of fainting is *mucchaniya*; likewise, *rajaniya*, *kamaniya*, *gamaniya*, *dussaniya*, and *dassaniya*.
357, 382. *Upamatthāyitattaṃ*.
The suffix *āyitatta* occurs after a word used in the sense of a comparison.
That forest which appears like smoke—that is *dhūmāyitatta*; that forest which appears like darkness—that is *timirāyitatta*.
358, 383. *Tannissitatthe* (in the sense of being dependent on that):
the suffix *-la* occurs in the sense of "that is its basis" (*tadassa ṭhānaṃ*).

*Duṭṭhu nissitaṃ* = *duṭṭhullaṃ* (badly dependent); *vedaṃ nissitaṃ* = *vedallaṃ* (dependent on the Veda). *Duṭṭhu ṭhānaṃ* = *duṭṭhullaṃ* (a bad basis); *vedassa ṭhānaṃ* = *vedallaṃ* (the basis of the Veda).
359, 384. *Ālu* when there is an abundance of that.
The suffix *ālū* occurs in the sense of an abundance of that [quality]. For example:
one whose nature is covetousness is *abhijjhālu*; or, one in whom covetousness is abundant is *abhijjhālu*. Likewise: *sītālu*, *dhajālu*, *dayālu*.
360, 387. *Ṇya*, *tta*, *tā* [are used] in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*).
These suffixes—*Ṇya*, *tta*, and *tā*—occur in the meaning of abstract state.
The state of being lazy is *ālasya*; the state of being healthy is *ārogya*. The state of being a wearer of rag-robes is *paṃsukūlikattaṃ*.
The state of one who is not gluttonous is *anodarikatā*. The state of one who delights in company is *saṅgaṇikārāmatā*; the state of one who delights in sleep is *niddārāmatā*.
By the inclusion of the suffix *-t*, the suffix *-tta* occurs: for example, *puthujjanattanaṃ* (the state of being a worldling) and *vedanattanaṃ* (the state of feeling).
[Pāṇini 5.1.121] *Ṇa* occurs after *viṣama*, etc.
The suffix *Ṇ* occurs after words such as *visa* (poison) in the sense of "the state of that" (*tassa bhāvo*).
The state of poison is *vesamaṃ*; the state of purity is *socaṃ*.
362, 389. After *ramaṇīya* and similar words, the suffix *kaṇ* is added.
In this way, from words such as *rāmaṇīya*, the suffix *ka* becomes a condition for the sense of "the state of that" (*tassa bhāvo*).
Thus, the state of being delightful is *rāmaṇīyaka*; the state of being agreeable is *mānuññaka*. 363, 390.
The suffixes *tara*, *tama*, *isi*, *ki*, *yi*, and *ṭṭha* are used in the sense of distinction (*visesa*).
The suffixes *tara*, *tama*, *isi*, and *ka* are used in the sense of distinction (*visesa*).
For example: "All these are evil; this one among them is especially evil" is *pāpatara*. Likewise: *pāpatama*, *pāpisika*, *pāpiya*, *pāpiṭṭha*. [Pāṇini 5.2.36] 364, 398.
[The suffix *matup* is added after a word ending in *tad* (a pronoun), and the final vowel of the base becomes *vī*.]
The suffix *vī* occurs in the sense of "that which has this" (*tadassatthi*).
One who has wisdom (*medhā*) or in whom it exists is "wise" (*medhāvī*). Likewise for "deceitful" (*māyāvī*).
By the inclusion of the particle *ca*, there is also the suffix *so*: one who has excellent wisdom (*sumedhā*) or in whom it exists is "one of excellent wisdom" (*sumedhaso*).
365, 399. *Tapādito si*.
The suffix *si* occurs after words beginning with *tapa*, etc., in the sense of "that which belongs to him" (*tadassatthi*).
One who has austerity (*tapas*) or in whom austerity exists is a *tapassī*. Likewise, *yasassī* (one who has fame) and *tejassī* (one who has splendor).
266, 400. *Ika* and *ī* after *daṇḍa*, etc.
These suffixes, *ika* and *ī*, occur after words such as *daṇḍa* in the sense of "that which belongs to him" (*tadassatthi*).
One who has a staff, or in whom a staff exists, is *daṇḍika* or *daṇḍī*. Likewise, *mālika* and *mālī*.
367, 401. *Madhvādito ro*.
The suffix *ra* occurs after words beginning with *madhu*, etc., in the sense of "that which belongs to it" (*tadassatthi*).
That which has honey, or in which honey exists, is *madhura*. Likewise: *kuñjara*, *muggara*, *mukhara*, *susira*, (*sīsara*, *sukara*, *suṅkara*), *subhara*, *sucira*, *rucira*.
368, 402. *Vantu* from *guṇa*, etc.
The suffix *vantu* occurs after *guṇa* and so forth in the sense of "that which has this" (*tadassatthi*).
One who has virtue (*guṇa*) or in whom virtue exists is "virtuous" (*guṇavā*). Likewise: glorious (*yasavā*), wealthy (*dhanavā*), wise (*paññavā*), powerful (*balavā*), and Blessed (*bhagavā*).
369, 403. The suffix *mantu* is added after words such as *sati*.
The suffix *mantu* occurs after [stems] like *sati* in the sense of "that belongs to him" (*tadassatthi*).
One who has mindfulness (*sati*) or in whom it exists is *satimā*; likewise, *jutimā*, *rucimā*, *thutimā*, *dhitimā*, *matimā*, and *bhāṇumā*.
370, 405. *Saddhādito ṇa*.
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after "saddhā" and other such words in the sense of "that which belongs to him" (*tadassatthi*).
One in whom faith exists is "faithful" (*saddho*); likewise, one who possesses wisdom is "wise" (*pañño*), and one who is not stingy is "generous" (*amaccharo*).
371, 404. Regarding *āyus* with the suffix *-mantu*:
when the suffix *-mantu* follows, the vowel *u* within *āyus* undergoes the substitution *as*.
Because he possesses life (*āyus*), or because it exists in him, he is called *āyasmā*.
372, 385. *Tappakativacane mayo*.
The suffix *maya* occurs in the sense of expressing that which has been made from something.

An object made from gold is *sovaṇṇamayaṃ*. Likewise, there are things made of silver (*rūpiyamayaṃ*), lac (*jatumayaṃ*), silver (*rajatamayaṃ*), brick (*iṭṭhakamayaṃ*), iron (*ayomayaṃ*), clay (*mattikāmayaṃ*), wood (*dārumayaṃ*), and cow-dung (*gomayaṃ*).
373, 406. *Saṅkhyāpūraṇe mo*.
The suffix *ma* occurs in the sense of completing a number.
That which completes five is *pañcamo*; likewise, *sattamo*, *aṭṭhamo*, *navamo*, *dasamo*.
374, 408. *Sa* optionally replaces *cha* when used in the sense of completing a number.
That which completes six is *saṭṭha* or *chaṭṭha*.
375, 412. *Ekādito dasassī*:
The suffix *ī* optionally occurs after the word *dasa* when preceded by *eka* and others, in the sense of completing a number.

*Eko ca dasa ca* = *ekādasa*; that which completes the eleven is *ekādasī*. *Pañca ca dasa ca* = *pañcadasa*; that which completes the fifteen is *pañcadasī*. *Cattāro ca dasa ca* = *catuddasa*; that which completes the fourteen is *cātuddasī*.
What is the purpose of [the term] *pūraṇa*? It is for the sake of eleven and fifteen.
376, 257. *Dase so niccañca*:
when the word *dasa* follows, *cha* always becomes *sa*.
Sixteen.
377. And the nasal *niggahita* at the end:
at the end of their enumeration, there is the addition of the nasal *niggahita*.
*Pañcadasī*, *cātuddasī*. 378, 414. *Ti*:
the suffix *ti* is added at the end of those numerals. *Vīsati*, *tiṃsati*.
379, 258. *La-darānaṃ*.
In the enumeration of the letters *da* and *ra*, there is the substitution of *la*. [Examples: *soḷasa* (sixteen), *cattālīsaṃ* (forty).
380, 255. *Vīsati dasesu bā dvissa tu*. But in the words *vīsati* and *dasa*, the substitution of *ba* for *dvi* occurs.
In these instances, such as *vīsati* and *dasa*, the substitution of *bā* occurs for *dvī*. Thus:
*bāvīsatindriyāni* (twenty-two faculties) and *bārasa manussā* (twelve humans).

By the inclusion of the term *tu*, the substitutions *du*, *di*, and *do* also occur for *dvī*: *durattaṃ* (two nights), *dirattaṃ* (two nights), *diguṇaṃ* (twofold), and *dohaḷinī* (longing for two [milk]).
381, 254. *Ekādito dassa ra saṅkhyāne*.
In enumeration, the letter *da* of the word *dasa* following *eka* and so forth optionally becomes the letter *ra*. Thus:
*ekārasa*, *ekādasa*; *bārasa*, *dvādasa*.
What is the purpose of "in enumeration" (*saṅkhyāne*)? [It is to indicate: "the twelve bases" (*dvādasāyatanāni*).
And from "eight" (*aṭṭha*) onwards, and likewise from "ten" (*dasa*) onwards, there is optionally a substitution of the letter *r* for the letter *d* of the word "ten" in enumeration.
*Aṭṭhārasa*, *aṭṭhadasa*.
For what purpose [is the rule] "beginning with *aṭṭha*"? [To show: *pañcadasa*, *soḷasa*.
For what purpose [is the rule] "in counting" (*saṅkhyāne*)? [To show: *aṭṭhadasiko*.
383, 253. The vowel *ā* may optionally be substituted for *dvi*, *eka*, and *aṭṭha* when forming numerals. Thus:
*dvādasa* (twelve), *ekādasa* (eleven), *aṭṭhārasa* (eighteen).
For what purpose is the term *saṅkhyāna* used? [Examples include: "two-tusked," "one-tusked," "single-roofed," "eight-pillared.
(384, 407) *Catu*, *cha*, *icca*, and *tha*, *ṭha*:
after these [stems], the suffixes *tha* and *ṭha* occur in the sense of completing a number.
The fourth, the sixth.
385, 409. From *dvi* and *ti*, *tiya*.
The suffix *tiya* occurs after *dvi* and *ti* in the sense of completing a number.
The second and third [rules].
386, 410. *Tiye dutāpi ca*.
For these [stems] ending in *dvi* and *tri*, *du* and *ti* respectively are the substitutes when the suffix *tiya* follows.
The second [and] the third.
By the inclusion of "api," the substitution of *du* for *dvi* occurs even in other instances. *Durattaṃ*.
By the inclusion of "ca," the form *di* is substituted for *dvi*. *Dirattaṃ*; having put on a double-layered (*diguṇaṃ*) outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*).
387, 411. *Aḍḍhūpapadena*: *aḍḍhuḍḍha*, *divaḍḍha*, *diyaḍḍha*, *aḍḍhatiya*.

For those [words]—the fourth, second, and third—when preceded by *aḍḍha*, the substitutes *aḍḍhuḍḍha*, *divaḍḍha*, *diyaḍḍha*, and *aḍḍhatiya* occur, arising together with the prefix *aḍḍha*. One who is a fourth part by means of a half is *aḍḍhuḍḍha*;
one who is a second part by means of a half is *divaḍḍha*; one who is a second part by means of a half is *diyaḍḍha*; one who is a third part by means of a half is *aḍḍhatiya*.
388. 68. *Sarūpānamekaseso asakiṃ*.
There is a single remainder (*ekasesa*) of words and phonemes that are identical in form, provided they do not occur more than once. For example: *puriso ca puriso ca* becomes *purisā*.
Why is it said "of those that are identical in form"? [Consider: *hatthī ca asso ca ratho ca pattiko ca* becomes *hatthi-assa-ratha-pattikā*.
What is the purpose of *asakinti*? [It is for the sake of] "a person" (*puriso*).

389, 413. In enumeration, for the numbers two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, and nine, there are the forms *vī*, *catto*, *paññā*, *cha*, *sattāsanavā*, and *yosu*, *yonañcīsamāsaṃ*, *ṭhi*, *ri*, *tī*, *tu*, *ti*.
In enumeration, for the numbers ten, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, and nine, which are identical in form...
For the remaining [numerals], according to their respective order, there are the substitutions *vī*, *cattāri*, *paññā*, *cha*, *satta*, *asa*, and *nava* for *asī* when followed by *yosu*;
and for *yonaṃ*, there are the substitutions *īti*, *uti*, and *āsanaṃ* for *īsaṃ*, *āsaṃ*, and *ṭhi*. Subsequently, they are further resolved [into their constituent parts]. Thus:
*vīsaṃ*, *tiṃsaṃ*, *cattālīsaṃ*, *paññāsaṃ*, *saṭṭhi*, *sattari*, *sattati*, *asīti*, *navuti*.
What is the purpose of *asakinti*? Ten.
What is the purpose of *gaṇanā*? Ten groups of ten men. 390, 256.
There is elision of the prefix in a four-syllable compound, and optionally the initial *cu* of the subsequent word as well.
In the counting of *catu* when it has a following word (*upapada*), there is the elision of the letter *t*; furthermore, the initial *c* of the subsequent word optionally becomes *cu*.
Thus: *cuddasa*, *coddasa*, *catuddasa*.

By the inclusion of the particle *api*, even when there is no following word, the initial *c* of the word is optionally elided; and for that [elided] *c*, *cu* is substituted as well. Thus: *tālīsaṃ*, *cattālīsaṃ*, *cuttālīsaṃ*, *cottālīsaṃ*.
391, 423. Those formations which are established through irregular derivation (*nipātana*) are successful.

These are words whose grammatical characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) have not been explicitly stated, whether by way of phonemes, words, and syllables; feminine, masculine, and neuter gender; noun, prefix, and particle; indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva*), compound, primary derivative (*taddhita*), and verb;

enumeration, number, tense, and the application of case-roles (*kāraka*); or by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), root-form (*pakati*), augmentation (*vuddhi*), elision (*lopa*), insertion (*āgama*), and metathesis (*viparīta*).
And through the analysis of case endings, those [words] are established by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
392, 418. *Dvādito ko’nekattheca*.
After *dvi* and similar words, the suffix *ka* occurs in the sense of plurality and as an irregular derivation; they are established by means of irregular derivation.
Two of a hundred is two hundred; three of a hundred is three hundred; four of a hundred is four hundred;
five of a hundred is five hundred; six of a hundred is six hundred; seven of a hundred is seven hundred;
eight of a hundred is eight hundred; nine of a hundred is nine hundred; ten of a hundred is one thousand.
393, 415. A hundred of ten-tens and a thousand of tens are in the *yo*. For that which is included in calculation, there is a hundred of ten-tens;
for a hundred of tens, there is a thousand in the subsequent *yo*. [The numbers] are a hundred, a thousand.
The terms beginning with "two" and those following it are formed according to their respective order.

Two hundred is *dvisataṃ* (this is what it becomes); likewise, three hundred, four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, seven hundred, eight hundred, nine hundred, ten hundred, which is a thousand (*sahassaṃ*).
394, 416. Up to ten times that and beyond.
One should continue multiplying by ten until the count of those numbers is exhausted. How so?
Having multiplied the number ten by ten, one hundred is produced; having multiplied the number one hundred by ten...
A thousand arises; multiplying the thousand tenfold, there is ten thousand; multiplying the ten thousand tenfold, there is one hundred thousand;
multiplying the hundred thousand tenfold, there is one million; multiplying the million tenfold, there is ten million;
multiplying the ten million by a hundred, there is a hundred million (*pakoṭi*). In this manner, the remaining [units] should also be applied accordingly.
The inclusion of the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of qualification. 395, 417.
By their own names: those enumerations whose designations have not been explicitly stated are formed by means of their respective individual names.
One hundred times one hundred thousand is a *koṭi*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭis* is a *pakoṭi*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is a *koṭipakoṭi*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭipakoṭis* is a *nahuta*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *nahutas* is a *ninnahuta*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *ninnahutas* is an *akkhobhiṇī*. Likewise, a *bindu*, an *abbuda*, and a *nirabbuda*.

363) There is no elision of the *ṇ* in these.

By one division: *ekadhā*. Likewise: *dvidhā*, *tidhā*, *caturdhā*, *pañcadhā*, *chadhā*.

That manner is *tathā*; that manner is *tathā*; by that manner is *tathā*; of that manner is *tathā*; from that [manner] is *tathā*.

In the word *pakāra*, [the suffix] *tathā* is applied; likewise, in *tassa pakārassa*, *tasmiṃ pakāre*, and so on. Similarly: *yathā*, *sabbathā*, *aññathā*, *itarathā*. What is the purpose of including the letter *t*?
It is so that the suffix *thaṃ* may occur there. Thus: *tathatthā*, *evamatthā*, *yathatthā*, *sabbathatthā*, *aññathatthā*, *itarathatthā*.
(399, 422) What is the purpose of these [suffixes ending in] *thaṃ*?
Why is it that the suffix *tham* occurs after these [words] in the sense of expressing a manner?
[Examples: *ko pakāro*—how; *kathaṃ*—how; *kaṃ pakāraṃ*—what manner; *kathaṃ*—how; *kena pakārena*—by what manner; *kathaṃ*—how; *kassa pakārassa*—of what manner;
*kathaṃ*—how; *kasmā pakārā*—from what manner; *kathaṃ*—how; *kassa pakārassa*—of what manner; *kathaṃ*—how; *kasmiṃ pakāre*—in what manner; *kathaṃ*—how; *ayaṃ pakāro*—this manner; *itthaṃ*—thus.

of this manner, in this way; in this manner, in this way. 400, 364.

401, 375. *Māyūnam-āgamo ṭhāne*.

In place of these initial sounds—*m*, *ā*, *u*, *n*, and *m*—there is no vowel-increment (*vuddhi*). However, among those [sounds], *e* and *o* become the increment of vowel-increment in their respective places.

One who studies grammar (*byākaraṇa*) is a *Veyyākaraṇika*; one who studies logic (*nyāya*) is a *Neyyāyika*; the offspring of one who is occupied (*vyāvaccha*) is a *Veyyāvaccha*; one appointed at the gate (*dvāra*) is a *Dovārika*.
In these cases, there is the substitution of *ātta*, and the vowel *i* is inserted in its place.

For example: the state of a seer (*isi*) is *ārisyaṃ*; the state of a debt (*iṇa*) is *āṇyaṃ*; the state of a bull (*usabha*) is *āsabhaṃ*; the state of one who is upright (*ujju*) is *ajjavaṃ*; and so forth—these should be applied accordingly.
What is the purpose of [the term] *yūnam*? It refers to one who has been born in the states of misery (*apāya*).
What is the purpose of [the term] *ṭhāne*? It refers to one who is doubtful, one who is guided, one who is illustrated by comparison, and one who is skillful in means.
403, 354. In certain cases, the long and short vowels of the initial, middle, and final [syllables] occur before suffixes.
In some cases, the first, middle, and last syllables of these words become long, whether they are suffixes or non-suffixes.
First, an example of a long initial syllable: *pākāro*, *nīvāro*, *pāsādo*, *pākaṭo*, *pātimokkho*, *pāṭikaṅkho*, and so forth.
An example of a long medial syllable: *aṅgamāgadhiko*, *orabbhamāgavīko*, and so forth.
First, those with a long final vowel (*uttaradīgho*): *khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā*, *añjanā giri*, *koṭarā vanaṃ*, *aṅgulī*, and so forth.
First, those with a short initial vowel (*ādirasso*): *pageva*, and so forth.
First, those with a medial vowel (*majjherasso*): *sumedhaso suvaṇṇadharehi*, and so forth.

First, regarding the *Uttararassa* [section]: "He is called a *bhovādi*, according to his actual qualities," and so forth. Other [examples] should also be joined in accordance with the words of the Jina.

By the inclusion of the particle *ca*, the sense "and in the case of suffixless forms" (*apaccayesu*) is conjoined. Among those [suffixless forms], there are [instances of] vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), modification (*vikāra*), and reverse substitution (*viparītādesa*).

Among those [syllables] at the beginning, middle, and end, in accordance with the words of the Jina, in some cases there is augmentation, in some cases elision, in some cases an addition, in some cases a modification, in some cases a reversal, and in some cases a substitution.
First, as for augmentation at the beginning: *ābhidhammiko*, *venateyyo*, and so forth.
First, as for augmentation in the middle: *sukhaseyyaṃ*, *sukhakāri dānaṃ*, *sukhakāri sīlaṃ*, and so forth.
First, *uttaravuddhi* (increment of the latter): such as *kāliṅgo*, *māgadhiko*, *paccakkhadhammā*, and so forth.
First, *ādilopa* (elision of the initial): such as *tālīsaṃ*, and so forth.
First, *majjhelopa* (elision of the middle): such as *kattukāmo*, *kumbhakāraputto*, *vedallaṃ*, and so forth.
First, elision in the middle (*uttaralopa*): “a bhikkhu,” “a bhikkhunī,” and so forth.
First, addition at the beginning (*ādiāgama*): “spoken by the Blessed One,” and so forth.
First, addition in the middle (*majjheāgama*): “possessing virtue,” “possessing wisdom,” and so forth.
The *uttarāgama* (subsequent derivation) consists, for instance, of *vedalla* and so forth.
The *ādivikāra* (initial modification) consists, for instance, of *āriśyaṃ*, *āṇyaṃ*, *āsabhaṃ*, and *ajjavaṃ*.
The *majjhevikāra* (middle modification) consists, for instance, of *varāriśyaṃ* and *parāriśyaṃ*.
First, regarding the alteration of the subsequent [words]: "those which... are pleasures," and so forth.
First, regarding the reversal of the beginning: "when the sun has risen, it rises," and so forth.
First, regarding the reversal of the middle: "it rises together; when the sun has risen together," and so forth.
First, the substitution at the end (*uttaraviparīta*): *digu*, *diguṇaṃ*, and so forth.
First, the substitution of the initial (*ādiādeso*): *yūnaṃ*, and so forth.
First, the substitution in the middle (*majjheādeso*): *nyāyogā*, and so forth.

First, the exceptions (*uttarādeso*): "the most excellent," "the most supreme," "mind" (*citta*), and so forth. Thus, they should be applied everywhere in accordance with the words of the Victor (*jina*).
405. **Vṛddhi of *a*, *i*, and *u* vowels:** *A* refers to the vowel *a*;

*i* and *ī* refer to the *i*-vowels; *u* and *ū* refer to the *u*-vowels. For these *a*, *i*, and *u* vowels, there are the *vṛddhi* substitutes *ā*, *ē*, and *ō* respectively—namely, the *vṛddhi* forms *ā*, *ī*, and *ū*.
*Ābhidhammika*, *venateyya*, *oḷumpika*.
Again, for what purpose is the enlargement of the suffix (*vuddhi*)? It is for the sake of expressing the enlargement of the subsequent word:
those who have come from Aṅga and Magadha are *aṅgamāgadhikā*; those born in market towns and districts are *negamajānapadā*; those born in the eastern districts are *porimajānapadā*.
“Attached to seven days” is *sattāhikā*; “attached to the four knowledges” is *cātuvijjikā*. In this manner, [other examples] such as these are to be applied.

What is the purpose of the rule "vuddhi" (vowel lengthening)? [It applies] to a long vowel (*vuddhi*) and so forth, when followed by a single consonant at the end of a word, and before the suffix *-saṇa*.

6. The Section on Verbs (ākhyāta), First Chapter.
(Ka) Today,
I shall churn the ocean of verbal roots, which has the tenses for its waves,
the suffixes and augments for its water, and the time-periods for its fish.
The wise poets cross to the further shore of the analysis of meaning— the method of eliding suffixes— by means of the broad ship of their intelligence.

Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One,
whose range is infinite, I shall explain this vast and complete sound of the word "vicitra," which is encompassed by various conditioned phenomena.
Listen to me as I speak of that which is a good range of conduct.
(Ga) It is used in the sense of a topic, in auspiciousness, in completion, and in restriction.

416, 429. Now, the six preceding forms of the personal endings (*parassapada*) for the case-terminations:
now, whichever six preceding forms there may be for all the case-terminations, those respective ones receive the designation "personal endings" (*parassapada*).
How so? *ti*, *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*.
What is the purpose of this designation "parassapada" (third person)? The third person (*parassapada*) is used for the agent (*kattari*).
407, 439. The others are the first person (*attanopada*).
Whichever are the last six case-endings (vibhatti) of all [the eight cases], they are designated as *attanopada*. For example: *te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, *mhe*.
What is the purpose of designating them as *attanopada*?
[It is for the application of] the rules concerning the *attanopada* endings in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the passive (*kamma*).
408, 431. Two by two, there are the first, middle, and highest persons.
For all those inflections, both in the *parassapada* (active) and the *attanopada* (middle), the two pairs of forms are designated as the first, middle, and highest persons.
How so? *Ti*, *anti* are the first person; *si*, *tha* are the middle person; *mi*, *ma* are the highest person.
*Atta*, *no*, and *padāna* are first-person endings; *se*, *vhe*, and *iti* are second-person endings; *e*, *mhe*, and *iti* are third-person endings. This applies everywhere.

What is the purpose of specifying "first, second, and third person"? Even when a noun is employed, the first person is used for a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), the second person for *tumhe*, and the third person for *amhe*. 409, 441. When all [persons] are expressed by a single word, the subsequent person is used.
In all three cases—first, middle, and last persons—the person following [the subject] is to be understood as "another person" (*paro puriso*).

Thus: *so ca paṭhati, tvañca paṭhasi, tumhe paṭhatha* ("He reads, you read, and you two read"); *so ca pacati, tvañca pacasi, tumhe pacatha* ("He cooks, you cook, and you two cook"). In this same manner, another person is to be joined in the remaining case-endings (*vibhatti*).
Even when a noun (*nāma*) is employed, the nominative case (*paṭhamā*) is used provided there is a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). (410, 432)
Whether the personal pronoun is employed or not employed, the third person is used when there is a common substratum (tulyādhikaraṇa). When it is employed:
*so gacchati* (he goes), *te gacchanti* (they go). When it is not employed: *gacchati*, *gacchanti*.
What is the purpose of the term "tulyādhikaraṇa" (having a common substratum)? In the example, *tena haññase tvaṃ devadattena* ("you are being struck by Devadatta"),
even when the [agentive] pronoun *tumhe* is employed or not employed, the second person (*majjhimapuruṣa*) occurs provided there is a common substratum.
"You go," "you (plural) go.
Even when not being employed [in a sentence]—"you go," "you go.
For what purpose is the condition "having a common substratum" (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) stated? [Example: "Rice is cooked by you."
412, 437. *Uttama* (first person).
Whether used or not used, when the grammatical subject (*adhikaraṇa*) is the same, the first person is employed. For example:
*ahaṃ yajāmi* (I sacrifice), *mayaṃ yajāma* (we sacrifice).
Even when not being applied—such as *yajāmi* (I sacrifice) or *yajāma* (we sacrifice).
For what purpose is the phrase "having a common locus" (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) used? [Example: *mayā ijjate buddho* (the Buddha is accomplished by me). 413, 427.
[The section on] Time (*kāla*).
“Kāle” (in time) should be understood as having the sense of a governing heading. 414, 428.
*Vattamānā* [is used] for the present.
The *vattamānā* case-ending occurs when referring to the present time.
"He goes to Pāṭaliputta; he enters Sāvatthī.
(415, 451) The fifth case ending occurs in the sense of command and in the sense of benediction when there is no subsequent word.
That is, the fifth case ending is used both in the sense of commanding and in the sense of wishing well, provided that it is not followed by another word.
May he perform what is wholesome; may happiness be yours.
(416, 454) The seventh case ending occurs in the sense of consent (*anumati*) and in the sense of supposition (*parikappa*).
In both the sense of consent and the sense of supposition, when not used in conjunction with another word, the seventh case ending is employed.
"You should go; what can I do? 417, 460. *Apaccakkhe parokkhātīte*.
When the past time is not witnessed (*apaccakkhe*), the *parokkhā* verbal suffix occurs.
Regarding this, it is said: thus indeed the ancients have stated.
418, 456. *Hiyyattanī* [is used] for the immediate past.
For the time that has passed beginning from yesterday—whether it be perceptible or imperceptible—the *hiyyattanī* case-ending occurs.
Thus he went on the path; they went on the path.

419, 469. The *ajjatanī* (present) tense occurs when expressing proximity, whether in the past time or in the present—whether the action is witnessed or not witnessed. When there is proximity, the *ajjatanī* case ending is used.
Thus: *maggaṃ agamī* (he went along the path), *te maggaṃ agamuṃ* (they went along the path).
420, 471. Regarding the use of *mā*:
both the aorist (*hiyyattanī*) and the present (*ajjatanī*) case-endings occur in all tenses when there is a connection with *mā*.
*Mā gamā*, *mā vacā*, *mā gamī*, *mā vacī*.
By the inclusion of *ca*, the fifth case ending (*pañcamīvibhatti*) is also included: *mā gacchāhi*. 421, 473.
*Anāgate bhavissantī* (in the future, they will be).
In the future tense, there is the analysis:
"He will go," "he will do"; "they will go," "they will do.
422, 475. In the past conditional, there is the lapse of time.
When the action is past and beyond the present (kriyātipanna), the conditional tense (kālātipatti) occurs.
For example: "If he had obtained that vehicle, he would have gone"; "If they had obtained that vehicle, they would have gone.
423, 426. The present tense endings are: *ti*, *anti*; *si*, *tha*; *mi*, *ma*; *te*, *ante*; *se*, *vhe*; *e*, *mhe*.
The term *vattamānā* (present tense) applies to these twelve suffixes: *ti*, *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, and *mhe*. What is the purpose of the word *vattamānā*?
It indicates that [these endings] belong to the present (*paccuppanne*).
But the fifth [tense, the imperative], consists of: *antu*, *hi*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *taṃ*, *antaṃ*, *ssu*, *vho*, *e*, *āmase*.
The designation *pañcamī* (the fifth case) applies to these twelve verbal suffixes: *tu*, *antu*, *hi*, *tha*, *mima*, *taṃ*, *antaṃ*, *ssu*, *vho*, *e*, *āmase*.
What is the purpose of the term *pañcamī*? It is for the sake of command (*āṇatti*) and exhortation (*āsīṭṭha*); the fifth case is used when there is no [past] tense marker (*nutta*).
425, 453. The seventh case (*sattamī*) consists of: *eyya*, *eyyuṃ*; *eyyāsi*, *eyyātha*; *eyyāmi*, *eyyāma*; *etha*, *eraṃ*; *etho*, *eyyāvho*; *eyyaṃ*, *eyyāmhe*.
The seventh [tense] is this designation for these twelve words: *eyya*, *eyyuṃ*; *eyyāsi*, *eyyātha*; *eyyāmi*, *eyyāma*; *etha*, *eraṃ*; *etho*, *eyyāvho*;
*eyyaṃ*, *eyyāmhe*. What is the purpose of the term "seventh"? It is for the meanings of consent (*anumati*) and possibility (*parikappa*). 426, 459.
The remote past (*parokkhā*) [is characterized by] *au* here, *aṃmha*, *tthare*, *ttho*, *vho*, *iṃ*, *mhe*.
The designation *parokkhā* applies to these twelve verbal endings: *a*, *u*, *ettha*, *aṃ*, *mha*, *ttha*, *re*, *ttho*, *vho*, *iṃ*, *mhe*. What is the purpose of the term *parokkhā*?
It refers to the past tense that is not witnessed by the speaker (*apaccakkhe atīte*).
The designation *hiyyattanī* applies to these [twelve endings]: *ā*, *ū*, *ottha*, *aṃ*, *mhā*, *tthatthuṃ*, *se*, *vhaṃ*, *iṃ*, *mhase*.

The past tense (*hiyyattanī*) consists of these twelve verbal endings: *ā*, *ū*, *o*, *ttha*, *aṃ*, *mhā*, *ttha*, *tthuṃ*, *se*, *vhaṃ*, *iṃ*, and *mhase*. What is the purpose of the term "past tense"?
The past tense refers to what occurred from yesterday onwards when it is within the range of direct perception.
The present tense (*ajjatanī*) consists of these endings: *ī*, *uṃ*, *o*, *ttha*, *iṃ*, *mhā*, *ā*, *ū*, *se*, *vhaṃ*, *aṃ*, and *mhe*.
The *ajjatanī* (present) tense consists of these twelve forms: *iti*, *ī*, *uṃ*, *o*, *ttha*, *iṃmhā*, *ā*, *ū*, *sevhaṃ*, *aṃ*, *mhe*.
What is the purpose of the term "present"? It refers to the immediate present (*samīpejjatanī*).
The *bhavissantī* (future) tense consists of: *ssati*, *ssanti*; *ssasi*, *ssatha*; *ssāmi*, *ssāma*; *ssate*, *ssante*; *ssase*, *ssavhe*; *ssaṃ*, *ssāmhe*.
*Bhavissantī*—this is the designation for these twelve word-forms: *ssati*, *ssanti*, *ssasi*, *ssatha*, *ssāmi*, *ssāma*, *ssate*, *ssante*, *ssase*, *ssavhe*, *ssaṃ*, *ssāmhe*.
What is the purpose of the term *bhavissantī*? It refers to those that will exist in the future.
430, 373. *Kālātipatti* (the past conditional): *ssā*, *ssasu*, *sse*, *ssatha*, *ssaṃ*, *ssāmha*, *ssatha*, *ssiṃsu*, *ssase*, *ssavhe*, *ssiṃ*, *ssāmhase*.

*Kālātipatti* is the technical designation for these twelve verbal endings: *ssā*, *ssaṃsu*, *sse*, *ssatha*, *ssaṃ*, *ssāmhā*, *ssatha*, *ssisu*, *ssase*, *ssavhe*, *ssiṃ*, and *ssāmhase*. What is the purpose of the term *kālātipatti*?
It refers to the past tense when an action has failed to take place (*kriyātipanne*).
[The suffixes] *hiyyattanī*, *sattamī*, *pañcamī*, and *vattamānā* apply to all roots (*sabbadhātukaṃ*).
The four case endings beginning with *hīyatta* (the dative-locative plural) are designated as *sabbadhātuka*. Examples:
*agamā*, *gaccheyya*, *gacchatu*, *gacchati*.
What is the purpose of designating them as *sabbadhātuka*? It is so that the augment *i* may be inserted before those that are not *asabbadhātuka*.
Thus ends the first section in the Ākhyātakappa.
Second Section. 432, 362.
Suffixes follow [roots] according to their verbal roots (dhātu) and genders (liṅga).
The suffixes beginning with *dhātu-liṅga-ic* follow these [roots]. He does;
he goes. Whoever does something, another says to him, "Do! Do!"—or else, one causes him who is doing it to act = *kāreti*.
The Saṅgha behaves like a mountain = *pabbatāyati*.
One treats oneself like a lake [is treated] like the ocean = *samuddāyati*; one treats oneself like the sound *cicciṭa* = *cicciṭāyati*;
the offspring of Vasiṭṭha is a *Vāsiṭṭha*. In this same way, others should also be applied. 433, 528.
The suffixes *kha*, *cha*, or *sa* are optionally added after the roots *tija*, *gup*, and *kita* when expressing honor.
After the verbal roots *tij*, *gup*, *kit*, and *mān*, the suffixes *kha*, *cha*, and *sa* optionally occur. Examples:
*titikkhati*, *jigucchati*, *tikicchati*, *vīmaṃsati*. Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated?
[To show that] otherwise it is *tejati*, *gopati*, *māneti*.
434, 534. After the roots *bhuja*, *ghasa*, *hara*, and *su-pā*, when they take the suffix *tum* (denoting desire), the suffixes *kha*, *cha*, and *sa* optionally occur.
For example: from the root *bhuja*, *bubhukkhati* (he wishes to eat); from *ghasa*, *jighacchati* (he wishes to eat);
from *hara*, *jigīsati* (he wishes to take); from *su-śru*, *sussūsati* (he wishes to hear); from *pā*, *pivāsati* (he wishes to drink).
What is the meaning of *vāti*? It means "he wishes to eat.
What is the purpose of [the rule] *tumicchatthesu*? [Example: *bhuñjati*.
435, 536. *Āya* is used after a noun denoting an agent or a standard of comparison in the sense of "conduct" (*ācāra*).
The suffix *āya* occurs in the sense of behaving (*ācāra*) after a noun that serves as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

*Saṅgho pabbatamiva attānamācarati* = *pabbatāyati* (the Saṅgha behaves toward itself as if it were a mountain); *taḷākaṃ samuddamiva attānamācarati* = *samuddāyati* (the pond behaves toward itself as if it were the ocean); *saddo cicciṭamiva attānamācarati* = *cicciṭāyati* (the sound behaves toward itself as if it were the *cicciṭa* noise). In this same way, other examples should also be applied. 436, 537.
And [the suffixes] *ī* and *ū* also [occur] after a standard of comparison.
The suffix *īya* occurs after a noun in the sense of acting like something, whether in the sense of a comparison or in the sense of conduct (*ācāra*).

*Acchattaṃ chattam iva ācarati* = *chattīyati* (he acts like one who has no umbrella as if he had one); *aputtaṃ puttam iva ācarati* = *puttīyati* (he acts toward one who has no son as if toward a son).
For what purpose is the term "comparison" (*upamāna*) stated? [To exclude cases such as: *dhammaṃ ācarati* (he practices the Dhamma).
For what purpose does one practice (*ācarati*)? One protects that which is not a parasol as if it were a parasol. In this same way, other [rules] should also be applied.
437, 538. Regarding "from a noun" (*nāmamhā*):
in the sense of desiring for oneself (*attano icchatthe*), the suffix *īya* occurs after a noun.
*Attano pattaṃ icchati* = *pattīyati*. Likewise, *vatthīyati*, *parikkhārīyati*, *cīvarīyati*, *dhanīyati*, *ghaṭīyati*.
[The question] "In *atticchatthe*, for what purpose? means: he desires the bowl of another. In this way, others should also be applied accordingly. 438, 540.
From verbal roots (*dhātu*), the causative suffixes *ṇe*, *ṇaya*, *ṇāpe*, and *ṇāpayā* are added in the sense of motive (*hetvatthe*).
After all roots (*dhātu*), the suffixes *ṇe*, *ṇāpe*, and *ṇāpayi* occur, and they are designated as *kārita* (causative) when used in the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe*).
Whoever performs an action, another person says to them, "Do it! Do it! (*karohi karohi*), or else one instigates (*payojayati*) the one who is acting;
thus: *kāreti*, *kārayati*, *kārāpeti*, *kārāpayati*. To those who perform any action, others say, "Do it! Do it! (*karotha karotha*).
Thus they say: *kārenti*, *kārayanti*, *kārāpenti*, *kārāpayanti*. Whoever cooks, another says to him, "Cook! Cook!

*gāyati*, *gāyanti*. 516, 466. Insertion of the letter *i*:
In every non-suffixal (asabbadhātuka) verbal form, there is the insertion of the letter *i*.
"He will go," "he will do," "he will obtain," "he will cook.
For what purpose [is the term] "in an uncommon verbal root" (*asabbadhātumhi*) used? [Examples: "he goes," "he does," "he obtains," "he cooks.
517, 488. In some instances, there are lengthening, substitution, elision, and augmentation of the verbal root, case endings, and suffixes.

In this context, when the grammatical means (sādhana) have not been explicitly stated in a verbal form, one should—in certain instances—apply these grammatical operations (kāriya)—namely, lengthening, substitution for the opposite, elision, augmentation, and so forth—to the root, the case-ending, or the suffix, in accordance with the Word of the Conqueror (jinavacana).

Examples such as *jāyati*, *kareyya*, *jāniyā*, *siyā*, *kare*, *gacche*, *jaññā*, *vakkhetha*, *dakkhetha*, *dicchati*, *agacchi*, *agacchuṃ*, *ahosi*, *ahesuṃ*, and other such formations should be constructed accordingly.
(518, 446) The middle voice endings (*attanopada*) are used in place of the active voice endings (*parassapada*).
In some instances, the *attanopada* (middle voice) endings take on the status of *parassapada* (active voice) endings.
[Examples are: *vuccati*, *labbhati*, *paccati*.
For what purpose is the word "in some instances" (*kvaci*) used? [To show: *karīyate*, *labbhate*, *paccate*.
519, 457. The augment *a* occurs in the past tense (*hiyyattanī*), the present day (*ajjatanī*), and the future (*kālātipatti*).
In certain instances, the augment *a* is inserted before these case endings: *hiyyattanī*, *ajjatanī*, and *kālātipatti*.
Examples: *agamā*, *agamī*, *agamissā*.
What is the purpose of [the word] *kvaci*? [Examples: *gamā*, *gamī*, *gamissā*.
520, 502. *Brūto ī timhi*:
The vowel *ī* is inserted after the root *brū* before the third case ending (*timhi*).
He says:
521, 425. Elision of the final [consonant] of a root that has more than one vowel.
In some cases, there is elision of the final [consonant] of a root that has more than one vowel.
*Gacchati*, *sarati*, *marati*.
For what purpose [is the suffix] *-aneka-sarasa-* used? *Pāti*, *yāti*, *vāti*.

522, 476. *Isu-yamu-antō ccho vā*.
For these roots, namely *isu* and *yamu*, the final letter becomes *ccha* optionally. [Examples: *icchati*, *niyacchati*.
Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated? [To show: *esati*, *niyamati*.
523, 526. *Kāritānaṃ ṇo lopaṃ*.
There is elision of the *ṇo* of these affixes called *kārita*.
[Examples: *kāreti*, *kārayati*, *kārāpeti*, *kārāpayati*.
This which has been pointed out for the sake of the Dispensation and briefly related by me,

7. The Section on Nominal Derivatives:
First Chapter.
Having first paid homage to the Buddha, that ocean of knowledge, the omniscient one whose wisdom for the sake of the world is inexhaustible,
I shall indeed explain the *Kitaka* method along with its supporting arguments.
(Kha) For they say that the root of practice is application,
and the root of application is the goal.
Those whose minds are confident regarding the meanings are considered by the Victor to be the upholders of the Dispensation.
(Ga)
Just as a blind man is destitute of his country and a pot is empty of honey and oil without its container,
so too is one who has perished like those things that have been lost.
Likewise, the meaning is deficient in its application.
(Gha) Therefore, for the sake of protecting the meaning of the Sage’s words, which are so difficult to obtain;
I shall explain that which is for the benefit of students, endowed with proof and appropriate for the ritual. 524, 561.
After a verbal root, when [the object] and so forth are present, the suffix *ṇa* occurs.
After a verbal root, when the object and so forth are present, the suffix *ṇa* arises.

One who performs an action is a *kammakāra* (worker); likewise, a potter (*kumbhakāra*), a garland-maker (*mālākāra*), a wood-worker (*kaṭṭhakāra*), a chariot-maker (*rathakāra*), a silversmith (*rajatakāra*), a goldsmith (*suvaṇṇakāra*), a bowl-collector (*pattaggāha*), a weaver (*tantavāya*), a grain-measurer (*dhaññamāya*), one who loves the Dhamma (*dhammakāma*), and one who walks in the Dhamma (*dhammacāra*).
525, 565. Regarding the suffix *-nu*:
After the verbal root *saññā* when it functions as the object of expression, the suffix *-a* is added to denote the object and so forth, and the augment *nu* is inserted before the noun.
He tames his enemies, thus he is Arindama, the king. He crosses over the state of a commoner, thus he is Vessantara, the king.
He creates craving, thus he is Taṇhaṅkara, the Blessed One. He creates wisdom, thus he is Medhaṅkara, the Blessed One. He creates a refuge, thus he is Saraṇaṅkara, the Blessed One.
He creates an island, thus he is Dīpaṅkara, the Blessed One.
526, 567. *Purindada* and *iṃ*.
When the word *pura* is at the beginning, the suffix *a* is added to the verbal root *dada*, and the letter *i* replaces the letter *a* of the word *pura*.
Because he gave a gift (*dāna*) in the city (*pure*), he is called *Purindada*, the king of the gods.
527, 568. *Sabbato ṇvu tvāvī vā*.
From every verbal root (*dhātu*), whether it has an object (*sakamma*) or no object (*akamma*), the suffixes *ṇvu*, *tu*, and *āvī* occur [after the root-final vowel] with the augment *a*.

That which performs this is a *takkara*; that which performs what is beneficial is a *hitakara*. That wherein one is led, or by means of which one is led, is *vinaya* (discipline); that which one dwells in depending upon is *nissaya* (support).

In the *ṇvu*-suffix: one who makes a chariot is a *rathakāraka* (chariot-maker); one who gives food is an *annadāyaka* (food-giver); one who leads beings is a *vināyaka* (leader); one who does is a *kāraka* (doer); one who gives is a *dāyaka* (giver); one who leads is a *nāyaka* (leader). In the *tu*-suffix:

one who does that is a *takkaṭṭhā* (doer of that), or "the doer of that" is *takkaṭṭhā*. One who gives food is a *bhojanadātā* (food-giver), or "the giver of food" is *bhojanadātā*. One who does is a *kattā* (doer). One who remembers is a *saritā* (rememberer). In the *āvī*-suffix: one who sees danger is a *bhayadassāvī* (one who sees danger), and so forth.
528, 577. *Vi*, *ruj*, *pad* and so forth: the suffix *ṇa* [is applied].
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after verbal roots such as *vi*, *ruj*, *pad*, and others.

*Pavisati* (he enters) → *paveso* (entry); *rujati* (he breaks/suffers) → *rogo* (disease); *uppajjati* (it arises) → *uppādo* (arising); *phusati* (he touches) → *phasso* (contact); *uñcati* (he covers) → *oko* (home/abode); *bhavati* (he becomes) → *bhāvo* (existence/state); *ayati* (he goes) → *āyo* (income/gain); *sammā bujjhati* (he perfectly awakens) → *sambodho* (enlightenment); *viharati* (he dwells) → *vihāro* (dwelling).
529, 580. *Bhāve ca*. The suffix *ṇa* occurs after all verbal roots when the abstract state (*bhāva*) is to be expressed. For example:
from *pacati*, *pāko* (cooking) or *pacanaṃ*; from *cajati*, *cāgo* (giving up) or *cajanaṃ*; likewise, *yāgo*, *yogo*, *bhāgo*, *paridāho*.
The suffix *kvip* occurs after all verbal roots (*sabbadhātu*).

That which comes into being is *sambhū*; that which exists in a distinguished manner is *vibhū*; that which moves by means of its arms is *bhujaga*; one who digs up oneself, or one who digs well, is *saṅkha*.
531, 589. *Rammo* by means of *dhara* and so forth.
The suffix *ramma* occurs after verbal roots such as *dhara* and the like.
That by which one upholds is *dhamma*; that which is performed is *kamma*.
532, 590. *Tassīlādīsu ṇītvāvī ca*.
After all verbal roots (*dhātu*), the suffixes *ṇī*, *tu*, and *āvī* occur in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth.
A king whose habit it is to praise what is dear is a king who praises what is dear (*piyapasaṃsī*); [likewise], one whose habit it is to practice the holy life (*brahmacariya*)...
The person for whom that individual is a celibate practitioner is one whose nature it is to prevail;
the king whose nature it is to prevail is a king who prevails; the ascetic whose nature it is to see fear is an ascetic who sees fear—and so forth.
533, 591. *Sadda-ku-dha-cala-maṇḍattha-rucādīhi yu*.
The suffix *yu* occurs after the verbal roots *sadda*, *ku*, *dha*, *cala*, *maṇḍa*, and those beginning with *ruca*, in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth.

One whose habit is shouting is *ghosana*; one whose habit is speaking is *bhāsana*. The analysis (*viggaha*) should be constructed in this manner. *Kodhana*, *dosana*, *calana*, *kampana*, *phandana*, *maṇḍana*, *vibhūsana*, *rocana*, *jotana*, *vaḍḍhana*.
534, 562. *Pārādigamimhā rū*:
From this verbal root *gam*, when preceded by the word *pāra*, the suffix *rū* occurs in the senses of "one whose habit is [that]," and so forth.

The further shore of existence (*bhava*) is the "further shore of existence" (*bhavapāra*). A person who has the habit of going to the further shore of existence is a "person who has gone to the further shore of existence" (*bhavapāragū*).
What is the purpose of [the rule] "after *tassa*, *ilādi*, etc."? [To form] *pāraṅgato*.
What is the purpose of [the rule] "after *pāra*, *ādi*, *gami*, etc."? [To form] *anugāmī*. 535, 593. And after *bhikkhā* and so forth.
The suffix *rūpa* occurs after verbal roots such as *bhikkha* in the senses of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth.
One who has the habit of begging, the habit of requesting, is a *bhikkhu*; one who has the habit of knowing is a *viññū*.
(536, 594) The suffix *ṇuka* occurs after [roots] such as *tan* in those same senses.
The suffix *ṇuka* occurs after roots such as *han* in the senses of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth.
One whose habit is to strike is an *āghātuka*; one whose habit is to act is a *kāruka*. 537, 566.
A nasalized vowel (*niggahita*) [is substituted] at the end of a word.
The augment *nukāra* (the letter *n*) at the end of a word becomes *niggahita*. For example:

"He tames his enemies" (*ariṃ dameti*) thus he is *arindamo*, the king. "He crosses over the *vessa*-caste" (*vessaṃ tarati*) thus he is *vessantaro*, the king. "He creates light" (*pabhaṃ karoti*) thus he is *pabhaṅkaro*, the Blessed One.
538, 595. Or, after *saṃhāna*, *ññā*, and *vā*, *ra* becomes *gha*.
The suffix *ra* is added to the root *hana* preceded by the prefix *sam*, or to any other root; furthermore, the substitution of *gha* occurs for *han*.

Thus, that which approaches the united action (*kamma*) is a *saṅgha*; that which is dug all around the city is a *parikhā*; that which makes an end is an *antaka*. For what purpose is the prefix *sam* used?
[To show] the act of striking down is *upaghāta*.
539, 558. *Ramhi ranto rādino*.
When the suffix *ram* follows, there is the elision of all consonants beginning with *r* at the end of a verbal root.
Examples include *antako*, *pāragū*, *satthā*, and *diṭṭho*, and so forth.
540, 545. *Tabba* and *anīya* suffixes in the sense of the passive and the gerundive.
In these senses—namely, the passive and the gerundive—these suffixes *tabba* and *anīya* occur after all verbal roots (*dhātu*).
Examples: *bhavitabbaṃ*, *bhavanīyaṃ*; *āsitabbaṃ*, *āsanīyaṃ*; *pajjitabbaṃ*, *pajjanīyaṃ*; *kattabbaṃ*, *karaṇīyaṃ*; *gantabbaṃ*, *gamanīyaṃ*.
The suffix *ṇya* occurs after all verbal roots in the senses of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the passive (*kamma*). For example:
*kātabbaṃ* (to be done) becomes *kāriyaṃ*; *jetabbaṃ* (to be conquered) becomes *jeyyaṃ*; *netabbaṃ* (to be led) becomes *neyyaṃ*, and so forth.

By the inclusion of *ca*, the suffix *teyya* occurs. For example: *ñātabbaṃ* (that which is to be known) becomes *ñāteyyaṃ*; likewise *daṭṭheyyaṃ* (that which is to be seen), *patteyyaṃ* (that which is to be attained), and so forth.

*Kattabbaṃ* means "that which is to be done.

After this root *bhū*, there is the substitution of *abbā* for the suffix *ṇya* together with the vowel *ū*, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*).
*Bhavitabbo* means "one who ought to become," *bhabbo* means "capable," and *bhavitabbaṃ* means "that which ought to be.
