That which is to be spoken is *vajja*; intoxicating drink is *majja*; that which is to be gone to is *gamma*; that which is to be joined is *yogga*;

that which is to be censured is *gārayha*; that which is to be given is *deyya*; that which is to be drunk is *peyya*; that which is to be abandoned is *heyya*; that which is to be measured is *meyya*; that which is to be known is *ñeyya*—and so forth. These are the *kicca* (verbal nouns).
Those suffixes beginning with *ta* that are devoid [of the sense of agent] should be understood as having the designation "function" (*kicca*).
What is the purpose of this designation "function"? It is for the sake of establishing the status of function in the cases of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*).
546, 562. Others are *kita*.
Other conditions are indeed *kita* suffixes.
What is the purpose of the *kita* suffix? It is used for the agent (*kattari*). 547, 596.
The suffix *yu* is added after [roots] beginning with *nand*.
The suffix *yup* occurs after roots such as *nand* and others in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*).

Thus: *nandīyate* becomes *nandanaṃ*; or that which is to be praised is *nandanaṃ*; that which is to be grasped is *gahaṇaṃ*; that which is to be practiced is *caraṇaṃ*. In this manner, it should be applied in all cases.
(548, 597) It also occurs in the case of the agent (*kattā*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The suffix *yup* occurs after these meanings: the agent (*kattā*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and so forth.
First, regarding the agent: that which carries away dust is "dust-carrying water" (*rajoharaṇaṃ toyaṃ*).
Regarding the instrument: that by which one acts is "an instrument" (*karaṇaṃ*).
Regarding "place" (*padese*) first: that in which something stands is a "place. This should be applied in all instances.
549, 550. *Rahādito ṇa*:
After verbal roots ending in the letters *ra* or *ha*, the *na* of the suffix *anā* becomes *ṇa*.

It is an instrument (*karaṇa*) because one acts by means of it; it is a fulfillment (*pūraṇa*) because one completes by means of it; it is a grasping (*gahaṇa*) because one grasps by means of it. In this same way, other [terms] should also be applied accordingly.
Thus ends the first section in the chapter on the formation of nouns (*kibbidhāna*).
The second section.
550, 546. The suffixes beginning with *ṇ* pertain to all three times.
It should be understood that the suffixes beginning with *ṇ*, ending with the suffix *yu*, pertain to all three times.

One who makes a pot—[has made, will make]—is a "pot-maker" (*kumbhakāra*). That by which one makes, has made, or will make is an "instrument" (*karaṇa*). In this same way, other [suffixes] should also be applied.
551, 598. *Dā* in the sense of perceiving (*saññā*).
When "perceiving" is the meaning to be expressed, the suffix *i* is added to the root *dā*.

That which is first taken up is *ādi*; that which holds water is *udami*; that which holds great waters is *mahodadhi*; that in which hair is held is *vāladhi*; that which is properly placed together is *sandhi*.
552, 609. *Ti kita cāsiṭṭhe*.
The suffix *ti* occurs after all verbal roots when expressing a command (*saññāya*) or an exhortation (*abhidheyyāyaṃ*), as well as *kita* in the sense of an exhortation (*āsiṭṭhe*). For example:
"May the Conqueror awaken the people" is *jinabuddhi*; "May wealth be his" is *dhanabhūti*; and "may he be" is *bhūto*.
"May he exist" is *bhāva*; "may he give Dhamma to people" is *Dhammadinna*; "may he increase" is *Vaḍḍhamāna*.
In this way, others should also be applied accordingly. 553, 599. *Itthiyamatiyavo vā*:
When a feminine referent is to be expressed, the suffixes *a*, *ti*, *yu*, and *va* optionally occur after all verbal roots.
One ages, thus it is aging (*jarā*); one conceives, thus it is conception (*mati*); one intends, thus it is volition (*cetanā*); one feels, thus it is feeling (*vedanā*).

In this same way, others should also be applied accordingly. The suffix *rirīya* occurs after the root *kara*. After the root *kara*, this suffix *rirīya* optionally occurs in the sense of "doing" (*karoto*) when there is a desire for a female or a male. Or rather, it is the suffix *rirīya* that occurs [in these instances].
*Kattabbā* means that which is to be done; *karaṇīyaṃ kiriyaṃ* means the action to be performed.
555, 612. *Atīte tatavantutāvī*: In the past tense, the suffixes *tavantu* and *tāvī* occur after all verbal roots (*dhātu*).
*Huta*, *hutavā*, *hutāvī*. *Vusita*, *vusitavā*, *vusitāvī*. *Bhutta*, *bhuttavā*, *bhuttāvī*.
(556, 622) Regarding the past tense of the causative and passive: the suffix *ta* occurs after all verbal roots (*dhātu*) when expressing the past tense in the causative and passive voices.
In the sense of the state (*bhāve*): his singing, dancing, acting, and laughing.
In the sense of the action (*kammani*): spoken by him, taught by him.
557, 606. In the case of the agent (*kattari*), [the suffix -ta is used] after roots such as *budha* and *gam*.
The suffix *ta* occurs after roots such as *budha*, *gamu*, and others, when their respective meanings are implied, denoting the agent (*kattar*) in all tenses. For example:

"He awakens, he awakened, he will awaken to all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena" is *buddho*; "He has gone to refuge, gone to tranquility, gone beyond the waves; he knows, he knew, he will know" is *ñāto*—and so forth.
(558, 602) The suffix *ina* is used everywhere [after the root *ji*].
The suffix *ina* occurs after a root ending in a long vowel (*ī*, *ū*, or *e*) at all times when denoting the agent.
One who conquers (*jināti*), has conquered (*ajini*), or will conquer (*jinissati*) evil and unwholesome states is a "Conqueror" (*jino*).
[Also] from the root *sup*. 559, 603. And from the root *sup*.
The suffix *in* occurs after a verbal root ending in *supa* (the causative marker) when expressing the agent (*kattar*) or the action itself (*bhāva*).
That which sleeps is a dream (*supinaṃ*); that which is slept is a dream (*supinaṃ*).
[Pāṇini 3.3.560, 604] After the prefixes *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *su*, the suffix *kha* is applied.
The suffix *kh* occurs after all verbal roots beginning with *īs*, *duss*, *suss*, and others. Examples:
*īsassayo*, *dussayo*, *sussayo* (by you); *īsakkaraṃ*, *dukkaraṃ*, *sukkaraṃ* (by you). 561, 636.
When the sense is that of desire and the agents are the same, the suffixes *tave* or *tuṃ* are used.
In the sense of desire (*icchattha*), when the agent is the same, these suffixes—*tum*, *itabba*, and *etu*—are applied to all verbal roots in all tenses to denote the agent:
*puññāni kātave* (he desires to do meritorious deeds), *saddhammaṃ sotum icchati* (he desires to hear the true Dhamma).
[Also] after roots such as *araha* and *sakka*. (562, 638)
The suffix *tuṃ* occurs after all roots when expressing meanings such as "worthy of" (*araha*) and "capable of" (*sakkā*). For example:
*Ko taṃ nindituṃ arahati?* ("Who is worthy to blame him? or *Sakkā jetuṃ dhanena vā.* ("Or it is possible to conquer by means of wealth"). In this way, other instances should also be applied.
(563, 639) [The suffix *tum* also occurs] in expressions of attainment (*patta-vacana*) and in the sense of sufficiency (*alam-attha*).
In the case of words expressing sufficiency (*alamattha*), the suffix *tuṃ* occurs after all verbal roots. For example:
*alam eva dānāni dātuṃ* (it is indeed sufficient to give gifts), *alam eva puññāni kātuṃ* (it is indeed sufficient to perform meritorious deeds).
564, 640. In the past tense, for those [roots] ending in *-aka*, the suffixes *tuna*, *tvāna*, and *tvāva* occur.
In ancient times, the suffixes *tun*, *tvāna*, and *tvā* optionally occur after verbal roots that have a single agent.
He goes having done the work; he suffers for merit not having done it; beings rejoice having heard the Dhamma;
he dwells having conquered the enemy; this thought occurred to him having heard the Dhamma; having heard from here, they speak there.
"Having heard, we shall know. In this manner, it should be applied in all instances.
565, 646. *Vattamāne mānantā*.
In the sense of the present tense, these suffixes—*māna* and *antā*—are added after all verbal roots (*dhātu*).
*Saramāno* means weeping. *Gacchanto gaṇhāti* means he takes while going.
566, 574. With roots such as *sāsadi*, the suffix *ratthu* occurs.
With roots such as *sāsaicc-*, the suffix *ratthu* occurs.
He teaches, thus he is a teacher (*satthā*); or, he harms, thus he is a teacher (*satthā*).
567, 575. *Pātitoritu*.
The suffix *ritu* occurs after the root *pā* (to drink).
"Pāti puttanti pitā" (He protects his son, thus he is a father).
568, 576. *Rātu* [is formed] from *māna* and so forth.
The suffix *rātu* occurs after verbal roots such as *māna* and others, as well as the suffix *ritu*.

She honors her son according to the Dhamma, thus she is a mother (*mātā*); he speaks first, thus he is a brother (*bhātā*); she is supported by her mother and father, thus she is a daughter (*dhītā*).
[Pāṇini 3.2.178] *Āgamā tuka*:
after the roots beginning with *āp*, the suffix *tuka* is applied when the sense of "gone" (*gata*) is conveyed.
"One who comes" is an *āgantuka* (a visitor), O monk.
570, 611. The suffix *ika* occurs after [the root] *bhabba* (capable).
From this root *gamu*, the suffix *ika* occurs when there is a sense of capability. One who will go, or one who is capable of going, is a *gamika* (a traveler), O monk.
Thus ends the second section, the Section on Flattery.
Third Section: 571, 624.
Desirable and undesirable forms are accomplished through the application of grammatical rules.

In the sections on numerals (*saṅkhyā*), nouns (*nāma*), compounds (*samāsa*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), *kit*, and *kapp* suffixes, those words which have undergone undesirable changes and possess suffixes are established as nipātas by being analyzed through their respective grammatical operations and then restored to their own original names.
First, regarding numerals: for the word *eka*, the vowel *e* becomes *etā*; and for the letter *d* of *das*, there is a substitution of the letter *r*.
Thus, *eka* and *das* become *ekārasa*. For the word *dvi*, it becomes *bā*; and for the letter *d* of *das*, there is a substitution of the letter *r*. Thus, *dve* and *das* become *bārasa*.
For *dvi*, it becomes *du*; for *daśa*, it becomes *viṃsa*. *Dve* and *viṃsa* become *bāvīsaṃ*.
For *ṣaṣ*, it becomes *so*; for *daśa*, the *da* becomes *ḷ*, thus *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* become *soḷasa*.
In the case of *ṣaḍāyatana*, the *ṣa* becomes *saḷ*, thus *saḷāyatanaṃ*. In this manner, the remaining numbers should be formed.

First, regarding *nāmika* (nominal) words: when preceded by *ima*, the suffixes *-ajja* and *-ajju* arise; furthermore, for the words *ima* and *samāna*, the substitutions *a* and *sa* occur [respectively].
Thus: at this time—*ajja*, *ajju*; at the same time—*sajja*, *sajju*; at another time—*aparajja*, *aparajju*. First, regarding compounds (*samāsa*):

*bhūmigato* (gone to the ground), *apāyagato* (gone to a state of loss), *issarakataṃ* (done by Īśvara). *Sallaviddho* (pierced by an arrow), *kathinadussaṃ* (stiff cloth), *corabhayaṃ* (fear of thieves), *dhaññarāsi* (a heap of grain), *saṃsāradukkhaṃ* (the suffering of saṃsāra), *pubbāparaṃ* (before and after).
First, regarding *taddhita* [secondary derivatives]: *vāsiṭṭho*, *bhāradvājo*, *bhaggavo*, *paṇḍavo*, *kāleyyo*.

First, regarding *ākhyāta* [verbs]: according to the rule "for the state of being" (*asa bhāve*) from the verbal root, when the present tense occurs in both the singular and plural numbers, for the singular, *ssa* replaces *ti* together with the final letter;
for the plural, *ssu* replaces *anti* together with the final letter. Thus it is for him.
"You should be addressed; thus you should be addressed.
For there is an injunction for him: "Go," or "Go forth. Now, regarding how many [forms]:

the suffix *ka* occurs after verbal roots such as *vad* ("to speak") and *han* ("to kill"); and for *vad*, it becomes *vāda*, and for *han*, it becomes *ghāta*. Thus: *vādaka* (a speaker), *ghātaka* (a killer).

From the roots *naṭ* and *daṭ*, the substitution of *tap* occurs together with the final letter [of the root]. Thus, *nattaṃ* (dancing) and *naṭṭaṃ* (perished), and other such forms, are established through these specific grammatical rules (*nipātanā*). 572, 625.
From the roots *sās*, *dis*, and others, the substitution of *riṭṭha* occurs for the suffix *tap* in its place.
That is to say, from the roots *sās*, *dis*, and so forth, the suffix *tap* undergoes the substitution of *riṭṭha*.
He was instructed by me; the form *diṭṭhaṃ* (seen) is [an example].

By the inclusion of "ca" (and), the substitutions *raṭṭha* and *raṭṭhuṃ* occur for the suffixes *kicca*, *tā*, and *tuṃ*. *Dassanīyaṃ* (worth seeing) and *daṭṭhabbaṃ* (to be seen). [They] go to the monastery to see the recluses (*daṭṭhuṃ*).
573, 626. [The suffix] *iṭṭha* occurs after roots such as *sādisa* (resembling), *puccha* (ask), *bhanja* (break), and *hansa* (go).

In the case of roots ending in *s*, such as *pucch* (to ask), *bhañj* (to break), *haṃs* (to go), and others, there is a substitution of *ṭh* for the consonant *s* of the *ta*-suffix in its place. Thus:

*tuṭṭho* (satisfied), *ahinā daṭṭho naro* (a man bitten by a snake), *mayā puṭṭho* (asked by me), *bhaṭṭho* (fallen), *pabhaṭṭho* (departed), *haṭṭho* (delighted), *pahaṭṭho* (exultant), *yiṭṭho* (sacrificed). In this manner, other roots should also be applied everywhere.
574, 613. From the root *vas* (to dwell), [the form] *uṭṭha*.
If this element [vassa] is followed by the suffix *ta*, there is the substitution of *u* for the consonant *t* and the following consonant in its place.
*Vassamvuṭṭho*.
575, 614. Or *vassa* becomes *vu*.
When the suffix *tap* follows the stem *vas*, the letter *v* may optionally be replaced by *u*. Thus:
*vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ* becomes either *uṭṭho* or *vuṭṭho*.
(576, 607) When *dha*, *ḍha*, *bha*, or *ya* follow, [the preceding *v*] becomes *dha* or *ḍha*.
The suffix *ta* undergoes the substitutions *dha* and *ḍha* respectively after verbal roots ending in *dha*, *ḍha*, *bha*, and *ha*. For example:

*buddho bhagavā* (the Blessed One is awakened), *vaḍḍho bhikkhu* (the monk has grown), *laddhaṃ me paṭṭacīvaraṃ* (a robe made of fine cloth has been obtained by me), *agginā daḍḍhaṃ vanaṃ* (the forest was burnt by fire).
577, 628. And [the suffix *ta* becomes] *gva* after the root *bhanja*.
When the suffix *ta* is elided from a verbal root beginning with *bhaj*, the substitute *gga* occurs before a consonant such as *sah*. [Result:
*bhaggo*.
(578, 560) In the case of roots beginning with *bhuj*, the final vowel becomes *no*, and the following consonant is doubled.
In the case of roots such as *bhuja* and others, the suffix *-no* does not occur; instead, there is doubling (*dvittāva*) of the *ta*-suffix. Thus:
*bhutto*, *bhuttāvī*, *catto*, *satto*, *ratto*, *yutto*, *vivitto*.
(579, 629) *Vaca* becomes *vāvu*.
In the verbal root *vaca*, the letter *va* is replaced by *u*, provided that the letter *c* does not occur at the end; furthermore, the suffix *tap* may optionally undergo reduplication.
As stated by the Blessed One: *vuttaṃ* or *uttaṃ*.
(580, 630) And [this applies] to *gup* and the others as well.
In the case of roots such as *gup*, etc., there is no final consonant, and the suffix *-ta* undergoes doubling. Thus:
*sugutto*, *catto*, *litto*, *santatto*, *utto*, *vivitto*, *sitto*. Other [roots] should be applied in the same way. 581, 616.
With *tar*, etc., the suffix *-inna* [is added].

After roots such as *tara*, the substitution of *iṇ* for the suffix *tap* occurs, and the final consonant is dropped. Thus: *tarati* becomes *tiṇṇo*; *uttarati* becomes *uttiṇṇo*; *sampūrati* becomes *sampuṇṇo*; *turati* becomes *tuṇṇo*; *parijīrati* becomes *parijiṇṇo*; *ākirati* becomes *ākiṇṇo*.
(582, 631) After roots beginning with *bhid*, the suffixes *inna*, *anna*, or *īṇa* are applied.
After roots such as *bhidi*, etc., the substitutes *inna*, *anna*, and *īṇa* optionally occur for the suffix *tap*, and the final consonant is dropped. Thus: that which is to be split is *bhinna*;

that which is being cut is *chinna*; that which was cut off is *ucchinna*; that which is given is *dinna*; that which sits is *nisinna*; that which is well-covered is *suchanna*; that which is worn out is *khinna*; that which weeps is *runna*; "birth is exhausted" (*khīṇā jāti*). Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated? [To show: that which breaks is *bhitti*.
583, 617. *Susa*, *paca*, *saka*, *icc-ādīhi*:
For roots such as *susa*, *paca*, *saka*, and so forth, the suffix *ta* undergoes the substitutions *kkha* and *kā*, and the final consonant is elided.
That which dries up is *sukkhaṃ* (dry); that which is cooked is *pakkaṃ* (cooked), as in the case of fruit. He who is capable or who honors is *sakko*, the Lord of the Sujās (*Sujampati*).
584, 618. *Pakkamādīhi nto ca*.
From verbal roots such as *pakkama* and others, the suffix *ta* undergoes the substitution *nta*, and it also becomes *no*. Thus:
one who goes forth is *pakkanto*; one who departs is *vibbhanto*; *saṅkanto*, *khanto*, *santo*, *danto*, *vanto*.
What is the purpose of including the word *ca* (and)? It is so that the suffix *ta* becomes *anti* by means of those same roots, and it also becomes *anto*. For example: *kanti*, *khanti*.
This applies in all such cases. 585, 619. *Janādīnamā timhi ca*:
In the case of roots such as *jana* and others, the final consonant is replaced by *ā* when the suffix *ta* follows, and also when the suffix *ti* follows.
*Ajani* means "born"; *jāti* is the act of being born.
[The suffix] *timhi*: for what purpose? To exclude the vowel *ā* even when another suffix follows. Examples include: *janitvā*, *janitā*, *janituṃ*, *janitabbaṃ*, and so forth. 586, 600.
[The suffix] *-anta* is applied to roots such as *gama*, *khana*, *hana*, *rama*, etc.
A consonant within roots such as *gama*, *khana*, *hana*, *ramu*, and so forth, does not become doubled when followed by the suffix *ta* or the suffixes ending in *ti*. For example:

*Sundaraṃ nibbānaṃ gacchatīti sugato* (He goes to the beautiful Nibbāna, thus he is "Well-Gone"). *Sundaraṃ nibbānaṃ gacchatīti sugati* (The state of going to the beautiful Nibbāna). *Khataṃ*, *khati*. *Upahataṃ*, *upahati*. *Rato*, *rati*; *mato*, *mati*. Why is the word "vā" (or) used?
[To indicate that doubling occurs] in cases such as *ramato*, *ramati*.
587, 632. And the letter *ra*. The letter *ra*, when forming the end of verbal roots (*dhātu*), does not become [a consonant] before the suffix *ta* or before the following suffixes *ti* and *mhi*.
That which is made by means of a method is "made" (*pakato*); that which is made first is "nature" (*pakati*); that which flows apart is "viscous" (*visato*) or "it flows" (*visati*).
588, 620. *Ṭhā* and *pā*: In these roots, the vowel *ā* at the end is replaced by *i* and *ī* respectively when followed by the suffix *ta*, and also in the case of *tim*. Examples:
*yattha ṭhito*, *ṭhiti*, *pīto*, *pīti*.
589, 621. *Hante-hi ho hassa ḷo vā adahanahānaṃ*.

After roots ending in *h*, there is the substitution of *h* for the suffix *tap*; furthermore, for a root-final *h*, there is optionally the substitution of *ḷ*, except in the case of *adahana* and *hāna*.
Examples: *āruhittha* (he has ascended) becomes *āruḷho*; *gāḷho*, *bāḷho*, *mūḷo*.
What is the meaning of *adahanahāna*? That which burns is "burnt" (*daḍḍha*); that which is well-fastened is "bound" (*sannaddha*).
Thus ends the third section on the rules for primary derivatives (*kibbidhāna*).
The fourth section.
590, 579. *Ṇamhi rañjassa jo bhāvakaraṇesu*.

When the suffix *ṇam* follows, the letter *j* undergoes the substitution of *y* for the *nj* that constitutes the final element of the root *rañj*, provided it occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Thus, *rañjanam* [becomes] *rāgo*; [and] "that by which they are colored" is *rāgo*.
What is the purpose of [the rule] "in the case of the agentive and instrumental suffixes"?
*Raṅga* means "that which colors. 591, 544.
*Ghāta* is the substitute for *hana*. For this root *hana*, the entire form *ghāta* is substituted when the suffix *ṇam* follows.
"It strikes" (*upahanati*) is *upaghāta*; "one who strikes cows" (*gāvo hanati*) is a cow-killer (*goghātaka*).
Alternatively, there is the substitution of *vadha* everywhere.
That is to say, for this verbal root *han*, the substitute *vadha* occurs in all instances.
*Hanati* means "he kills," thus it is *vadha*, *vadhaka*, *avadhi*, or *ahani*.
593, 564. *Ākārantānamāyo*:
For roots ending in long *ā*, the substitution of *āy* occurs for the final *ā* when the suffix *ṇa* follows.
One who gives is a *dāyaka*; one whose habit is to give gifts is a *dānadāyī*; one whose habit is to give intoxicants is a *majjadāyī*; one whose habit is to go to the city is a *nagarayāyī*.
594, 582. *Pura*, *saṃ*, *upa*, and *pari*: for the root *karoti*, there are optionally the substitutions *kha* and *kha-ra* when followed by a *ta*-affix or the affix *ṇam*.

When the roots *pura*, *saṃ*, *upa*, and *pari* precede the root *karoti*, the substitutions *kha* and *khara* optionally take the place of *karoti* when a *ta*-affix follows, as well as when the affix *ṇam* follows.

It is made pure, thus it is *purakkhata*; it is made correctly, thus it is *saṅkhata*; it is made by approaching, thus it is *upakkhata*; it makes all around, thus it is *parikkhāra*; it is mixed together, thus it is *saṅkhāra*. Why [is there] *va*?
It makes by approaching, thus it is *upakāra*.
(595, 637) In *tave*, *tunā*, etc., [the suffix] *kā* [applies].
In forms such as *tava tunā* and so forth, the substitution of *kā* for the verbal root *karoti* optionally occurs before suffixes beginning with *tu*.
Thus: *kātave*, *kātuṃ*, or *kattuṃ*; *kātuna*, or *kattuna*.
(596, 551) However, for roots such as *gam*, *khan*, and *han*, the substitution does not occur before suffixes beginning with *tu* or *tabba*.
The letter *n* optionally occurs at the end of verbal roots such as *gam*, *khan*, *han*, and others, when followed by suffixes beginning with *tuṃ*, *tabba*, and so forth.

Examples: *gantuṃ*, *gamituṃ*; *gantabbaṃ*, *gamitabbaṃ*. *Khantuṃ*, *khanituṃ*; *khantabbaṃ*, *khanitabbaṃ*. *Hantuṃ*, *hanituṃ*; *hantabbaṃ*, *hanitabbaṃ*. *Mantuṃ*, *manituṃ*; *mantabbaṃ*, *manitabbaṃ*.
What is the purpose of including "and others" (*ādiggahaṇa*)? It is for the purpose of including the suffix *tuna*: *gantuna*, *khantuna*, *hantuna*, *mantuna*.
597, 641. *Sabbehi tunādīnaṃ yo*:
After all verbal roots (*dhātu*), the letter *y* optionally replaces the initial *t* of the suffixes beginning with *tu*.
Examples: *abhivandiya*, *abhivanditvā*; *ohāya*, *ohitvā*; *upanīya*, *upanetvā*; *passiya*, *passitvā*; *uddissa*, *uddisitvā*; *ādāya*, *ādiyitvā*.
598, 643. *Canantehi raccaṃ*:
After verbal roots ending in the letter *c* or the letter *n*, there is optionally the substitution of *racca* for the suffixes beginning with *tu*.
Examples: *vivicca*, *āhacca*, *uhacca*.
For what purpose does it flow (*vāti*)? To strike (*hantvā*).
599, 644. *Disā* and the substitution of *svāna* for *svā*.
For this root *dis*, the suffixes beginning with *tu* undergo the substitution of *svāna* for *svā*, and there is also the elision of the final vowel (*antalopa*).
*Disvāna*, *disvā*.

(600, 645). After verbal roots ending in *ma*, *ha*, *da*, *bha*, *m*, *ya*, *jja*, *bbha*, *ddha*, and *ca*, the suffixes beginning with *tun* undergo the substitutions *mma*, *yha*, *jja*, *bbha*, *ddhā* respectively, or else there is elision of the final vowel (*antalopa*).
Having come, having approached, having descended. Having descended, having taken up, having grasped, having arisen, having arisen, having undertaken, having begun, undertaken, begun.

601, 334. Words ending in *taddhita*, *samāsa*, *kit*, and *taka* suffixes, as well as those ending in *tave*, *tuna*, *tvāna*, *tvā*, etc., should be regarded as nouns (*nāman*), with the exception of those ending in the suffixes *tave*, *tuna*, *tvāna*, *tvā*, and so forth.
"Vāsiṭṭho," "pattadhammo," "kumbhakāro"—and so forth.
602. 6. Regarding a syllable in a *dum* [consonant cluster]: whichever syllable precedes within a *dum*, that should be regarded as heavy (*garuka*) alone.
Having pierced, having cut, having given, having sacrificed. 603, 7.
And long: a long vowel should be regarded as if it were heavy.
Food, river, bride—these are the bases; [the suffix] *opanayika*.
604, 684. With respect to letters:
when there is an application, the suffix *kāra* occurs after words denoting letters (*akkhara*) or the meanings of letters (*akkharattha*).
The letter *a* itself is the augment *akāra*; the letter *ā* itself is the augment *ākāra*;
the letter *ya* itself is the augment *yakāra*. 605, 647.
Regarding the augment *ikāra*: according to the tradition, the augment *ikāra* occurs after all verbal roots (*dhātu*) before all suffixes (*paccaya*).
*Kāriyaṃ*, *bhavitabbaṃ*, *janitabbaṃ*, *viditabbaṃ*, *karitvā*, *icchitaṃ*.
(606, 642) *Dadhantato yo kvaci*:
After a verbal root ending in the letter *da* or *dha*, the augment *ya* is inserted according to the grammatical tradition before certain suffixes such as *tun* and others.
"Buddha" means having arisen in the world and having awakened to the Dhamma.
"Dadhanta-to" (giving) means for what purpose? Having obtained [it].
"Kvacī" (where) means for what purpose? Having produced [it].
Thus ends the fourth section of the *Kibbidhānakappa*.
Fifth Section: 607, 578.
[Rules concerning] the elision (*niggahita*) of a conjunct consonant and so forth.
The letter *n*, when occurring at the beginning of a conjunct consonant, becomes a *niggahita* (anusvāra).
Examples: *raṅgo*, *bhaṅgo*, *saṅgo*.
In all cases, *ge* becomes *gī*.
In every instance where [the suffix] *ge* occurs, the substitution of *gī* takes place for the element *cetassa*.
*Gītaṃ gāyati* ("he sings a song").
609, 484. The substitution of *sīda* for *sada* [occurs].
In every instance where [the suffix] *ṭhā* occurs, the substitution of *sīda-* for *sad-* takes place throughout. Thus:
*nisinno*, *nisīdati*.
(610, 627) In the case of *yaj*, there is the substitution of *sar-* when *ṭhā* follows.
In place of the vowel *i* of this root *yaj*, there is the substitution of the vowel *i* when followed by the suffix *ṭṭha*.
Thus: *yiṭṭho*, *yiṭṭhā*.
For what purpose is *ṭṭha* specified? [To exclude cases such as] *yajanaṃ*.
611, 608. *Do* replaces the final consonants of roots ending in a fourth-class consonant when followed by *dhe*.
For roots ending in a fourth-class consonant, *do* is the substitute before the suffix *dhe*.
Examples: *sannaddho*, *kuddho*, *yuddho*, *siddho*, *laddho*, *āraddho*.
612, 615. Regarding *ḍa* and *ḍha*:
when the letter *ḍha* follows, the substitution *ḍa* occurs for the fourth letters (*ja*, *bha*, *ga*, *dha*) at the end of a verbal root.
Thus, from *dayhati* comes *daḍḍho*; from *vaḍḍhati* comes *vuḍḍho*.
What is the meaning of *ḍhākāra*? It means burning (*dāha*).
613, 583. *Gahassa ghara ṇe vā*.
For the root *gaha*, there is optionally the substitution of *ghara* for the whole [root] when the suffix *ṇa* follows.
*Gharaṃ*, *gharāni*.
Why does it flow (*vāti*)? For the purpose of grasping (*gāha*).
614, 581. *Daha* becomes *ḷa*.
Furthermore, the letter *da* of this root *dah* optionally becomes *ḷ* when followed by the suffix *ṇa*.
*Paridahanaṃ* (the act of burning all around) is *pariḷāho*.
Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated? [To show that] *paridāho* (burning) also occurs.
615, 586. Elision of the final of a verbal root before *kvim*.
When the suffix *kvim* follows, there is elision of the final consonant of a verbal root.
Thus: "he goes by means of arms" is *bhujaga*; "he goes by means of the belly" is *uraga*, *turaga*, and *saṅkha*.
616, 587. *Vidante ū*.
The vowel *ū* is inserted after the root *vid* when the suffix *kvip* follows.
One who knows or understands the world (*loka*) is called a *lokavidū* (a knower of the world).
617, 633. *Na makarānamantānaṃ niyuttamhi*:
There is no elision of the final *n*, *m*, *k*, or *r* sounds at the end of verbal roots when followed by the suffix *ta* joined with the vowel *i*.
Examples: *hanitabbaṃ*, *gamito*, *ramito*, *sakito*, *sarito*, *karitvā*.
What is the purpose of [the rule] "iyuttatamhīti"? It means "gone" (gato), [and] "mindful" (sato).
618, 571. There is no *ka* in the case of *ṇvuṃ*. When the suffix *ṇvuṃ* follows, the letters *ja*, *ka*, *ga*, and *ga* do not undergo the change to *ṇva*.
One who cooks is a *pācaka*; one who sacrifices is a *yājaka*. 619, 573. Regarding the root *kṛ*:
there is the substitution of *t* for the letter *r* at the end of the root *kṛ* when the suffix *tu* follows.
One who does is a *kattā* (agent); those who do are *kattāro* (agents).
620, 549. *Tuṃ*, *tuna*, or *tabba*:
The letter *r* at the end of this verbal root *kar-* optionally becomes *t* before the suffixes *tuṃ*, *tuna*, or *tabba*.
*Kattuṃ*, *kātuṃ*, *kattuna*. *Kātuna*, *kattabbaṃ*, *kātabbaṃ*. 621, 553.
A suffix with the letter *ṇ* as its *anubandha* (indicatory letter) should be regarded as if it were *kārita* (causative).
Or, a suffix having the letter *ṇ* as its *anubandha* is to be seen as equivalent to a causative.
Dāho, deho, vāho, bāho, cāgo, vāro, cāro, parikkhāro, dāyako, nāyako, lāvako, bhāvako, kārī, ghātī, dāyī. [The suffix] *vāti* is used in what sense?
It signifies "an instrument" (*upakkharo*).
622, 570. The suffixes *ana*, *ka*, *yu*, *ṇu*, *ūna*.
When these suffixes (*paccaya*) ending in *u*, *ṇ*, *v*, *i*, or *cc* follow, the substitutions *a*, *na*, *ka*, and *gā* respectively take their place.
Examples: *nandanaṃ*, *kārako*.
Rule 623, 554: *Ka gā ca jānaṃ*.
Furthermore, for these endings of verbal roots, the substitutions of *ka* and *ga* occur when a suffix with the marker *ṇa* follows. For example:
*pāko* (cooking), *yogo* (union).
Thus ends the fifth section in the chapter on euphonic combination (*kibbidhāna*).
The Kitakappa is finished.
8. The Uṇādi Section:
The Sixth Chapter.
624, 563. *Kattari kita*.
The suffix *kita* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattar*).
Examples: *kāru*, *kāruka*, *kāraka*, *pācaka*, *kattā*, *janitā*, *pacitā*, *netā*.
625, 605. The suffixes *kicca*, *tta*, and *khattha* occur after verbal roots (*bhāva*) and passive bases (*kamma*).
Regarding these meanings of verbal roots and passive bases, the suffixes *kicca*, *tta*, and *khattha* are employed. For example:

"that which is to be ordained by you" (*upasampādetabbaṃ upasampādanīyaṃ bhavatā*), "that which is to be reclined by you" (*sayitabbaṃ bhavatā*), "that which is to be done by you" (*kattabbaṃ bhavatā*).
Rice must be eaten by you; food must be consumed by you; you have eaten; you have slept; you have cooked;
you have consumed what was to be eaten; you have slept on what was to be slept upon; rice has been cooked by you;
you have [prepared] some cloth, some fine cloth, some bad cloth, or some coarse cloth.
626, 634. *Kammani dutiyāya tto*.
In the sense of the object (*kammani*), when the second case (*dutiyā*) is used, the suffix *tta* occurs after the agent (*kattari*). For example:

*Dānaṃ dinno Devadatto* (Devadatta was given a gift), *Sīlaṃ rakkhito Devadatto* (Devadatta was protected in virtue), *Bhattaṃ bhutto Devadatto* (Devadatta ate the meal), *Garuṃ upāsito Devadatto* (Devadatta attended upon his teacher).
627, 652. *Khyādīhi māna ma ca to vā*.

The suffix *mana* occurs after verbal roots such as *khi*, *bhī*, *su*, *ru*, *hu*, *vā*, *dhū*, *hi*, *lū*, *pī*, *ada*, *icc-eva-m-ādīhi*; and for the letter *m* of that suffix, *t* optionally occurs. [Examples:
*khema* (safe), because calamities (*upaddava*) are destroyed (*khīyanti*) therein; *bhema* (terrible), because it is to be feared (*bhāyitabba*), or because they fear (*bhāyanti*) from it.

It is *soma* because it flows forth as rays (*raṃsiyo abhissaveti*); it is *roma* because it moves or goes (*ravati gacchati*); it is *homa* because one offers or sacrifices with it (*huvati juhvati etenāti*);
it is *vāma* because it moves or goes in a contrary direction (*paṭilomavasena vāti gacchati*), or it is *vāma* because it moves or proceeds in a base manner (*lāmakavasena vāti gacchati pavattati*);

it is *dhūma* because it shakes or trembles (*dhunāti kampati*); it is *hema* because the mind is impelled or set in motion therein by way of its excellence (*seṭṭhabhāvena hinoti pavattati cittaṃ etasmiṃ*); and it is [called] *lunitabbo* because it is to be shorn.

*Loma*: it is called *loma* because it shaves (*lunāti*) or cuts away the flesh and skin; *pema*: it is called *pema* because of its fondness (*piyana*) or because it is an object of love (*piyāyitabba*);
*attā*: it is called *attā* because it consumes (*adati*) pleasure and pain, or because it is consumed (*adīyate*) and devoured by birth, aging, death, and so forth; *ātumā*.
[In the formation of these words, the suffixes *tha* and *mā* are added after the root *sam-ā-dā*.]
The suffixes *tha* and *ma* occur after verbal roots such as *sam*, *dam*, *dar*, *rah*, *du*, *hi*, *si*, *bhī*, *dā*, *yā*, and *ṭhā*.
It calms, thus it is *samatha*; it tames, thus it is *damatha*; or else, the act of taming is *damatha*; or that which is to be tamed is *damatha*.
It causes distress, thus it is *daratha*. It will take up or seize the state of being worn out, thus it is *ratha*; it takes up or seizes the constituent parts of a chariot, thus [it is *ratha*].
Or, a chariot (*ratha*); it moves swiftly, thus it is a tree (*duma*); growth, increase, and development proceed and continue, thus it is a tree (*uddhaṃ vā dumo*);
it goes upon or falls upon the earth, mountains, and so forth, thus it is snow (*himo*); that wherein one is bound by the formal act of speech (*kammavācā*) is a boundary (*sīmā*);
or, a boundary (*sīmā*) is that which is to be bound. It is terrifying, thus it is formidable (*bhīmo*); it cuts off and obstructs sentient beings.
*Dāma*: by this it is given; or, it is eaten or bitten off by mice and the like, thus *dāma*. *Yāma*: it goes or moves, thus *yāma*. *Sāma*:
it is capable of seizing the minds of others, thus *sāma*. *Thāma*: they stand by means of this, thus *thāma*. *Bhasmā*: it is spat upon or reduced to ashes, thus *bhasmā*.
(629, 569) [The suffix *a* is added] after the root *gah* or after a root ending in a short vowel (*upadha*).
For the vowel *a* of this root *gah* (to take), *etta* optionally occurs.
One who takes the materials for construction is a *gehaṃ*, [also] *gahaṃ*.
630, 654. For the *su* of *masu*, *cchara* and *ccherā* [occur].
In place of *masuicce* and *tassa*, there are the substitutes *pāṭipadika* and *sussa*.
[The word] *macchara* is that which is stingy (*maccharati*); thus is *macchera*.
631, 655. And also for *car* preceded by *ā*.
The substitute *cchariya* occurs for the root *car* preceded by *ā*, and there is the substitution of *acchara* and *acchera*. Furthermore, when preceded by *ā*, the vowel becomes short (*rasso*).
"That which is to be practiced thoroughly" (*ābhuso caritabba*) is *acchariya*. Thus [are formed] *accharaṃ* and *accheraṃ*.
By the inclusion of the particle *ca*, the substitution *cchariya* also occurs for the root *mas* with the prefix *su*; thus, *macchariyaṃ*.
632, 656. *Ala-kala-sal-icce-tehi la-yapaccayā honti.* The suffix *la* occurs after the verbal roots *ala*, *kala*, and *sala*. Because it is capable (*alati*), it is *alla* (moist).
Because it is to be reckoned (*kalitabba*) or counted, it is *kalla* (suitable). Because it moves, goes, or enters (*salati*), it is *salla* (an arrow). Thus: *alyaṃ*, *kalyaṃ*, *salyaṃ*.
633, 657. *Yāna* and *lāṇa*.
With those roots beginning with *kala* and *sala*, the suffixes *yāna* and *lāṇa* occur.

That which is to be reckoned or counted is *kalyāṇa*. That wherein one settles (*salanti*) after withdrawing from the crowd (*gaṇato paṭikkamitvā*) is *paṭisallāṇa*. Thus [are formed] *sallāṇa* and *paṭisallāṇa*.
634, 658. *Mathissa tha-lassa la*.
For the *tha* of this root *math*, there is a substitution of *la*. [The word] *malla* means "he who churns or agitates one another"; thus, *mallaṃ*.
By the inclusion of the particle *ca*, there is the augment *la* after the root *math*. Thus, *mallaka*, *mallakaṃ*.
635, 559. *Pesa*, *atisagga*, *pattakāla*:
the suffix *kicca* occurs in these senses: *pessa*, *atisagga*, and *pattakāla*.

That which is to be done is an action (*kamma*) for you; that which is to be performed is a duty (*kicca*) for you; that which is to be eaten is food (*bhojana*) for you; that which is fit to be eaten is food for you; that which is to be studied is a lesson (*ajjheyya*) for you; that which is fit to be studied is a lesson for you.
636, 659. *Avassaka* and *adhammiṇa*: the suffix *ṇī* occurs after these two meanings, and the suffix *kicca* as well. First, regarding *avassaka*:
"He must perform my work" (*avassaṃ kārīsi me kammaṃ*); "He must carry my burden" (*avassaṃ hārīsi me bhāraṃ*).
*Adhamiṇe*: "You owe me a hundred in debt; you owe me a thousand in debt. *Kiccā ca*:

"A hundred in debt must be paid by you to me; a thousand in debt must be borne by you for me. A house must be built by you for me; a task must be performed by you for me; a bed must be made by you for me.
[The suffix] *tuṃ* is used after [verbal roots] such as *araha*, *sakka*, etc.
When there are such verbal forms as *araha*, *sakka*, and *bhabba*, the suffix *tuṃ* occurs after all roots. For example:

*arahā bhavaṃ vattuṃ* (you are able to speak), *arahā bhavaṃ kattuṃ* (you are able to do), *sakkā bhavaṃ hantuṃ* (it is possible for you to kill), *sakkā bhavaṃ janetuṃ* (it is possible for you to produce), *janituṃ* (to produce), *bhavituṃ* (to become), *sakkā bhavaṃ dātuṃ* (it is possible for you to give), *sakkā bhavaṃ gantuṃ* (it is possible for you to go), *tabbo bhavaṃ janetuṃ* (you are capable of producing), and so forth.
638, 660. From *vajja* and other roots, words such as *pabbajjā* are derived.
Words such as *pabbajjā* (renunciation) and others are derived from verbal roots like *vajati*, as well as from prefixes (*upasagga*) and suffixes (*paccaya*).

It is called *pabbajjā* because it is to be departed from (*vajitabba*) at the very outset; *ejjā* is movement (*iñjana*); *samajjā* is gathering (*samajjana*); *nisajjā* is sitting down (*nisīdana*); *vijjā* is knowing (*vijānana*);
*visajjā* is relinquishing (*visajjana*); *pajjā* is going (*padana*); *vajjhā* is killing (*hanana*); and *icchā* is desiring (*esana*).
*Atiesanaṃ* is *aticchā*; *sadanaṃ* is *sajjā*; it is called *seyyā* because they lie (*sayanti*) upon it; it is called *saddhā* because by means of it one rightly deposits (*nidheti*) the mind;
*caritabbā* is *cariyā*; *karaṇaṃ* is *kiriyā*; *rujanaṃ* is *rucchā*;
*padanaṃ* is *pacchā*; *riñcanaṃ* is *ricchā*; *tikicchanaṃ* is *titicchā*; *saṃkocanaṃ* is *saṃkucchā*; *madanaṃ* is *macchā*; *labhanaṃ* is *lacchā*.
*Radhabba* means a street (*racchā*); *radana* or *vilekhana* (scratching) is *vāracchā*; it goes by way of the lower part, thus it is *tiracchā* or *tiracchāna*;
*ajana* (not coming) is *acchā*; it endures, thus it is *titikkhā*; it comes together, thus it is *sāgacchā*; bad eating is *dobhacchā*;
bad angering is *durucchā*; questioning is *pucchā*; fainting is *mucchā*; dwelling is *vacchā*.
*Kacana* becomes *kacchā*; *saha-kathana* becomes *sākacchā*; *tudana* becomes *tucchā*; *visana* becomes *vicchā*; *pisana* becomes *picchillā*.
That which gladdens (*mudati*) and devours (*bhakkhati*) pleasure and pain is *maccho*. That which steals (*museti*) and abandons (*cajeti*) the life-breath of beings is *maccu*.
*Satana* becomes *sacca*. That which shakes upward (*uddhaṃ dhunāti*) is *uddhacca*. *Naṭana* becomes *nacca*; *nitana* becomes *nicca*; *tathana* becomes *taccha*, and so forth.
639, 585. *Kvilopo ca*.
There is an elision of *kvi*, and it arises again.

It is called *vibhū* because it exists through various qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth; or, it is called *vibhū* because it exists in a distinguished manner; [it exists] by itself, through its own nature.
He becomes by himself, thus he is *sayambhū*; having overcome, he becomes, thus he is *abhibhū*; he shakes or trembles well and thoroughly, thus he is *sandhū*;
he shines or appears especially, thus he is *vibhā*; he shines or appears without remainder, thus he is *nibhā*; he shines or appears in a particular manner, thus he is *pabhā*;
they speak together therein, thus it is *sabhā*; he shines or appears abundantly, thus he is *ābhā*; with a curved arm...
It goes, thus it is a *bhujaga* (snake); it goes very swiftly, thus it is a *turaga* (horse); it digs the earth well, thus it is a *saṅkha* (conch);
it especially restrains and ceases, thus it is a *viya* (a type of bird); it remembers and knows well, thus it is a *sumo*;
it extends and spreads out all around, thus it is a *parito*—and so forth.
640. *Sacajānaṃ kagā ṇānubandhe*:
For the roots beginning with *sa* and *ja*, and for those ending in *ca* and *ja*, the substitutions *ka* and *ga* occur respectively when a suffix having *ṇ* as its *anubandha* follows.
Examples: *oko*, *pāko*, *seko*, *soko*, *viveko*, *cāgo*, *yogo*, *bhogo*, *rogo*, *rāgo*, *bhāgo*, *bhaṅgo*, *raṅgo*, *saṅgo*.

641, 572. From roots such as *nuda*, *sūda*, *jana*, *su*, *lū*, *hu*, *pu*, *bhū*, *ñā*, *a*, *sa*, and *samuicc*, and from causatives such as *phanda*, *citi*, and *āṇa*, the suffixes *yu* and *ūna* [are applied], and the substitutions *ana*, *āna*, *na*, *aka*, and *ānaka* occur respectively.

From the roots *nuda*, *sūda*, *jana*, *su*, *lū*, *hu*, *pu*, *bhū*, *ñā*, *a*, *sa*, and *samuicc*, and from causatives such as *phanda*, *citi*, and *āṇa*, the suffixes *yu* and *ūna* are applied, and the respective substitutions *ana*, *āna*, *na*, *aka*, and *ānaka* take place.

[The suffix -ana] occurs after a verbal root in the sense of the agent (*kattar*), and also in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). First, regarding the agent: that which drives away (*panudati*) is a *panūdano*. Likewise: *sūdano*, *janano*, *savaṇo*, *lavano*, *havano*, *pavano*, *bhavano*, *ñāṇo*, *asano*, *samaṇo*.

Regarding the abstract state: that which is driven away is *panūdanaṃ*. Likewise: *sūdanaṃ*, *jananaṃ*, *savaṇaṃ*, *lavanaṃ*, *havanaṃ*, *pavanaṃ*, *bhavanaṃ*, *ñāṇaṃ*, *asanaṃ*, *samaṇaṃ*, *sañjānanaṃ*. That which is made is a *kānanaṃ*.

And in the sense of causing (*kārite*): that which is made to quiver is "quivering" (*phandāpana*); that which is caused to be bought is "causing to buy" (*cetāpana*); that which is commanded is "commanding" (*āṇāpana*).

In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*): that by which they push is "pushing" (*nūdana*); likewise, "cleansing" (*sūdana*), "begetting" (*janana*), "hearing" (*savaṇa*), "tasting" (*lavaṇa*), "offering" (*havana*), "purifying" (*pavana*), "speaking" (*bhagana*), "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*), "eating" (*asana*), and "listening" (*savaṇa*).

Again, in the sense of the agent (*kattari*): he who pushes is "a pusher" (*nūdaka*); he who cleanses is "a cleaner" (*sūdadhaka*); he who begets is "a progenitor" (*janaka*); he who hears is "a listener" (*sāvaka*).

One who cuts is a cutter (*lāvaka*); one who offers is an offerer (*hāvaka*); one who purifies is a purifier (*pāvaka*); one who becomes is a becoming-one (*bhāvaka*); one who knows is a knower (*jānaka*); one who exists is an existing-one (*asaka*); one who attends upon is an attendant (*upāsaka*);
one who comes together is a coming-together-one (*samaka*). In the causative, however:
one who causes to quiver is a causer of quivering (*phandāpayaka*). Likewise: a causer of commanding (*āṇāpayaka*), a causer of sending (*cetāpayaka*), a causer of perceiving (*sañjānanaka*).
642, 588. The final vowel of the pronouns *iya*, *ta*, *ma*, *ki*, *e*, and *sā* becomes long in certain instances;
in the case of the verbal root *du*, the letter *u* undergoes *guṇa*;
the letter *da* becomes *ra*; and the *s* at the end of the root becomes *kkha*.
These substitutions occur as far as possible. These words subsequently emerge again within the Buddha’s teaching according to their respective names and without obstruction:
*īdiso* (such-like) from "he sees it as like this," *yādiso* (what-like) from "he sees it as like what," and *tādiso* (that-like) from "he sees it as like that."
"He sees him as like me" is *mādiso*; "in what way does he see him? means "of what kind"; "he sees him as like this" is *ediso*; "he sees him as like the same" is *sādiso*.
"He sees him as like this one" is *īriso*; "he sees him as like that which" is *yāriso*;
"he sees him as like that which" is *tāriso*; "he sees him as like me" is *māriso*; "in what way does he see him?"...
"Of what kind? is *eriso*, meaning "he sees him as such. "Equal-like" is *sāriso*, meaning "he sees him as equal.
"Like this one" is *īdikkho*; "like whom" is *yādikkho*; "like that" is *tādikkho*;
likewise, *mādikkho*, *kīdikkho*, *edikkho*, and *sādikkho*. [The corresponding feminine forms are: *īdī*, *yādī*, *tādī*, *mādī*, *kīdī*, *edī*, and *sādī*.

By the inclusion of the word "ca" (and), it is said that for those very sounds such as *iya* and so forth, the final vowel sometimes serves the purpose of lengthening (*dīghattha*). Examples: *īdikkho*, *yādikkho*, *tādikkho*, *mādikkho*, *kīdikkho*, *edikkho*, *sādikkho*; *idisō*, *sadisō*, *sariso*, *sarikkho*. 643, 635.
From roots beginning with *bhī* and from *mati*, *budhi*, *pūjā*, etc., the suffix *tta* occurs.
From roots such as *bhī* and so forth, [the suffix] *mati* [occurs]; and from *budhi*, *pūjā*, and others, the suffix *tta* is applied.
"Bhāyitabbo" means one who is to be feared, thus "bhīto" (one who is afraid). "Supitabbo" means one who is to be slept with, thus "sutto" (one who is asleep).
"Mijjitabbo" means one who is to be loved, thus "mitto" (a friend). "Sammannitabbo" means one who is to be honored; it is "sammato" because he is to be well-honored (suṭṭhu mānitabbo) or worshipped.

It is "sammato" because he has been honored. "Saṅkappīyati" means he is intended, thus "saṅkappito"; it is "saṅkappito" because he has been intended. "Sampādīyati" means he is accomplished, thus "sampādito"; it is "sampādito" because he has been accomplished.
It has been accomplished, thus it is "accomplished" (*avadhārīyata*); it has been determined, thus it is "determined" (*avadhārīyita*); it has been determined, thus it is "determined" (*avadhārīta*).

It is to be awakened to and known, thus he is "Awakened" (*buddha*). It is to be studied, thus "from this" (*ito*); it is to be gone to, thus "gone from here" (*ito*). It is to be understood and known, thus it is "known" (*vidita*). It is to be reasoned about, thus it is "reasoned" (*takkita*);
it is to be honored, thus it is "honored" (*pūjita*); it has been honored, thus it is "honored" (*pūjita*). It is to be venerated, thus it is "venerated" (*apacāyita*); it is to be revered.
*pūjetabbo* means "to be honored" (*mānito*); *apacīyati* means "is respected," thus *apacito*; *vandīyati* means "is saluted," thus *vandito*;
*vandīyittha* means "was saluted," thus *vandito*; *sakkarīyati* means "is revered," thus *sakkārito*; *sakkarīyittha* means "was revered," thus *sakkārito*.
(644, 661) [The suffixes] *thu*, *ttima*, *ṇimā* arise after roots such as *vepu*, *sī*, *dava*, *vamu*, *ku*, *dā*, *bhū*, *hvā*, etc., when something is produced.
The suffixes *thu*, *tti*, and *maṇi* occur after roots such as *vep*, *sī*, *dav*, *vam*, and *ku*—as appropriate—to express the sense of "produced by that" (*nibbatta*).
*Trembling* is *vepo*; that which is produced by it is *vepathu*. *Lying down* is *sayo*; that which is produced by it is *sayathu*. *Burning* is *davo*;
that which is produced by it is *davathu*. *Vomiting* is *vamo*; that which is produced by it is *vamathu*. *Cutting* (*kutti*) is the act of making.
*Kutta* is cutting; that which is produced by that is *kuttima*. *Dāti* is cutting; that which is produced by that is *dattima*. *Bhūti* is being;
that which is produced by that is *bhottima*. *Avahuti* is carrying away; that which is produced by that is *ohāvima*. 645, 662.
In the sense of abuse, there are the suffixes *-nam* and *-ha*.
When the negative particle *na* is used in the sense of prohibition (*akkosacittasmiṃ atthe*), the suffix *ani* occurs after verbal roots. For example:
*na gamitabbaṃ agamāni te jamma desaṃ* (you should not go to that place, you wretch), *na kattabbaṃ akarāṇi te jamma kammaṃ* (you should not do that deed, you wretch).
Why is it said "when *na* is used"? [To exclude cases such as: *vipatti te jamma*, *vikati te jamma*.
For what purpose does he revile? "That which is not a proper course for you, you must not go.
(646, 419) From one's own side, it occurs once;
from one's own side, it occurs once.
For one meaning, once at a time means “once”; for two meanings, once at a time means “twice”;

for three meanings, once at a time means “thrice. In this way, [the words] “four times,” “five times,” “six times,” “seven times,” “eight times,” “nine times,” and “ten times” should be applied accordingly. Such are the terms to be joined.
647, 663. *Suna-ssu-na-ss-oṇa-vānu-vān-ūna-unakha-una-ā-ānādesā honti*.
For the word *suna* (dog), when it is the first member of a compound, there are the following substitutions for the final *u*: *oṇa*, *vāna*, *uvāna*, *ūna*, *unakha*, *una*, *ā*, and *āna*.
One who hears the master’s voice is *soṇo*; one who hears the master’s voice is *svāno*; likewise, *suvāno*, *sūno*, *sunakho*, *suno*, *sā*, and *sāno*.
648, 664. *Taruṇassa susū ca*.
For the word *taruṇa*, when it means "the first day of the lunar fortnight" (*pāṭipadika*), there is the substitution *susū*.
*Susū* means "having black hair."
649, 665. *Yuvassuvassuvuvānunūnā*.
For this word *yuva*, when it is in the nominative singular (*pāṭipadika*), the substitutes *uva*, *uvauva*, *una*, and *ūna* occur.
[Examples: *yuvā*, *yuvāno*, *yuno*, *yūno*.
650, 651. *Kāle vattamānātīte ṇvādayo*.
The suffixes *ṇu*, *yu*, and *tap* occur in the sense of both present time (*vattamāna*) and past time (*atīta*). For example:
"he did" (*akāsi*) and "he does" (*karoti*) is *kāru*; "he went" (*agacchi*) and "he goes" (*gacchati*) is *vāyu*; "it was" (*abhavi*) and "it is" (*bhavati*) is *bhūtam*.
651, 647. *Tavissati gamādīhi ṇī ghiṇa*.
The suffixes *ṇī* and *ghiṇa* occur after verbal roots such as *gam*, *bhaj*, *su*, *ṭhā*, and others, in the sense of the future tense (*bhavissatikāla*).
One whose nature it is to go in the future is "one who goes" (*gāmī*); one whose nature it is to associate in the future is [one who associates] (*bhājī*).
One whose nature is to see the future is *passāvī*; one whose nature is to establish [the practice] for the future is *paṭṭhāyī*.
In these instances, the suffix *-ṇvu* is used after a verbal root (*tavo*).
In the sense of action (kriyā), these suffixes *ṇvu* and *tu* occur in the future tense:
*kārako gacchati* (“he goes as one who will do”), *bhoktā gacchati* (“he goes as one who will eat”).
When expressing the abstract state (bhāva), the dative case is used.
In the future tense, the fourth case ending occurs in verbal nouns (*bhāvavācin*):

*pacissate*, or "cooking" (*pacana*) or "the act of cooking" (*pāka*); he goes for the sake of cooking (*pākāya vajati*). He will eat (*bhuñjissate*), or "eating" (*bhojana*) or "food" (*bhoga*); he goes for the sake of food (*bhogāya vajati*). He will dance (*naccissate*), or "dancing" (*naccana*) or "a dance" (*nacca*); he goes for the sake of dancing (*naccāya vajati*). 654, 649.
The suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of the object (*kamma*).
When a *kamma* (object) is the *upapada*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs in the future tense.

Thus: "he will build a city" becomes *nagarakāro vajati*; "he will reap rice" becomes *sālilāvo vajati*; "he will sow grain" becomes *dhaññavāpo vajati*; "he will give wealth" becomes *bhogadāyo vajati*; "he will drink the Sindhu river" becomes *sindhupāyo vajati*. 655. 650.
In the remaining cases, the suffixes *-ssaṃ*, *-ntu*, *-māna*, and *-āna* [occur].
In this remaining sense, when there is a future time and a word denoting an object (kamma) as an upapada, these suffixes—*ssaṃ*, *ntu*, *māna*, and *āna*—occur.
For example: *kammaṃ karissati*, *kammaṃ karissaṃ*; likewise, *kammaṃ karonto*, *kammaṃ kurumāno*, *kammaṃ karāno gacchati*.
Similarly: *bhojanaṃ bhuñjissati*, *bhojanaṃ bhuñjissaṃ*; likewise, *bhojanaṃ bhuñjanto*, *bhojanaṃ*...
While eating, he goes while eating food. He will eat a snack; I will eat a snack—thus, while eating a snack, while consuming a snack, while partaking of a snack, he goes.
He will walk the path; I will walk the path—thus, while walking the path, while traversing the path, while traveling the path, he goes. Alms...

"He will beg for alms" (bhikkhissati), "he will beg for alms" (bhikkhissaṃ); thus, while begging for alms (bhikkhaṃ bhikkhanto), while begging for alms (bhikkhaṃ bhikkhamāno), while begging for alms (bhikkhaṃ bhikkhāno), he goes.
656, 666. *Chavādī* means "therein."

The suffixes *tana* and *ica* occur after such verbal roots as *cha*, *da*, *ci*, *ti*, *su*, *nī*, *vi*, *da*, *pada*, *tanu*, *yata*, *ada*, *mada*, *yuja*, *vatu*, *mida*, *mā*, *pu*, *ka*, *la*, *vara*, *ve*, *pu*, *gu*, and *pā*, according to their respective applicability. Because it covers heat (*ātapaṃ chādeti*), it is a *chattaṃ* (an umbrella); [in Sanskrit] a *chatraṃ*.

Because it thinks upon an object (*ārammaṇaṃ cinteti*), it is a *cittaṃ* (mind); [in Sanskrit] a *cittraṃ*. Or alternatively, because associated states (*sampayuttadhammā*) think by means of it, it is a *cittaṃ*;

[in Sanskrit] a *cittraṃ*. Because it flows forth toward meanings (*atthe abhissaveti*), it is a *suttaṃ* (thread/sūtra); [in Sanskrit] a *sutraṃ*. Or alternatively, because it indicates meanings (*atthe sūceti*), it is a *suttaṃ*.
*Sutta*, *sūtra*. It leads beings (*satte neti*), thus it is a "guide" (*netta*, *netra*). Or, by means of this, beings are led to their desired destination, thus it is a "guide" (*netta*, *netra*).

It knows thoroughly (*pākārena vidati*), thus it is "purified" (*pavitta*, *pavitra*). It purifies (*punāti*) or cleanses (*sodheti*) evil (*maṅga*) in various ways, thus it is "purified" (*pavitta*, *pavitra*).
Or, it attains a state of purity (*sucibhāva*), thus it is "purified" (*pavitta*, *pavitra*).
It is called *patto* (a bowl) because one reaches [food] with it (*pāpuṇāti*), thus *patro*; or, it is a *patta* (bowl) because food falls (*patanti*) into this vessel, thus *patraṃ*.

Or, it is a *patta* (bowl) because it moves or proceeds (*padati pavattati*), thus *patraṃ*. It is called *tantaṃ* (a thread) or *tantraṃ* (a loom/continuity) because it stretches or extends (*tanoti vitthāreti*); or, it is a *tantaṃ* or *tantraṃ* because it is that which is to be stretched or extended (*tanitabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ*).
It is called *yattaṃ* (restrained/self-controlled) because it restrains itself (*yatatīti*). Or, it is a *yattaṃ* because by means of it one exerts effort (*yatati vīriyaṃ karoti*).

*Yatram*: *Yatanaṃ* (exertion) or *yattaṃ* (striving), thus *yatram*. It consumes (*adati*) pleasure and pain, thus it is *attā*; [the form] *atrā*. It intoxicates (*madati*), thus *mattaṃ*; [the form] *matraṃ*.
By means of this, things are joined (*yujjanti*) to a basis (*vatthuṃ*), thus *yottaṃ*; [the form] *yotraṃ*. It proceeds (*vattati*), thus *vattaṃ*; [the form] *vatraṃ*.
It gladdens (*midati*) and produces affection (*sinehaṃ*), thus *mittaṃ*; [the form] *mitraṃ*. One gladdens or feels affection by means of this, thus *mettā*; [the form] *metrā*. *Pari*...
It is called *mattā* or *matrā* because by means of it they measure (*minanti*) everything in every way. Or else, the act of measuring is *mattaṃ*, *matraṃ*.

It is called *putto* or *putro* because it purifies (*punāti*) and cleanses its own family (*kula*). It is called *kalattaṃ* or *kalatraṃ* because it is to be reckoned (*kalitabba*) and counted (*saṅkhyātabba*).

It is called *varattaṃ* or *varatraṃ* because one restrains (*vāreti*) well (*saṃ*) by means of it. It is called *vettaṃ* or *vetraṃ* because it trembles (*vepati*) and shakes. It is that which is to be protected (*gopitabba*).
*rakkhitabbaṃ* means "protected" (*guttaṃ*). *Gutraṃ*, *gottaṃ*, *gotraṃ* [are synonyms]. *Dāti* means "it cuts" (*avakhaṇḍati*) by means of this; thus, *dāttaṃ*, *dātraṃ*, and so forth. 657, 667.
With roots such as *vada* and others, the suffix *ṇi* occurs in the sense of a group (*gaṇa*).
The suffix *ṇi* is applied after verbal roots such as *vada*, *cara*, *vara*, and so forth, in the sense of a class or group.
The group of musical instruments is *vādittaṃ*. Likewise, there are *cārittaṃ*, *vārittaṃ*, and so forth.
658, 668. The suffixes *tti* and *ti* come after roots such as *mida*.
These suffixes, namely *tti* and *ti*, occur after verbal roots (*dhātu*) such as *mida*, *pada*, *ranja*, *tanu*, *dhā*, and others.

*Metti* is so called because it moistens with affection (*sinehati*). *Patti* is so called because it goes or proceeds (*padati gacchati*). *Ratti* is so called because one delights therein (*ranjati*).
*Tanti* is so called because it stretches or extends (*tanoti vitthāreti*); or alternatively, it is *tanti* because it stretches or extends one’s own lineage.
*Dhāti* is so called because she bears the child of others’ wives; or *dhāti* because she bears milk; or *dhāti* because she bears her own essential nature (*sabhāva*), and so forth.
659, 669. *Usu*, *ranja*, and *daṃsa*: for these roots, the substitute *daḍḍha* occurs in place of *daṃsa*, and the suffixes *ḍha* and *ṭha* also occur. Thus: *usīyate* becomes *uḍḍho*;
"they color therein" (*rañjanti ettha*) becomes *raṭṭhaṃ*; and "it is bitten" (*daṃsīyati*) becomes *daḍḍho*.
660, 670. *Sūvusānamūvusānamatothoca*.
For these roots beginning with *sū* and *ū*, there is a substitution of *a* for the final vowel, and the suffix *tha* is added.

That by which one cuts or harms is *satthaṃ* (a weapon); that by which one restrains shame and fear of wrongdoing is *vatthaṃ* (clothing). The meaning is: it becomes non-existent (*asati*) in accordance with the sound [of the root].

661, 671. From roots such as *rañj*, *ud*, *id*, *cad*, *mad*, *khud*, *chid*, *rud*, *dal*, *sus*, *suc*, *vac*, *vaj*, and others, the suffixes *dha*, *da*, *idda*, *ka*, and *ira* occur; in some instances, there is also the elision (*lopa*) of *ja* and *da*, and thus they are further produced.
That which is to be colored is *randhaṃ*; or, that which was colored is *randhaṃ*. [It refers to] the fish and sea-monsters residing within oneself...
It is called the ocean (*samudda*) because it moistens, pours forth, and generates rapture and joy.
It is called Indra (*indo*) because it exercises supreme sovereignty, or because it exercises lordship and dominance. It is called the moon (*canda*) because it is to be desired or longed for.

It is called the mild one (*manda*) because it gladdens, or because it is to be gladdened. It is called the hungry one (*khudda*) because it hungers and thirsts; it is also [called] that which is to be cut.
*Chiddo* means "one who pierces. *Ruddo* means "one who weeps and harms. *Daliddo* means "one who breaks apart" or "one who falls into a state of wretchedness.
*Sukkaṃ* means "that which withers. *Soko* means "one who sorrows. *Vakkaṃ* means "that which is to be spoken. *Vajiraṃ* means "that which goes or moves unimpededly," and so forth. 662, 672.
For *heraṇa* and *hīraṇa* are derived from the root *paṭi* (to fall).
For from this root *paṭi*, there are the substitutions *heraṇa* and *hīraṇa*.
Because it goes toward (*āgacchati*) and proceeds (*pavattati*) by overcoming its opposite (*paṭipakkha*), it is called *pāṭihera* or *pāṭihīra*. 663, 673.
[The suffix] *ko* is added after *kaḍi* and other roots.

The suffix *ka* arises after such verbal roots as *kaḍ*, *ghaḍ*, *vaḍ*, *karaḍ*, *maḍ*, *saḍ*, *kuṭh*, *bhaḍ*, *paḍ*, *daḍ*, *raḍ*, *taḍ*, *isiḍ*, *caḍ*, *gaḍ*, *aḍ*, *laḍ*, *meḍ*, *eraḍ*, and *khaḍ*, along with the corresponding suffixes, as appropriate. That which is to be split or cut is a *kaṇḍa*;
that which is to be struck or joined is a *ghaṇḍa*; that wherein they gather is... [a *vaṇḍa*].
*Vaṇḍo*: that which is to be cut (*karaṇḍitabbo*) and divided (*bhājetabbo*) is *karaṇḍo*. *Maṇḍo*: that by which one is adorned (*maṇḍīyate*) or beautified (*vibhūsīyate*) is *maṇḍo*.

*Saṇḍo*: that wherein things cluster (*saṇḍanti*) or grow thick (*gumbanti*) is *saṇḍo*. *Kuṭṭhaṃ*: that which numbs (*kuṇṭhati*) or cuts away (*chindati*) limb after limb is *kuṭṭhaṃ*. *Bhaṇḍaṃ*: that which is to be quarreled over (*bhaṇḍitabbaṃ*) is *bhaṇḍaṃ*. *Paṇḍako*:
that which becomes deficient in sexual characteristics (*liṅgavekallabhāvaṃ gacchati) is *paṇḍako*. *Daṇḍo*: that by which one exercises authority (*āṇaṃ karoti*) is *daṇḍo*.
He harms and injures, thus he is a *raṇḍa*; he specifically agitates and moves the hearts of wise people, causing them to tremble, thus he is a *vitaṇḍa*;
he crushes and subdues others, thus he is an *isiṇḍa*; he is fierce and displays ferocity, thus he is a *caṇḍa*;
it is called a *gaṇḍa* because one accumulates or forms a mass therein; it is called an *aṇḍa* because it is produced or brought forth; it is to be spat out (*laṇḍitabba*).
*Jigucchitabba* means excrement (*laṇḍa*). *Meṇḍa* means that which goes toward a crooked state; it "meṇḍati. *Eraṇḍa* means that which destroys disease;
it "eraṇḍati. *Khaṇḍa* means that which is to be broken or cut; thus, and so forth. 664, 674.
For *khādā*, *agama*, and *māna*, the substitutes are *kha*, *ndha*, *ndha*, and *gandha*.
The suffix *kha* is applied to these roots (*dhātu*) to form the words *khandha*, *andha*, and *gandha*, and the suffix *ka* also occurs.
It is called a *khandha* because it is devoured (*khāditabbo*) by the sufferings of saṃsāra, such as birth, aging, and death;

it is called *andha* because it goes (*amati*) to a state of being broken in its various limbs, or because it is broken (*rujjati*) by the eye, or because it moves (*gacchati*) from place to place by means of the wind.
Gandho. Thus: khandhako, andhako, gandhako.
665, 675. Enough with paṭa and the others.
Paṭa, kala, kusa, kada, bhaganda, mekha, vakka, takka, palla, sadda, mūla, bila, vida, caḍaṃ, pañca.

The suffix *ala* occurs after roots such as *vasa*, *paci*, *maca*, *musa*, *gotthu*, *puthu*, *bahu*, *maṅga*, *baha*, *kamba*, *samba*, *agga*, *icca*, and so forth, as well as after individual nouns (*pāṭipadika*) when used as subsequent members of a compound;
subsequently, they emerge again [as complete words]. For example: *paṭe alaṃ* becomes *paṭalaṃ*;
*kale alaṃ* becomes *kalalaṃ*; and "one who cuts off (*kusati*) evil, unwholesome states" [becomes *kusala*].

*Kusala* means "sufficient" (*ala*) with respect to wholesome states (*kusabhūta*) that possess their own intrinsic nature; or *kusala* means "sufficient" for the giving directed toward the *kusa* grass;
or *kusala* means "sufficient" for the accumulation of a collection of phenomena. *Kadala* means "sufficient" (*ala*) for the soft mud (*kadde madde*).

*Bhagandala* means "sufficient" (*ala*) for the oozing of filth (*bhagande secane*); or alternatively, *bhagandala* means "sufficient" for the evacuation of urine and feces (*bhagande muttakarīsaharaṇe*).

In the sense of "girdle" (*mekha*) at the variegated waist, there is *mekhalā*; in the sense of "bark" (*vakkha*) of a tree, there is *vakkalā*; in the sense of "curd" (*takkha*) or tree-resin, there is *takkalā*;
in the sense of a "pool" (*palla*) or low-lying place, there is *pallalā*; in the sense of "sound" (*sadda*) or greenery, there is *saddalā*;
in the sense of a "root" (*mūla*) or foundation, there is *mulālā*; in the sense of a "hole" (*biḷa*) or support, there is *bilālā*; in the sense of "existing" (*vida*), there is *vidalā*.
*Vidala*: it means "split. *Caṇḍāla*: *caṇḍe* (in violence) and *alanti* (they act), thus *caṇḍāla*. *Pañcāla*: *pañcannaṃ rājūnaṃ* (of five kings) and *alanti*, thus *pañcāla*.
*Vāla*: *vā* (in going and smelling) and *alanti*, thus *vāla*. *Vāḷa*: *vā* (in walking on foot) and *alanti*, thus *vāḷa*. *Vasala*: *vase* (in covering) and *alanti*, thus *vasala*.
*Pacala*: *pace* (in expansion) and *alanti*, thus *pacala*. *Macala*: *mace* (in thievery) and *alanti*, thus *macala*. *Musala*: *muse* (in theft) or *muse* (in taking life) and *alanti*.
From *musala*, with the suffix *ala* in the sense of a lineage or clan, comes *gotthula*; in the sense of being broad or wide, *puthula*;
in the sense of a large number, *bahula*; or in the sense of great increase, *bahula*;
in the sense of a lucky omen or movement, *maṅgala*; in the sense of great increase, *bahala*; and in the sense of moving or shaking, *kambala*.
In *sambamhi maṇḍale*, it becomes *alanti* [thus] *sambalaṃ*; in *agge gatikoṭille*, it becomes *alanti* [thus] *aggaḷaṃ*. There are other words as well, such as these. 666, 676.
For *puthu*, there are the substitutes *puthu* and *patha*, or *mo*.
For this word *puthu*, which is a synonym for *pāṭipadika* (the first day of the lunar fortnight), the substitutes *puthu* and *patha* occur; in some instances, the suffix *am* occurs.

"Born as one who is distinct" (*putha hutvā jāta*) means "the first-born among the earth" (*pathavī*); thus *pathavī* or *paṭhama*. Or, because he generates manifold defilements (*puthu kilese janeti*), he is a "worldling" (*puthujjana*). Because he is born as one who is distinct, he is *pathavī*;
or [alternatively], *pathavī*. 667, 677. Regarding the suffixes *dava*, etc.:
the suffixes *du* and *icca* occur after verbal roots such as *sas*, *dada*, *ada*, *mada*, and so forth.
One who hisses at or injures other beings is a *sattu*; one who gives suffering is a *daddu*;

that wherein one eats or consumes suffering is an *addu*, or alternatively, an *addu* is so called because people eat or experience suffering through it; or an *addu* is so called because it produces (*bhāveti*) a vessel or receptacle for suffering;
one who intoxicates or makes one insane is a *maddu*, or alternatively, a *maddu* is so called because it intoxicates or brings about a state of madness.
668, 678. *Jhādīhi īvaro*.
The suffix *īvara* occurs after roots such as *ci*, *pā*, *dhā*, and so forth.

That which is accumulated (*cīyati*) is *cīvara*; that which drinks (*pivati*) is *pīvara*; or alternatively, that which is to be drunk or protected is *pīvara*. One who bears (*dhāreti*) or, having borne [the burden], maintains his life is *dhīvara*; [thus] *dhīvara*.
669, 679. *Munādīhi* (from *muna* and so forth).
The suffix *-ipa* occurs after verbal roots such as *muna*, *yata*, *agga*, *pata*, *kava*, *suca*, *ruca*, *mahāla*, *bhaddāla*, *mana*, and others, as well as after primary nouns (*pāṭipadika*).

One who knows what is beneficial and what is not beneficial, or who knows the phenomena to be known by way of their characteristics and so forth, is a *muni*. One who exerts effort (*yatati*) is [a *yati*].
He restrains himself, thus he is a *yati*; he goes forward, moving toward a crooked state, thus he is *aggi*; he goes before, having become preeminent, thus he is a *pati*;
he composes poetry, thus he is a *kavi*, or alternatively, he speaks words that are lovely and pleasing, thus he is a *kavi*.
It becomes pure, thus it is *suci*; it shines, thus it is *ruci*; it takes a great manifestation, a mass of enjoyments, thus he is *Mahāli*.
One who brings (*lāti*) auspicious fame (*bhaddaṃ yasaṃ*) is Bhaddāli; one who leads (*nayati*) the mind (*manaṃ*) toward that jewel (*ratanaṃ*) is Maṇi.
(670, 680) The suffix *ūra* occurs after roots such as *vida*, *valla*, *masa*, *sida*, *dukka*, *pu*, *maya*, *udi*, *khajja*, and *kuraicci*, as well as after primary nominal stems (*pāṭipadika*).
It is called *vidūra* because it is capable of being known (*vidituṃ alaṃ*); *vedūro* is that which grows in a place distant from [the sea];

*vallūro* is so called because it exists as something desirable (*vallabhāvena bhavati*), or alternatively, because it binds things together (*aññamaññaṃ bandhati*); *masūro* is that which is to be touched (*āmasitabbo*);

*sindūro* is so called because it goes toward a state of passion (*siṅgārabhāvaṃ gacchati*), or alternatively, because it gleams (*virocati*); and *dūro* is so called because it is incapable of being approached due to its distance (*anāsannattā*).

It is called *kūra* because it makes a sound (*saddaṃ karoti*). It is called *kappūra* because by its own fragrance it overcomes (*kapati*), destroys (*hanati*), or harms (*hiṃsati*) other fragrances;

or alternatively, it is called *kappūra* because it is suitable (*kappati*) and capable of removing diseases. It is called *mayūra* because it cries out (*ravati*) on the earth (*mahiyaṃ*); or it is called *mayūra* because it moves or goes (*yāti gacchati*) on the earth.
It is called *undūra* because it burrows into or produces (*undati pasavati*) dust (*paṃsuṃ*). It is [called] *khajjaka* because it is to be chewed (*khajjitabba*) or eaten (*khāditabba*).
*Khajjūra*: that which eats; *kurūra*: one who cries out or reviles. 671, 681.

The suffixes *nu*, *ṇu*, and *tu* [are added] after roots such as *hana*, *jana*, *bhāri*, *khanu*, *ama*, *ve*, *vedhā*, *siki*, *hi*, and so forth. These suffixes—namely *nu*, *ṇu*, and *ku*—occur after verbal roots such as these.

*Haṇu* (the jaw) is so called because it strikes (*hanati*) or destroys (*hiṃsati*) with this. *Jāṇu* (the knee) is so called because it produces going (*gamanaṃ janeti*). *Bhāṇu* (the sun) is so called because it shines (*bhāṇu dibbati*).
*Reṇu* (dust) is so called because it moves (*reti*) or goes in a windless place (*nivāte*). *Khāṇu* (a stump) is so called because it is to be dug out (*khaṇitabbo*) or split open (*avadāritabbo*).

*Aṇu* (an atom) is so called because it moves toward or reaches the state of breaking and piercing each limb (*aṅgamaṅgassa rujjanabhāvaṃ vijjhanabhāvaṃ amati*). *Veṇu* (a bamboo) is so called because it exists in the continuity of fibers (*veti tantasantāne bhavati*).
A bamboo is *veṇu*; that which flows outside and inside is *vahi-sāra-anta-vāhi-veṇu*. That which causes one to drink is *dhenu* (a cow); that which holds its meaning is *dhātu* (a root).
Alternatively, it is *dhātu* because it holds actions such as going and cooking. That which cools and binds is *setu* (a bridge). That which goes upward and proceeds is *ketu* (a banner).
That which impels its own fruit and proceeds is *hetu* (a cause).
672, 682. *Kuṭādīhi ṭho*.
The suffix *ṭha* occurs after verbal roots such as *kuṭ*, *kusa*, *kaṭ*, and others, as well as after primary nouns (*pāṭipadika*).
That which cuts or lops off limb by limb is *kuṭṭha* (leprosy). That which is to be covered or filled with grain is *koṭṭha* (a granary). That which is to be cut or crushed is *kaṭṭha* (wood).
673, 683. *Manu*, *pūra*, *suṇādīhi* [the suffixes] *ussa*, *nus*, and *isa*.

From verbal roots (*dhātu*) such as *manu*, *pūra*, *suṇa*, *kusu*, *ila*, *ala*, *maha*, *si*, and so forth, as well as from primary nouns (*pāṭipadika*), the suffixes *ussa*, *nus*, and *isa* occur, and they are subsequently produced.

One who thinks (*manati*) and knows (*jānāti*) wholesome and unwholesome phenomena (*dhamma*) is a *manusso* (human), a *mānuso*. One who thinks and knows cause (*kāraṇa*) by means of a cause (*kāraṇā*) is... [a *kāraṇusso*].
Or, he is a *manusso* (human) because he thinks and knows what is beneficial and what is harmful; thus he is a *mānusso*. He fills the hearts of his mother and father, thus he is a *puriso*;
or he fulfills his own desires, thus he is a *puriso*; or he nourishes (*pūreti*), thus he is a *poso*.
She is to be heard from and to be harmed by her fathers-in-law, thus she is a *suṇisā*; or she establishes the lineage of two families that know [her].
*Suṇisā*: that which is to be despised is *karīsa* (excrement); it releases the womb (*gabbha*), thus it is *surisa*;

it pacifies (*surati*) and destroys (*hiṃsati*) the fear of beings by dispelling darkness, thus it is *sūriya* (the sun); it destroys disease, thus it is *sirīsa* (the śirīṣa tree); it moves (*ilati*) and trembles (*kampati*), thus it is *illisa*;
or, having become weak through craving (*taṇhā*), it moves and trembles, thus it is *illigha*; it is capable (*alati*) and able (*samattheti*) in the performance of evil deeds.

One who is lazy (*alasa*) is to be honored (*mahitabba*) and worshipped (*pūjetabba*), thus he is a buffalo (*mahisa*); one is chilled (*sīyati*) and bound (*bandhīyati*), thus it is the head (*sīsa*); that which is to be made thin (*kitabba*) or harmed (*hiṃsitabba*) is emaciated (*kisa*). Such are these examples.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on the *uṇādi* Suffixes, within the Chapter on Derivative Nominal Forms (*kibbidhāna-kappa*).
The *Uṇādi-kappa* is completed.
The Kaccāyana-pakaraṇa is completed.
